paras.html: Why Called Brushless?
No brushes — no slip rings — nothing transfers electricity from stationary to rotating parts
All electrical transfer is by induction (exciter) and rotating rectifiers carry the DC internally on shaft
Advantages: No brush sparking (safe in hazardous areas), no brush wear, no slip ring maintenance, suitable for UMS
Better suited for humid marine environment — no carbon brush dust

SOLAS Regulation for AVR
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Asked by Sanjib, Upendra Kumar, Deswal
SOLAS II-1/Reg 40.3: Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) must maintain voltage within ±2.5% of rated voltage under any load condition from no-load to full-load.
AVR must also regulate voltage during load transients — sudden load pickup or shedding must not cause more than ±10% transient excursion before recovering to ±2.5%.
This applies to all alternators connected to the main busbar.

Why remove AVR during IR test: AVR contains sensitive thyristors, transistors, and capacitors — megger voltage (500V–1000V DC) can permanently damage these components. Also, AVR may back-feed voltage into the winding, giving a false IR reading.
Brushless Excitation System — Safeties
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Cross-questions after brushless alternator explanation
Rotating diode failure detection: stroboscope check during running — check for discoloured or pitted diodes. Also: unbalanced output voltage or ripple on output indicates a failed diode.
Overvoltage protection on exciter output: Zener diode suppressor across diode bank — clamps transient voltages.
Overcurrent protection on main field winding: included in AVR — limits excitation current to prevent winding overheating.
Thermistor protection: embedded in stator winding — trips if temperature exceeds Class F limit (155°C).
No slip rings — advantage: eliminates brush wear, arcing, and brush-dust contamination. Reduces maintenance significantly.
Slip Ring Pitting Marks — Action
Causes of pitting: high current sparking from worn/misaligned brushes, contamination, incorrect brush grade.

Action: (1) Reduce load to minimum. (2) Inspect brush pressure — must be 150–200 g/cm² typically. (3) Use fine emery cloth to smooth pits during running (carefully, with insulated holder). (4) Check brush grade — must match manufacturer spec. (5) If severe → machine slip rings in lathe during dry dock.
After dressing: check contact surface is smooth and bright. Monitor brush sparking for 30 minutes.
Press Breaker on Idle (Non-Running) Generator — What Happens?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Trick question — asked by multiple surveyors
Answer: Nothing useful. An idle generator has no voltage — if you close its ACB, no power flows from it onto the busbar.

What ACTUALLY happens: The running generator back-feeds the idle generator's windings through the closed breaker. The idle machine runs as an induction motor (motoring effect) — draws current from busbar.
Protection: Reverse power relay detects the reverse power flow and trips the ACB within seconds. If reverse power relay fails → overcurrent may develop.
Why this matters: Closing ACB without synchronising (and without running) is a common exam trick — surveyor wants to hear 'motoring + reverse power trip'.

Alternator Routine Maintenance — Winding Cleaning
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple candidates asked about alternator routine maintenance
Routine maintenance of ship alternator:
Check insulation resistance (IR) using megger — record in maintenance log
Clean air filters and ventilation ducts — blocked filters cause overheating
Blow out dust/carbon deposits using dry compressed air (low pressure)
Oil contamination in windings: clean using approved electrical contact cleaner (not water)
Check and tighten all terminal connections — vibration causes loosening
Inspect bearing condition — lubricate or replace per schedule
Test AVR output voltage and stability under load
Record all readings in PMS (Planned Maintenance System)
Motor Running on 280V Instead of 440V — Effect
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: What happens if 440V motor receives only 280V?
Torque reduces as square of voltage ratio: (280/440)² = 0.4 → only ~40% rated torque produced
Under load: motor may fail to start or stall — cannot overcome load torque
Current rises 2–3× rated value to compensate — severe overheating risk
Speed drops, slip increases — inefficient operation
Overload relay should trip — but only if correctly set
Exam answer: "Under-voltage → excessive current, overheating, reduced torque, possible stalling"
Why Generator Not Placed on Bottom Platform (Tank Top)
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Wad — generator placement in engine room
1. FLOODING RISK: Bottom of ER floods first — generator submerged if placed at tank top level
2. SOLAS II-1/Reg 40: Main electrical power source must be protected against flooding
3. VIBRATION: Tank top level has highest structural vibration from ME and propeller shaft
4. MAINTENANCE: Upper platforms allow overhead crane access for motor/generator overhaul
5. VENTILATION: Upper platforms have better forced/natural airflow for cooling
Emergency generator: MUST be above bulkhead deck, OUTSIDE machinery space — SOLAS requirement
Alternator Safeties — Complete List
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple surveyors — "what are the safeties on an alternator?"
Over-current relay (OCR): trips if output current exceeds rated — protects windings
Over-voltage relay: trips if terminal voltage exceeds ~110% rated — protects insulation
Under-voltage relay: trips if voltage drops below ~85% rated — prevents motor stalling
Differential protection relay: compares current in vs out — detects internal winding faults
Reverse power relay: prevents motoring — trips if prime mover fails and power flows backward
Earth fault relay: detects stator winding earth faults (95% stator earth fault protection)
Over/under frequency relay: trips on abnormal speed (over-speed or under-speed)
Bearing temperature: PT100 sensors — alarm ~80°C, trip ~95°C
Winding temperature: PT100 in stator slots — alarm and trip on overheating
Preferential trip: sheds non-essential loads before tripping generator on sustained overload

HV Rubber Gloves — Identification by Class
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Asked whenever HV working procedure is discussed
HV insulating gloves are classified by the voltage they protect against:
Class 00: Max use voltage 500V AC — colour: beige
Class 0: Max use voltage 1,000V AC — colour: red
Class 1: Max use voltage 7,500V AC — colour: white
Class 2: Max use voltage 17,000V AC — colour: yellow
Class 3: Max use voltage 26,500V AC — colour: green
Class 4: Max use voltage 36,000V AC — colour: orange

How to check before use: Inflate by rolling cuff — check for holes/cracks. Inspect visually for cuts, contamination. Check date stamp — must be within test interval (typically 6 months). Store away from oil, ozone, and UV.
Electrical Bonding — Purpose and Procedure
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal asks this in nearly every session on tankers/HV ships
Definition: Connecting all metal parts electrically using a bonding conductor to equalise electrical potential between them — prevents static spark ignition.
Tanker cargo ops sequence: (1) Connect bonding cable — ship to jetty FIRST, before anything else. (2) Connect cargo hose — bond both ends before coupling. (3) Only then begin cargo transfer.
Why: Cargo flow creates static charge (streaming current). If potential difference exists between ship and jetty → spark → ignition of vapour.
Ship's own bonding: All pipework, tanks, pumps are bonded to ship's hull. Hull is the common reference.
HV equipment bonding: All metallic enclosures, cable armour, motor frames bonded to ship's earth bar — prevents shock if insulation fails.

HV System — Advantages and Disadvantages
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Vallatho — always asked when HV ship is mentioned
ADVANTAGES:
1. Lower current for same power → thinner cables → significant weight saving on large ships
2. Lower I²R losses in cables → improved efficiency
3. Smaller cable cross-sections → easier routing, less space
4. Better voltage regulation over long cable runs
5. Suitable for large loads (thrusters, cargo pumps, cranes) — impractical at 440V
DISADVANTAGES:
1. Greater danger to personnel — stricter safety procedures required
2. More expensive switchgear (VCB, SF6 breakers)
3. More complex insulation monitoring and protection systems
4. Specially trained personnel required — HV authorisation needed
5. Higher cost of cables, terminations, and joints
Shaft Earthing System — Why Used
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sudhir — 'why do we use shaft earthing system?'

Problem: Main engine shaft and propeller are insulated from hull by oil film in bearings. Stray electrical currents (from alternator, VFD harmonics) can flow through bearings → electrolytic corrosion → pitting of bearing surfaces and shaft.
Solution: Shaft earthing device — a carbon brush assembly that rides on the propeller shaft and provides a direct electrical path from shaft to hull earth.
Maintains shaft at hull potential → no potential difference → no galvanic current through bearings.
ETO responsibility: Check brush condition and contact, clean slip ring surface on shaft, measure shaft-to-hull resistance (should be near zero Ω).

Front access clearance: minimum 1000 mm (1 m) — operator working space in front of panel
Rear access clearance: minimum 600 mm — safe working access for cable entries and busbar connections
Insulating rubber mat thickness: minimum 6 mm for 440V systems — placed in front and rear of MSB

Number of Busbars in MSB and Their Purpose
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "How many busbars in MSB and what are they for?"
Standard MSB: 3 main phase busbars (L1, L2, L3) + 1 neutral busbar = 4 busbars total
Split-busbar MSB: 6 busbars (3 per section) + bus-tie breaker between sections
L1 (Red/Brown): Phase 1 — 440V line-to-line between phases
L2 (Yellow): Phase 2
L3 (Blue/Black): Phase 3
Neutral (N): NOT directly earthed on ship — IT (Insulated Terra) system
Earth busbar: Hull earth connection — separate from neutral on insulated neutral system
Ship uses IT system: neutral NOT earthed → first earth fault does not trip → IRM alarms instead
200% Insulation — What Is the Value?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "What is 200% insulation?"
"200% insulation" = measured IR must be at least TWICE the minimum acceptable value
IEC standard minimum: 1 MΩ per kV of working voltage + 1 MΩ (for voltages below 1kV: minimum 1 MΩ)
For 440V system: minimum 1 MΩ → 200% means minimum 2 MΩ before returning to service
For newly installed/rewound equipment: much higher expected — typically >100 MΩ
Context: surveyor wants you to know the test standard and what "passing" IR looks like
IRM — Insulation Resistance Monitor — Working Principle
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Wad — "explain how IRM works on ship system"
IRM = Insulation Resistance Monitor (also: Earth Fault Indicator). Ship uses IT (Insulated Neutral) system.
Working: Injects a low-level voltage (1–5V AC or DC) between neutral and hull earth
Measures impedance between live system and earth — high impedance = healthy insulation
If insulation deteriorates or earth fault develops: impedance drops → leakage current increases → IRM alarms
Alarm threshold: typically set at 50–100 kΩ — below this value, alarm activates
IRM does NOT identify which circuit is faulty — used with earth fault locator to trace faults
After IRM alarm: switch off non-essential circuits one by one until IRM clears → identifies faulty circuit

Double Cage (Double Squirrel Cage) Induction Motor
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — where used on ships and why
Construction: Two rotor cages — outer cage (high resistance, low reactance) and inner cage (low resistance, high reactance).
During starting: High frequency rotor currents flow mainly in outer cage (skin effect) → high resistance → high starting torque. Reduced inrush compared to full cage.
During running: Low slip → low frequency → currents shift to inner cage → low resistance → efficient running, low losses.
Used on ships for: windlass, mooring winch, anchor windlass, bow thruster auxiliary motors, cargo crane hoisting motors — all need HIGH STARTING TORQUE under load.
Advantage over single cage: Better starting torque without requiring external resistance starter. Better PF at starting.
Motor Crawling — Cause and Prevention
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kolkata surveyors, Sanjib — 'motor runs at slow speed after starting'
Definition: Motor runs stably at approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed instead of accelerating to full speed.
Cause: 7th harmonic component in the air-gap flux creates a reluctance torque dip at 1/7 × Ns. Motor locks into this stable operating point instead of pulling through to full speed.

Prevention: (1) Skew rotor slots — reduces harmonic content of air-gap flux. (2) Proper stator slot/rotor slot combination — avoid slot harmonics. (3) Chording of stator winding — reduces 5th and 7th harmonics.
How to recognise: Motor starts, accelerates to ~1/7 speed, stops accelerating, runs noisily at low speed. Overcurrent relay may trip.

2. Power rating: kW
3. Voltage: 440V / 6.6kV / 11kV
4. Frequency: 60 Hz or 50 Hz

Self-Synchronous Motor (Synchro / Selsyn)
A transmitter-receiver pair that maintain exact angular correspondence. No power circuit — signal circuit only.
Working: AC supply to transmitter rotor. Stator outputs 3-phase signal proportional to rotor angle. Receiver stator receives same 3-phase signal → receiver rotor aligns to same angle.
Used on ships for: remote position indicators — rudder angle indicator, valve position indicator (remote), fuel tank level gauges, hatch cover position.
Advantage: Continuous, accurate position feedback over long distances without mechanical linkage.
Motor After Rewinding — Checks Before Returning to Service
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal: 'Motor came back from shore after rewinding — what checks do you do?'
1. Insulation resistance (IR) test — all 3 phases to earth and between phases. Minimum 1 MΩ at 500V DC megger. Warm the winding first if damp.
2. Resistance balance — measure DC resistance of all 3 phases with bridge meter. Should be equal within 2%.
3. Check terminal markings — confirm U1/U2, V1/V2, W1/W2 correctly labelled. If markings missing → find by test.
4. Phase rotation check — use phase rotation meter. Confirm same as original before connecting.
5. No-load trial run — check starting current, running current (should be less than FLA). Check vibration, bearing temperature after 30 minutes.
6. Check end-shield alignment — ensure air gap is uniform after reassembly.
7. Confirm IP rating maintained — check all cable gland seals, terminal box cover.
Motor Coupling Check Procedure
1. Alignment check: Use dial gauge on coupling face (angular and parallel). Also check with straight edge across coupling flanges.
2. Coupling bolts: Check torque to manufacturer spec. Check anti-vibration rubber insert condition (for flexible couplings).
3. End float check: Measure axial movement — must be within spec to avoid thrust bearing overload.
4. After brief run: Check vibration (compare to baseline), bearing temperature. No abnormal noise.
5. Record: Log alignment readings, bolt torques, date in maintenance file.
IP Rating — Requirements by Location
Engine room (general): Minimum IP44 — protected against solid objects >1mm and water splashes from any direction.
Cargo deck / exposed areas: IP55 — dust tight + protected against water jets from any direction.
Wash-down areas / car deck: IP56 — powerful water jets.
Bilge area / intermittently submerged: IP68 — continuous submersion.
Pump rooms, hazardous areas (Ex zones): IP55 or IP56 + Ex certification (EEx d, EEx e).
Battery rooms: IP44 minimum + ventilated enclosure.
Insulation Class — Generator and MCSW Pump
Insulation class defines maximum operating temperature of the winding insulation:
Class B: 130°C maximum. Class F: 155°C maximum. Class H: 180°C maximum.
Ship's alternator/generator: typically Class F (155°C) — operated at Class B temperature (130°C) for reliability margin.
Main cooling seawater pump (MCSW) motor: typically Class F. Pump room motors in wet/humid environment need Class F minimum.
Why asked: Surveyor checks you know the motor's thermal limits — important for IR test interpretation and alarm setpoints.
Eddy Currents in Motors — Cause and Reduction
Eddy currents: Circulating currents induced in the stator/rotor iron core by changing magnetic flux (Faraday's law).
Effect: I²R losses in core → heat. Reduces efficiency. Called iron losses or core losses.
Reduction: Core made of thin laminated silicon steel sheets (0.3–0.5mm), insulated from each other. Eddy current path is broken — magnitude greatly reduced. Silicon increases resistivity of iron.
Cannot be eliminated completely — only minimised.
Also present in transformers for the same reason — same solution (laminated core).

Motor Overheating — Causes and Actions
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple surveyors — "why is motor overheating?"
1. OVERLOAD: Motor driving excessive load — current exceeds rated → I²R heat in windings
2. SINGLE PHASING: One phase lost — remaining two phases carry ~2× current — severe heating
3. UNDER-VOLTAGE: Low supply voltage → higher current for same torque → overheating
4. VENTILATION FAILURE: Blocked filters, failed cooling fan, dirty housing — heat cannot escape
5. HIGH AMBIENT: Engine room temperature exceeds design limit (usually 45°C) — less cooling margin
6. FREQUENT STARTING: Each start = 6–8× FLC inrush — frequent starts prevent cooling
7. BEARING FAILURE: Seized bearing increases mechanical load → thermal overload
8. PHASE IMBALANCE: Unequal voltages → negative sequence currents → additional rotor heating
Action: Stop motor → check cause → inspect overload relay setting → inspect bearings → check supply
Single Phasing — Effect and Detection
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal, Kamath — "what is single phasing and how do you detect it?"
Single phasing: one of three phases is lost (fuse blown, contactor contact failure, cable break)
Running motor continues on two phases — draws heavy current in remaining phases (~2× normal)
Motor cannot develop full torque — will stall under heavy load
Vibration increases — negative sequence currents produce counter-rotating torque
Stopped motor in single-phase condition: CANNOT restart — starting torque is zero on two phases
Detection: (1) Ammeter per phase — missing phase shows zero. (2) Phase failure relay — trips on loss of any phase. (3) Negative sequence relay. (4) 3-element overload relay.
Protection: Use 3-element thermal overload relay with phase-sensitive protection — single-element will NOT protect
Fuse Selection for 440V Circuit
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "What fuse do you use for a 440V circuit?"
440V ship circuits: HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse — NOT rewirable or cartridge type
HRC fuse rating: based on circuit FLC and motor starting characteristics
Motor circuits: fuse rated at 1.5–2.5× motor FLC (allows starting surge without blowing)
HRC internals: ceramic/glass body, silver fusing element, silica sand arc-quenching filler
Breaking capacity: typically 80–100 kA — can safely interrupt high fault currents
HRC is "current limiting" — interrupts fault before first current peak → limits damage
Never use rewirable fuse on 440V MSB feeder — unsafe, inaccurate rating, slow operation
5kW 440V 50Hz Motor — Specs & Starter Selection
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked motor nameplate data and starter selection
5 kW, 440V, 3-phase, 50Hz induction motor — key specifications:
Starting current (DOL): approximately 6–8× FLC = 51–68 A
Speed: ~1450 rpm (4-pole, 50Hz synchronous = 1500 rpm, ~3% slip)
Autotransformer starter: reduces voltage to 65–80% → reduces current and torque as V². Use when load needs medium starting torque but lower current stress required.
Soft starter: electronic phase-angle control gradually ramps voltage 0→100%. Smooth start, adjustable ramp. Modern preference.
Selection: Autotransformer — older installation, higher torque needed. Soft starter — pumps/fans (variable torque), reduced mechanical stress, precise control.
For 5 kW pump: soft starter preferred — gentle ramp, no water hammer, protects pipe fittings
ER Crane — Speed Control Methods & Motor Overhauling
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple candidates asked about crane motor speed control
ER crane speed control methods:
1. POLE CHANGING (Dahlander winding): 2-pole = high speed, 4-pole = low speed. Simple, two fixed speeds only.
2. ROTOR RESISTANCE (Slip ring motor): External resistance in rotor → increases slip → reduces speed. Steps depend on resistance steps. Good torque control for crane hoists.
3. VFD (Variable Frequency Drive): Full variable speed, smooth control, regenerative braking. Modern cranes.
4. CASCADE CONTROL: Two coupled motors — auxiliary motor fed from rotor circuit. Less common.
Motor overhauling procedure:
1. Isolate, permit to work — lock off, tag out, verify dead
2. Disconnect all cables — mark with identification tags
3. Remove motor from mounting — support shaft during removal
4. Disassemble: end shields, extract rotor, inspect bearings
5. Clean windings — dry compressed air, check IR, inspect for burn marks
6. Replace bearings (standard practice during overhaul)
7. Reassemble, align, refit to mounting
8. Megger test before energising — record IR value
9. Commission: check rotation direction, measure running current all three phases
Back EMF — Principle and 3-Pole Double-Throw Switch
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "What is back EMF?" and reversing switch operation
Back EMF: Voltage generated by rotating motor opposing supply voltage — increases as motor accelerates
At no load: back EMF ≈ supply voltage → very small current (magnetising + friction losses only)
At full load: load slows rotor → back EMF drops → larger net voltage → more current → more torque
Starting: back EMF = 0 → full supply across winding resistance → 6–8× FLC starting current
DC motor: back EMF = φ × N × K (proportional to speed) — used in DC speed control
3-pole double-throw (reversing) switch: swaps two phases → reverses motor rotation direction
Used for reversing duty: bilge pumps, windlass, crane. MUST stop motor before switching — never switch under load
Bearing Identification — Reading Bearing Numbers
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "How do you read a bearing number?"
Standard ISO bearing number: e.g. 6205-2RS
First digit(s) = type: 6=deep groove ball, 7=angular contact, 2=spherical roller, 3=cylindrical roller
Next two digits = bore: multiply by 5 for bore in mm. Example: 05 = 05×5 = 25 mm bore
Width/series: 0=extra light, 2=light, 3=medium, 4=heavy
Suffix: 2RS = two rubber seals. ZZ = two metal shields. C3 = larger clearance (high temperature). E = reinforced cage.
Example: 6205-2RS = deep groove ball bearing, 25mm bore, light series, double rubber sealed
Ordering: quote full number from old bearing. If unreadable: measure bore diameter, outer diameter, width
Synchronous Motor (SG Motor) — Safety Features
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked SG motor safety features
Field failure relay: trips if DC excitation is lost — motor loses synchronism, pulls high current as induction motor
Out-of-step protection: detects when rotor falls out of synchronism — trips motor
Under-voltage trip: protects on supply failure
Overcurrent protection: standard motor protection
Starting protection: During asynchronous starting, field winding must be short-circuited or loaded with resistance — prevents high induced voltage damaging field insulation
Includes: Batteries, UPS, Emergency Generator, Sequential Load Restoration

MSB Safeties — Complete List
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Asked by ALL surveyors — most common switchboard question
1. Dead-front panel construction: Cannot open live panel door — physical/electrical interlock prevents access to live conductors.
2. IDMT Over-current relay (OCR): Inverse Definite Minimum Time — trips FASTER for higher fault current. Protects busbars and feeders.
3. Under-voltage (UV) trip relay: Trips generator ACB if voltage drops below ~85% rated. Prevents motoring.
4. Reverse power relay: Detects power flow FROM busbar INTO generator — trips ACB. Prevents motoring of alternator.
5. Earth fault indicator lamps: Three lamps in star configuration. Normal = all glow equally. Fault = earthed phase lamp goes dim/dark.
6. Bus-tie (BT) interlock: Prevents wrong buses being paralleled. Ensures only correctly synchronised sections connected.
7. Preferential trip relay: Sheds non-essential loads sequentially (in stages) to prevent overload and blackout.
8. Standby start interlock: Auto-starts standby generator on overload or main generator failure.
9. Emergency stop push button: Trips all generator ACBs simultaneously for emergency shutdown.
10. Overvoltage relay: Trips generator if output voltage exceeds ~110% rated — protects connected equipment.
HRC Fuse Types — Full Detail
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Deswal, Sanjib — difference between fuse types
1. Rewirable (Kit-Kat) fuse: Rating unknown (depends on wire gauge used). NOT safe for high fault current. Cheapest, least reliable. Replaced by inserting new wire element.
2. Cartridge fuse: Rating known (printed on body). NOT safe for high fault current. Reliable rating but may not clear high fault safely.
3. HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse: MOST IMPORTANT. Rating stamped on end cap. Blows in 0.25–3 cycles. SAFE for high fault current.
HRC internals: Ceramic or glass body, silver fuse element (calibrated cross-section), silica sand filler (quenches arc), riveted brass end caps.
HRC advantage: Current limiting (arc extinguishes before current reaches peak), no arc flash, accurate and repeatable operation.
Used for: MSB feeder protection, motor feeder protection, HV system protection.
Overload Relay vs Overcurrent Relay — Difference
Overload relay: Thermal bimetallic type. Protects motor from sustained overload (overcurrent < 10× FLA). Slow to trip — reflects thermal heating of motor winding.
Overcurrent relay (OCR): IDMT type. Protects against fault currents and heavy short circuits. Fast trip proportional to current magnitude.
Key difference: Overload = thermal protection (motor). OCR = fault protection (cables, busbar). Both may be present — different trip times.
Fuse vs OCR: Fuse is sacrificial (single-use), trips on overcurrent, protects cables. OCR resets after fault clearance, more precise, can be tested.
Differential Relay — What It Is and vs Fuse
Differential relay: Compares current flowing IN versus current flowing OUT of a protected zone (transformer, generator, busbar section).
If IN ≠ OUT → fault inside the zone → relay trips. Even small fault currents can be detected — VERY sensitive.
Used for: Large generators, large transformers, main busbar sections.
vs Fuse: Fuse only protects against overcurrent. Differential relay detects internal faults (earth fault, winding fault) even with small fault current that wouldn't blow a fuse.
PI Test — Why Wait 10 Minutes?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: ALL surveyors — follow-up after IR test
PI (Polarisation Index) = IR at 10 minutes ÷ IR at 1 minute.

Firing angle (α): The angle in the AC cycle at which the gate pulse is applied to turn the thyristor on.

1.1 Working Principle — Photocell / Light Extinction Method

An Oil Mist Detector (OMD) continuously monitors the crankcase atmosphere of a diesel engine for elevated oil mist concentration. Oil mist forms when bearing surfaces begin to overheat — the oil film vaporises and condenses into fine droplets. This is an early warning of impending failure, occurring well before a catastrophic crankcase explosion. The OMD provides the crucial minutes needed to slow down or stop the engine safely.

The working principle is photoelectric light extinction (opacity measurement). A rotary sampling valve draws gas from each crankcase unit in sequence and passes it through a measuring tube. A calibrated light source (lamp) shines through the tube onto a photocell at the other end. When oil mist concentration is elevated, the mist droplets scatter and absorb the light beam, reducing the intensity reaching the photocell. The photocell output decreases in proportion to mist concentration. This signal is compared against a sealed reference tube containing clean air at the same optical path length — the differential measurement gives the true mist reading independent of lamp aging.

2.1 Purpose and Need for Viscosity Control

Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO) used in marine diesel engines must be heated before injection. The purpose of heating is to reduce viscosity to a level where the fuel can be properly atomised through the injector nozzle. Atomisation quality directly determines combustion efficiency, exhaust temperature, carbon deposit formation, and specific fuel consumption. Too high a viscosity means the fuel jet does not break into fine droplets — incomplete combustion follows. Too low a viscosity (over-heated) means reduced lubrication between the fuel pump plunger and barrel, accelerating wear and allowing fuel to blow past the plunger, causing injection timing errors.

The correct injection viscosity is 10–14 cSt (centistokes) for most main engines, and 14–20 cSt for auxiliary diesel engines. This does not correspond to a fixed temperature — different HFO grades (e.g. RMG 380 with 380 cSt at 50°C, versus RME 180 with 180 cSt at 50°C) reach the same injection viscosity at different temperatures. This is the fundamental reason a viscosity controller is used rather than a temperature controller.

In the follow-up system, the hunting gear linkage generates a signal proportional to rudder position and uses it to cancel the solenoid valve command when the demanded angle is reached. If this linkage is disconnected, worn, or misadjusted, the solenoid never sees the cancellation signal and drives the rudder continuously.

🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Deswal, Vishwanathan — most critical gap identified
This is DIFFERENT from automatic blackout recovery. Dead ship = no power, no compressed air, no running machinery. Manual process only.
Step 1: Check all necessary valves and lines are open (fuel, cooling water, lube oil to AE).
Step 2: Start emergency generator from emergency switchboard (battery start).
Step 3: Using emergency power, start emergency air compressor to build air pressure.
Step 4: Once main air bottles at sufficient pressure, attempt to start first auxiliary engine by compressed air.
Step 5: Check and confirm voltage, frequency, and phase rotation of AE output.
Step 6: Close ACB of first AE — power on main busbar. Inform bridge: 'Main power restored.'
Step 7: Start second AE, synchronise and parallel onto main bus.
Step 8: Load essential services one by one — in sequence: steering gear, bilge pumps, cooling pumps, then non-essential.
Step 9: Switch off emergency generator once main power confirmed stable.
Step 10: Restore all normal distribution — log event, notify C/E and bridge, investigate root cause.
IGBT in cycloconverter note: If thruster uses cycloconverter drive — cannot restart until main power fully restored and drive re-initialised.
Boiler Electrical Alarms and Troubleshoot — ETO Role
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Sudhir — 'what is your role in boiler fault?'
ETO owns: All sensors (PT100 temperature sensors, pressure transmitters, level gauges/DP transmitters), solenoid valves, ignition transformer, FD fan motor, burner management controller (PLC/BMS).
C/E owns: Mechanical issues — tube leaks, pump failures, combustion tuning.
Flame failure alarm: Check UV/IR flame detector (clean lens), check ignition transformer output voltage, check solenoid valve energises (test with 24V), check BMS controller output signal.
High/low water level alarm: Check DP transmitter calibration, check reference leg isolation valve open, check drain valve closed, compare with sight glass.
FD fan motor fault: Check motor overload relay reset, check thermistor resistance (normal: 100–200Ω, tripped: >3kΩ), check starter contactors, check duct pressure switch.
BMS power fault: Check 24V DC supply rail, check MCB/fuse, check supply cable earth fault.
Boiler FD fan motor vs normal motor contactor: FD fan has high inertia → uses star-delta starter or soft starter. Normal motor may use DOL. Key difference for exam.
Turbocharger RPM Sensor — Type and Working
Type: Magnetic pickup (variable reluctance) sensor — most common. Some high-speed TCs use eddy current or optical sensors.

Working: Ferromagnetic toothed wheel (phonic wheel) on TC shaft rotates past sensor tip. Each tooth passing changes magnetic flux through sensor coil — induces voltage pulse. Frequency of pulses = RPM of TC.
Calibration: Count teeth × pulses per tooth × conversion factor = RPM. Usually preconfigured in tachometer.
Faults: Oil on sensor tip → weak signal. Air gap too large (>2mm) → no signal. Broken tooth → erratic RPM. Cable fault → zero reading. Clean tip, check gap during maintenance.
Anti-Heeling System — ETO Role
Purpose: Transfers ballast between port and starboard tanks to maintain ship upright during one-sided cargo loading/discharging.
ETO controls: Motor-driven centrifugal pump (transfers ballast). Remote valve actuators on cross-flooding valves. Heel angle sensor (inclinometer) input to control panel.
Safeties ETO must know: Pump motor overload protection, tank overfill alarm, remote stop from bridge and CCR, limit switches on valves.
Monitoring: Check heel angle display matches inclinometer reading. Check transfer pump current for correct value. Verify tank level sensors reading correctly.
TEV — Thermostatic Expansion Valve (Reefer System)
Function: Regulates refrigerant flow into evaporator to maintain constant superheat at evaporator outlet.

Working: Sensor bulb on suction line detects superheat temperature. Bellows transmit pressure to valve needle. High superheat → valve opens more → more refrigerant flow → superheat reduced. Low superheat → valve closes → less flow.
Typical superheat setting: 4–6°C above saturation temperature at evaporator pressure.
ETO check: Measure suction line temperature and suction pressure → calculate actual superheat → compare to set value. Adjust TEV if needed.
Mooring Winch Autotension — Working and ETO Maintenance

Working: Motor drives drum. Load cell or current sensing detects rope tension. When tension > setpoint → motor reverses/brakes → pays out rope. When tension < setpoint → motor hauls in. Maintains constant tension automatically during tidal/current changes.

ETO maintenance: Check motor IR, check brake condition (air gap of electromagnetic brake), check limit switches (inboard/outboard), check hydraulic pressure if hydraulic drive type, verify load cell calibration.
Autotension interlock: Must be manually cancelled before departure — if left in auto, winch will keep paying out rope as ship moves away.
Lube Oil Low Pressure Alarm — ETO Action
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: 'Generators running, suddenly LO low pressure alarm — ETO action?'
Step 1: Do NOT immediately stop engine. Inform C/E and bridge.
Step 2: Check local LO pressure gauge — confirm alarm is genuine (not sensor fault).
Step 3: Check LO pump running (listen, check ammeter, check local pressure).
Step 4: Check LO sump level — if low, immediate risk of bearing damage.
Step 5: Check LO pump inlet strainer — blocked strainer = low pressure.
Step 6: If pressure keeps dropping → prepare to switch to manual emergency stop to prevent bearing damage. Log all actions.
ETO scope: Check LO pressure sensor calibration, check LO level sensor, check pump motor running (electrical side). C/E handles mechanical cause.

Steering Gear — Electrical Alarms and Trips
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Gopikrishna, Sudhir — very commonly asked
ALARMS (warning only — no trip):
1. Hydraulic oil low level alarm
2. Hydraulic oil high temperature alarm
3. Phase failure alarm (loss of one phase to motor)
4. Pump motor overload alarm — before trip
5. Control power failure alarm
TRIPS (automatic shutdown):
6. Motor overload trip — sustained overcurrent
7. Hydraulic oil high pressure trip — relief valve plus electrical trip
8. Rudder hunting trip — rudder oscillates continuously without reaching setpoint → NFU trip
9. Power unit isolation trip — emergency shutdown from bridge

Governor Types — Which Used Where
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Wad — 'types of governors? which type on main engine?'

1. MECHANICAL (Centrifugal / Flyball) governor: Rotating flyweights driven by engine. As speed increases → flyweights fly out → fuel rack reduces. Simple, robust, no external power. Used on older main engines and some AEs.
2. HYDRAULIC-MECHANICAL (Woodward type): Flyball + hydraulic servo amplifier. More precise than pure mechanical. Used on most diesel generators onboard.
3. ELECTRONIC (PID-based): Speed sensor (magnetic pickup) → electronic controller → actuator on fuel rack. Most precise. Used on modern DGs and electronically controlled main engines.
Main engine governor type: Most 2-stroke slow-speed diesels use hydraulic-mechanical (Woodward) or electronic governor. Modern MAN B&W/Wartsila → electronic.
Exam answer: 'DG typically uses hydraulic-mechanical Woodward governor. ME uses electronic governor on modern ships.'
Overspeed Relay Test Procedure
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Wad — 'how do you test overspeed relay?'

Method 1 (Setpoint reduction): Slowly reduce governor speed setpoint using speed trim while engine is running → engine speed falls, overspeed relay does NOT activate (this tests governor, not overspeed relay).

Method 2 (Mechanical lift test — CORRECT for overspeed relay): While engine runs at governed speed → manually lift the overspeed trip lever → confirm trip activates → engine shuts down. Reset manually after test.
Method 3 (Electronic test where available): Press 'Overspeed test' button on governor panel → electronic unit simulates overspeed signal → confirm relay trips.

Why two separate systems: Governor adjusts fuel to maintain speed. Overspeed trip is a BACKUP — activates if governor fails and speed runs away. They are independent — testing one does not test the other.
After test: Reset trip manually. Restart engine. Record test in log with date, time, speed at which trip activated, and who witnessed.

JCW (Jacket Cooling Water) System — Operation
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked ETO about JCW system — "explain JCW system and your role"
What is JCW?

JCW = Jacket Cooling Water. A CLOSED-LOOP fresh water system that cools the cylinder liners, cylinder heads, exhaust valve cages, and turbocharger casing of main and auxiliary diesel engines. It prevents overheating of hot parts and maintains ideal liner temperatures for efficient combustion and to prevent cold corrosion.
JCW System Flow Path:
1. JCW PUMP (centrifugal): Circulates FW through engine jackets under pressure (typically 2–4 bar).
2. ENGINE JACKETS: Water passages in cylinder liner and head castings — absorbs heat from combustion.
3. FRESH WATER COOLER (FWC): Shell-and-tube heat exchanger — JCW (hot) cooled by sea water (cold side).
4. THERMOSTATIC 3-WAY VALVE: Bypasses or routes through FWC to maintain correct JCW outlet temperature.
5. EXPANSION TANK: Above engine — maintains system pressure head, allows thermal expansion, vents air. Contains immersion heater for pre-heating.
6. PRE-HEATER: Electric immersion heater in expansion tank keeps JCW at 50–60°C while engine stopped — prevents cold-start thermal shock.
7. DOSING UNIT: Adds nitrite/molybdate corrosion inhibitor — prevents liner pitting and galvanic corrosion.
Operating temperatures and why they matter:
JCW inlet to engine: ~60–70°C. JCW outlet from engine: ~75–85°C.
Too cold (<55°C): Combustion gases condense on liner → sulphuric acid formed → cold corrosion of liner — very expensive damage.
Too hot (>90°C): Risk of localised boiling in cylinder head passages → hot spots → thermal cracking.
Correct temperature is critical — thermostatic valve maintains this automatically.
ETO Responsibilities:
1. Immersion heater (pre-heater): Test element resistance with megger, check thermostat setpoint, verify temperature at expansion tank.
2. Temperature sensors (PT100/thermocouple): Calibrate against reference thermometer, check cable integrity.
3. High-temperature alarm and trip: Test with simulated signal — verify alarm activates at correct value and engine trip works.
4. Low-level alarm on expansion tank: Test float switch or level sensor function.
5. JCW pump motor: Scheduled megger test, bearing greasing, impeller inspection.
6. Inhibitor concentration: Test monthly with kit, top up as required, record in chemical log.
7. Fresh water cooler: Inspect SW side for scale/fouling, check tube plate for leaks across to JCW side.
Reefer Compressor — LO Pressure Sensor Measurement and Calibration
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked how ETO measures and calibrates the reefer compressor LO pressure sensor
Why is LO pressure monitoring critical on reefer compressor?

The lubricating oil pressure sensor protects compressor bearings. If LO pressure drops below minimum (typically 1.5–2 bar), the compressor must trip immediately — without LO, bearings seize within minutes causing catastrophic mechanical failure and refrigerant leak. The trip is a safety-critical function.
Calibration procedure (electronic 4–20mA transmitter):
1. Permit to work — notify C/E, stop compressor, allow LO pressure to equalise to zero.
2. Isolate sensor at 3-valve manifold: close PROCESS ISOLATION valve (stops live pressure). Open EQUALISING BYPASS valve to safely vent residual pressure.
3. Connect calibrated reference gauge (dead-weight tester or certified digital pressure calibrator) to test tapping on manifold.
4. Apply increasing test pressures in steps — 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% of sensor range.
5. At each step: compare panel/DCS reading with reference gauge. Acceptable error: ±2% of full scale.
6. If deviation exists: use HART communicator or trim screws to adjust zero and span.
7. Test TRIP SETPOINT: Slowly reduce test pressure — note exact pressure when compressor trip alarm activates on panel.
8. Verify trip setpoint matches maintenance record. If wrong: adjust via relay calibration or DCS setpoint change (with C/E approval).
9. Typical setpoints: LO pressure alarm at ~2 bar, trip at ~1.5 bar.
10. Restore manifold: close equalise valve, open isolation valve. Verify normal system pressure on panel.
11. Document: test pressures, panel readings, deviations, setpoint confirmation, date, calibration cert reference.
Bilge Injection Valve — Purpose and Emergency Fire Pump Priming
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked about bilge injection valve — "what is it and when do you use it?"
What is the Bilge Injection Valve?

The bilge injection valve is a large-bore valve (100–150 mm) fitted to the SUCTION SIDE of the main sea water cooling pump, connecting the SW cooling pump suction directly to the engine room bilge. It exists for ONE purpose: emergency dewatering of the engine room when normal bilge pumps cannot cope with the rate of flooding.
Why it matters — comparison of capacities:
Dedicated bilge pump capacity: typically 10–50 m³/hr
Main SW cooling pump capacity: typically 200–600 m³/hr (depending on engine size)
In a serious flooding situation — a broken sea chest valve or large pipe fracture — only the main pump has the capacity to keep up
The bilge injection valve allows the main pump to switch from sea suction to bilge suction instantly
Precautions and procedure:
Valve is sealed or wired shut under normal operation — label says "EMERGENCY BILGE SUCTION — AUTHORISED USE ONLY"
Opening procedure posted at valve location (SOLAS II-1/Reg 35 requirement)
Before opening: Inform C/E and Master. Close SW cooling pump discharge to coolers (to avoid pumping bilge water through engine cooling systems).
After flooding controlled: Close bilge injection valve, restore SW cooling suction, reseal valve, log usage.
NEVER use for normal bilge pumping — it is not designed for regular use and uses the main cooling pump, which cannot simultaneously cool the engine
Emergency Fire Pump — Priming:
Emergency fire pump is typically self-priming — positive displacement (gear pump) type or jet-assisted centrifugal.
Located in emergency fire pump room OUTSIDE and SEPARATE from main engine room (SOLAS II-2/Reg 10).
Self-priming: Internal mechanism maintains liquid seal in pump body. Foot valve on suction line retains water when stopped.
If prime is lost (after long idle): Fill priming chamber through priming cock at top of pump casing. Use bucket or hose — prime with sea water.
Operational check (monthly): Start pump, open fire main valve, check discharge pressure (typically 4–5 bar at fire main). Record in log.
Smoke Density Meter — Working Principle and ETO Maintenance
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how does a smoke density meter work?"

The smoke density meter (opacity meter) measures the density of exhaust gases from boiler or engine stacks. It serves two purposes: (1) monitoring combustion quality — black smoke means incomplete combustion and wasted fuel; and (2) MARPOL Annex VI compliance — excessive visible smoke is prohibited under Reg 14.
Working Principle (Optical Transmission type):
1. LIGHT SOURCE: LED or halogen lamp mounted on one side of exhaust duct — projects a beam across the flue gas path.
2. DETECTOR: Photodiode or photocell on opposite side — measures received light intensity.
3. AIR PURGE SYSTEM: Compressed air continuously purges across lamp and detector optical windows — prevents soot deposit on lenses. Critical — without purge, readings are false high.
4. OPACITY CALCULATION: Opacity % = (1 − I_received / I_reference) × 100. 0% = clear flue gas. 100% = completely opaque (black smoke). Typically alarmed above 30–40%.
5. CLEAN AIR REFERENCE: Unit autozeros against clean air reading — compensates for ambient light and lens condition changes.
ETO Maintenance:
1. Verify compressed air purge pressure and flow — this is the most common failure mode. Purge pressure typically 0.3–0.5 bar.
2. Clean optical windows monthly (or as per PMS) — remove lens covers and wipe with lens tissue when purge is off.
3. Calibration check with reference filters (zero and span) — typically quarterly. Record values.
4. Verify alarm setpoint at DCS/alarm panel.
5. Check cable connections — high-temperature resistant cables near exhaust duct, inspect for heat damage annually.
UMS Checks and Pre-Arrival Procedures for ETO
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple candidates — "what are your pre-arrival duties as ETO?" and "how do you transfer from UMS?"
Transfer from UMS (Unmanned Machinery Space) to manned watch — typically 4 hours before arrival at port or anchorage:
1. POST ENGINE ROOM WATCHKEEPER: Official entry in engine room log — time and name of watchkeeper. Inform bridge.
2. TEST UMS ALARM EXTENSION: Check all ER alarms extend to bridge and accommodation. Walk-around — verify audible/visual alarms present at all required locations (bridge, C/E cabin, duty mess).

6. MOORING WINCH MOTORS: Test-run each winch motor. Check brake — apply and release. Verify control from local pendant AND from remote station. Check PLC status — no fault codes.
7. SHORE CONNECTION EQUIPMENT: Inspect shore power cable — no damage to insulation, correct connector type. Lay out near gangway if cold ironing expected.

13. EMERGENCY GENERATOR: Check fuel, oil, cooling water levels. Confirm in AUTO-START mode.

Drydock Duties — ETO Responsibilities and Working Aloft Safety
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what are your duties during drydock?"
ETO Drydock Duties — comprehensive list (typically scheduled over 10–14 day drydock):
1. PRE-DRYDOCK BASELINE IR: Megger test ALL motors, generators, cables before ship enters dock. Record values. Repeat post-drydock. Detect any damage caused during docking operations.

2. ICCP SYSTEM: Set to MANUAL/OFF before docking — hull must be in water for ICCP to work. With hull in air: clean reference electrode faces, inspect cable connections from electrodes to control panel, inspect anode condition and record remaining material.

3. SHAFT EARTHING DEVICE: Access is only possible in drydock. Inspect carbon brush condition, brush spring pressure, contact surface on propeller shaft. Replace brush if worn below 50% length. Clean slip ring surface on shaft.

4. HULL TRANSDUCERS (echo sounder, Doppler log, ADCP): Inspect hull fitting condition, antifouling paint around transducer face, zinc anodes fitted to transducer frame. Check cable penetration seals (deck glands). Record any damage.
5. SACRIFICIAL ANODES: Inspect all zinc/aluminium hull anodes. Record remaining mass as % of original. Renew anodes below 50% remaining. Class surveyor may require anode renewal records.
6. NAVIGATION LIGHTS: Physical inspection — corrosion, cracked lens, water ingress in fitting. Replace lamps/LEDs per schedule. Test complete system from bridge panel with surveyor present.
7. MOORING WINCH AND WINDLASS: Electrical overhaul if on schedule — new motor bearings, winding IR test, contactor renewal, control panel inspection.
8. FIRE DETECTION: Class survey may require full system test — every detector tested. ETO prepares detector map, operates system, witnesses test alongside class surveyor.
9. EMERGENCY GENERATOR CLASS SURVEY: Typically done in drydock — overspeed test, blackout test, load test, fuel consumption check. Surveyor witnesses and issues endorsement.
10. DEFECT LIST: Maintain running drydock defect list — all jobs, materials used, test results. Class-relevant work must be surveyor-witnessed and documented with class certificate.
Working Aloft Safety Requirements:
Working Aloft Permit (WAP): Required for ANY work at height — mast, funnel, radar platform, bridge wings above main deck level. Master signature required.
Weather check: Wind speed within limits (typically <10 knots). Check weather forecast before starting.
Buddy system: Minimum two persons. No lone working at height. One standby on deck below.
PPE: Full-body safety harness with two lanyards (100% attachment while moving — one always clipped). Hard hat. Safety footwear. High-visibility vest.
Tool control: ALL tools secured with lanyards or in tool bags. No loose items. Exclusion zone on deck below with barrier and signage.
Electrical isolation: Radar scanner motor isolated, navigation light circuits locked off, antenna discharge devices in place — before approaching any electrical equipment at height.
Communication: Portable radio — contact maintained with bridge and ER throughout.
Rescue plan: Established BEFORE starting. Stretcher, first-aid kit, rescue harness accessible. Personnel trained in working-at-height rescue.
After work: Remove all tools and materials from height, restore all isolations, cancel permit, inspect work area is clear.
Air Bottle in Lifeboat — Purpose and Lifeboat Sprinkler System Design
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what is the compressed air bottle in the lifeboat for?"
Air Bottle in Lifeboat — Two Distinct Purposes:

1. ENGINE STARTING AIR: Backup starting method if electric starter motor or battery fails. Compressed air (200–300 bar) is piped directly to the engine starting air valve — acts like a large air starter. Essential for ensuring lifeboat engine starts even with flat battery after long storage.

2. BREATHING AIR SUPPLY (Fire-protected lifeboats on tankers/dangerous goods ships): SOLAS requires totally enclosed lifeboats on these ships to have fire protection. When the lifeboat is launched through burning oil on water surface with all hatches closed, occupants need breathable air. Air bottle provides this supply for minimum 10 minutes — enough time to clear the fire zone.
Specifications and calculation:
Breathing air requirement: 40 litres/minute per person × 10 minutes × number of persons = required cylinder volume at working pressure.
Example: 26 persons × 40 L/min × 10 min = 10,400 litres at standard pressure. At 300 bar cylinder: capacity ≈ 10,400/300 ≈ 35 litres water capacity cylinder.
Pressure gauge: Must be readable from inside lifeboat without opening hatch.
Reduction valve: Steps down 300 bar cylinder pressure to low-pressure breathing air for distribution system.
Safety relief valve (burst disc): Protects against overpressure if cylinder exposed to heat.
Maintenance checklist:
1. Monthly: Check pressure gauge — must be at or above minimum working pressure. Record in lifeboat maintenance log.
2. If pressure low: Recharge using Class E (breathing quality) air compressor only. NEVER use industrial or workshop compressed air — oil contamination risk.
3. Annual: Inspect cylinder body for corrosion, dents, heat exposure. Any damaged cylinder must be withdrawn and condemned.
4. 5-year (or per regulation): Hydrostatic pressure test — cylinder filled with water and tested at 1.5× working pressure. Certificate required for class/SOLAS survey.
5. Pressure reduction valve and safety valve: Overhaul per manufacturer schedule.
Lifeboat Sprinkler (Water Spray Fire Protection) System:
Purpose: Protects lifeboat from radiant heat and direct contact with burning oil on sea surface during embarkation and escape through fire area.
Design: Engine-driven centrifugal pump draws sea water through hull sea cock → distributes to piping system → spray nozzles covering entire outer hull surface including windows.
Spray pattern: Full coverage — top, sides, and bottom covered with continuous water film.
Activation: Manual valve inside lifeboat (coxswain opens when required). Some designs automatic on engine start.
SOLAS LSC 4.4 / IMO MSC.218(82): Totally enclosed lifeboats on oil and chemical tankers in regular service must have fire protection system.
Test procedure: Start lifeboat engine → open sea cock → open spray valve → verify all nozzles operating, no blockages, adequate pressure. Test quarterly per PMS. Record date and result.
ER Crane — Speed Adjustment in Detail
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how do you adjust the speed of the ER crane?"
The answer depends on the type of drive installed. ETO must identify the system first. Common types on ship engine room cranes:

TYPE 1 — POLE CHANGING (DAHLANDER) MOTOR: Speed is fixed at two steps (typically low = 6 or 8 pole / high = 2 or 4 pole). No adjustment possible beyond selecting HIGH or LOW from pendant. Maintenance: check both speed contactors, check Dahlander winding connections U1/U2, V1/V2, W1/W2, check motor IR value for both winding configurations.

TYPE 2 — ROTOR RESISTANCE CONTROL (WOUND ROTOR / SLIP RING MOTOR): Speed varies by switching resistance in or out of rotor circuit. More resistance = more slip = lower speed. Typically 3–5 fixed speed steps. Speed adjustment by ETO: change resistance tap connections to alter step values — requires isolating control circuit, changing wiring at resistance bank terminal board. Detailed procedure: isolate crane (lockout), open resistance panel, change tap position, restore, test each speed.

TYPE 3 — VFD (VARIABLE FREQUENCY DRIVE): Full variable speed from 0–100%. Speed controlled by pendant potentiometer or up/down buttons. ETO adjustment parameters via VFD keypad: Maximum frequency (Hz) to limit top speed. Minimum frequency to set creep speed. Acceleration ramp time (seconds from 0 to max). Deceleration ramp time. These can be changed in the VFD parameter menu — refer to VFD manual for parameter numbers (e.g. Siemens MICROMASTER P1082 = max frequency).

TYPE 4 — HYDRAULIC (motor-driven hydraulic power pack): Motor speed is fixed. Crane speed controlled by hydraulic proportional valve. ETO role: maintain electric motor driving pump, not the crane speed setting itself — hydraulic valve adjustment is a mechanical job.
SOLAS II-1/3-13 — Lifting Appliances and Anchor Handling Winches (New 2026 Regulation)

🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Effective January 1, 2026, SOLAS Regulation II-1/3-13 formally brings shipboard lifting appliances and anchor handling winches under SOLAS statutory regulation for the first time. Previously governed only by a patchwork of classification society rules and ILO conventions. Surveyors will ask about SWL marking, load testing, and Safety Construction Certificate implications.
What the New Regulation Covers

Scope: All lifting appliances and anchor handling winches onboard ships subject to SOLAS. This includes: deck cranes (stores crane, provision crane, rescue boat davit winch), engine room overhead cranes (ER crane), anchor windlass, mooring winches used for anchor handling operations, and any other winch or lifting device used to lift loads or persons.
Key Requirements Under SOLAS II-1/3-13

1. Thorough load testing based on IMO guidelines: All lifting appliances must be load-tested to the proof load specified in the IMO guidelines (typically 125% of Safe Working Load for cranes, or as specified by class). Load test must be documented, witnessed by class surveyor, and the certificate retained onboard. Subsequent periodic proof tests required at intervals specified by class (typically every 5 years).

2. Permanent SWL marking: Every lifting appliance must be permanently and legibly marked with its Safe Working Load (SWL) in tonnes. The SWL must be visible to the operator at the control position. Variable SWL (e.g. crane at different radii) must show the SWL at each radius on a clearly readable load chart. Faded, damaged, or missing SWL markings are now a statutory deficiency under SOLAS.

3. Impact on Safety Construction Certificate: This is the key change. Mechanical failure of a crane now directly impacts the vessel's statutory Safety Construction Certificate (the main SOLAS certificate). A crane found to be defective, not load-tested, or with missing SWL markings can now trigger a condition of class and a deficiency on the Safety Construction Certificate — potentially preventing the ship from sailing until rectified. Previously, a crane defect was a class-only matter that did not directly affect statutory certificates.
Background — Why This Change Was Made

Before 2026, shipboard cranes and winches were regulated by a fragmented framework: classification society rules (e.g. Lloyd's Register, DNV crane rules), ILO Convention 152 (Occupational Safety and Health in Dock Work), and national port regulations. Ships could have cranes that were never load-tested to a unified standard, with SWL markings applied by the manufacturer only and never re-verified. Several crane collapses and falls resulting in crew fatalities prompted IMO to bring lifting appliances directly under SOLAS, giving port state control (PSC) officers the authority to detain ships where lifting appliances are not certified.
ETO Responsibilities Under SOLAS II-1/3-13
1. Maintain all electrical systems of lifting appliances in safe and serviceable condition — motor, VFD/controller, limit switches, EM brake, overload protection, pendant controls.
2. Verify SWL markings are legible at each crane and at the ER overhead crane — report to C/E if markings are faded or damaged. This is now a SOLAS statutory requirement.
3. Ensure overload limit switch (hoist cut-out at SWL) is functional — this is the primary electronic safety preventing overloading. Test annually. Calibrate to correct SWL value if load cell-based.
4. Ensure load test certificate is onboard, current, and available for PSC inspection. Flag to C/E and Master if certificate is approaching expiry (typically 5-year cycle).
SOLAS II-1/3-13 — Quick Revision Summary

Effective: 1 January 2026. Covers: all lifting appliances and anchor handling winches. Requirements: (1) Load-tested to IMO guidelines (125% SWL proof load). (2) Permanently marked with SWL — legible at control position. (3) Certificate of test onboard. Key change: crane defect now directly impacts Safety Construction Certificate — a SOLAS statutory certificate. PSC can now detain ship for crane defects. ETO: maintain electrical systems, verify SWL markings, ensure overload switches calibrated, flag certificate expiry to C/E.
1.1 Why Ships Corrode — The Electrochemical Cell

A ship's steel hull in seawater forms a natural electrochemical galvanic cell because seawater is an excellent electrolyte (salt concentration ~3.5%, conductivity ~50 mS/cm). Different areas of the hull surface have slightly different electrical potentials due to variations in steel grain structure, mill scale, weld joints, stress concentrations, and surface contamination. The more negative (active) area becomes the anode and corrodes, while the more positive (noble) area becomes the cathode and is protected. Without intervention, this causes accelerated corrosion at anodic areas, thinning the hull plating, pitting around welds, and degrading the propeller and rudder.

The corrosion reaction at the anode is: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (iron dissolves into solution). At the cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (oxygen reduction). The electrons released at the anode travel through the metal to the cathode, while ionic current flows through the seawater. This sets up a self-sustaining corrosion circuit that progressively destroys the hull. The rate of corrosion depends on the conductivity of the electrolyte, the potential difference between anodic and cathodic areas, temperature, and dissolved oxygen content.
1.2 Two Methods of Cathodic Protection

Cathodic protection works by making the entire hull surface act as a cathode by supplying electrons externally, stopping the anodic dissolution reaction. There are two methods: sacrificial anode method (passive, galvanic) and impressed current cathodic protection (ICCP, active). Both methods force the hull potential to a negative value (typically –800 mV to –1050 mV relative to Ag/AgCl reference electrode) where steel corrosion effectively stops. The choice between methods depends on vessel size, dry dock interval, trade route, and maintenance capability.
2.1 Main Components of ICCP System

The ICCP (Impressed Current Cathodic Protection) system consists of four main components working as a closed-loop control system: the power supply/controller unit, the impressed current anodes, the reference electrodes, and the connecting cables. The controller unit is typically located in the engine control room or electrical panel room and contains a transformer-rectifier that converts ship's AC supply to adjustable DC current. It continuously monitors the hull potential via reference electrodes and automatically adjusts the DC output to maintain the hull at the set protection potential.

The system operates on the principle that by forcing the hull to act as a cathode (by making it more negative), the anodic dissolution reaction (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) is suppressed. The controller supplies DC current from the external power supply through the cables to the anodes, which are mounted flush with the hull below the waterline. Current flows from the anodes through the seawater to the hull, converting the hull into a cathode. The reference electrodes continuously measure the hull-to-seawater potential and feed this information back to the controller, which adjusts the output to maintain the setpoint.
2.2 Reference Electrode — The Heart of ICCP

The reference electrode is the most critical sensing element in the ICCP system. It measures the electrochemical potential between the hull (cathode) and seawater, providing continuous feedback to the controller. Without an accurate reference electrode, the controller cannot determine whether the hull is under-protected (corrosion occurring) or over-protected (risk of hydrogen embrittlement and paint damage). The reference electrode must have a stable, predictable potential that does not change with temperature, salinity, or current flow — this is called a non-polarisable reference electrode.

The Ag/AgCl (Silver/Silver Chloride) reference electrode is the most commonly used type because it is stable in seawater, has a well-defined potential of +0.222 V vs. Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and has a long service life. It consists of a silver wire coated with silver chloride, immersed in a gel electrolyte and sealed in a protective housing with a porous ceramic junction allowing ion exchange with seawater. The zinc reference electrode is simpler and less expensive but less stable than Ag/AgCl. Reference electrodes are replaced at every dry dock interval because the gel electrolyte becomes depleted and the porous junction may become contaminated, leading to potential drift and inaccurate control.
3.1 Automatic Control Loop Operation

The ICCP system works as a closed-loop automatic control system. The reference electrode continuously measures the hull-to-seawater potential (typically in the range –700 mV to –1100 mV vs Ag/AgCl). This measured potential is compared with the setpoint (typically –850 mV Ag/AgCl) in the controller. If the measured potential is more positive than –850 mV (under-protection), the controller increases the DC output current, driving more current through the anodes into the seawater and to the hull, making the hull more negative (cathodic). If the measured potential is more negative than –850 mV (approaching over-protection), the controller reduces the output.

This feedback mechanism ensures that despite changes in seawater temperature, salinity, vessel speed, fouling conditions, and paint degradation, the hull potential is continuously maintained within the protective range. The system includes alarms for high current output (indicating large areas of paint breakdown), low output (indicating possible anode circuit fault), and deviation from protection potential. The controller also has an automatic/manual mode — manual is used during dry dock or when specific areas are being inspected.

The relationship between seawater temperature and ICCP parameters is an important cross-examination topic. As seawater temperature increases (e.g., sailing from temperate European waters to tropical Indian Ocean), the electrical conductivity of seawater increases significantly — this is because ion mobility (Na⁺, Cl⁻) increases with temperature. Higher conductivity means lower resistance in the ionic path from anodes through seawater to the hull. For the same controller setpoint (–850 mV), a lower resistance path means less voltage is required to drive the same current — therefore the ICCP output voltage decreases in warmer waters.

Conversely, in cold waters (Arctic routes, winter North Atlantic), seawater conductivity decreases, increasing the ionic path resistance. The controller must increase output voltage to maintain the required protection current, so the ICCP output voltage increases in cold waters. Additionally, in warm tropical waters the cathodic reaction rate increases (higher temperature accelerates electrochemical reactions), so a slightly higher current may be needed to maintain the same protection potential. The ETO should monitor these trends on the ICCP panel and understand that a gradual change in output voltage does not necessarily indicate a fault — it may simply reflect the change in operating environment. The seawater temperature effect also means that the controller setpoint may need to be reviewed when the vessel changes trading routes.
5.1 Stray Current Corrosion Explained

Stray current corrosion is corrosion caused by electrical current flowing through an unintended path in the structure. In the context of a ship berthed at port with ICCP running, the impressed DC current can leak from the hull into the mooring lines (steel wire ropes or chains), the gangway, shore power cables, and through the seawater into the jetty steel piling. When this current exits any metallic component back into the seawater (completing the circuit), it causes accelerated corrosion at the exit point. The rate of stray current corrosion can be extremely rapid — 10 amps of stray DC current can dissolve approximately 10 kg of steel per year.

Shore power connections are particularly problematic because the shore earth is connected to the ship's hull at the shore supply plug, effectively linking the ICCP circuit to the entire shore electrical earthing system. This creates unpredictable current paths. To prevent stray current damage in port, the ship's SMS requires: ICCP to be switched off before arriving alongside; an insulating flange or galvanic isolator to be fitted in the shore earth conductor; and the ship to maintain an earthing log showing ICCP status. Some modern ports have impressed current cathodic protection systems of their own (for dock structures) which can interfere with the ship's ICCP — an additional reason to isolate while alongside.
5.2 Electrical Bonding

Electrical bonding is the practice of connecting all metallic structures on the ship with low-resistance copper conductors to ensure they are at the same electrical potential. This serves two purposes in the context of cathodic protection: preventing bimetallic corrosion between dissimilar metals, and ensuring that the ICCP system can protect all metallic hull appendages uniformly. Without bonding, the bronze propeller (more noble, +0.3 V vs SHE) and the steel hull (less noble, –0.5 V vs SHE) would form a large galvanic cell with the seawater as electrolyte, causing rapid corrosion of the hull steel adjacent to the propeller.

The intermediate shaft earthing brush (or shaft bonding) connects the propeller shaft to the hull, ensuring the propeller is at the same potential as the hull and is included in the ICCP circuit. Similarly, the rudder stock is bonded to the hull using flexible copper jumper cables to ensure the rudder receives cathodic protection. If these bonds are broken — for example, if the shaft brush is worn out, or the rudder jumper cable is corroded — these components become cathodically isolated and may corrode rapidly, particularly the propeller boss area and rudder pintles. This is why the shaft earthing resistance is checked regularly (should be < 1 Ω) and the rudder bonding cables are inspected at each dry dock.

MGPS (Marine Growth Prevention System) is an electrochemical system that prevents marine biological growth (barnacles, mussels, algae, tubeworms) inside sea chests, sea water pipe systems, and heat exchanger inlet/outlet pipework. Without MGPS, biological fouling inside cooling water systems causes progressive blockage of pipes, heat exchanger tubes, and sea strainers, leading to reduced cooling efficiency, increased pump power consumption, and potential overheating of machinery. In port and in warm tropical waters, bio-fouling can block sea chest gratings within days.

MGPS works by generating biocidal ions (copper ions Cu²⁺ and sometimes aluminium ions Al³⁺) through electrolytic action. Low-voltage DC current (typically 0.5–4V, 0.5–4A per anode) is passed between copper anodes (mounted in the sea chest or inlet piping) and the surrounding seawater/pipework (which acts as cathode). The copper anode slowly dissolves, releasing Cu²⁺ ions into the seawater at a controlled concentration of approximately 2 ppb (parts per billion). This low concentration of copper ions is sufficient to be toxic to marine organisms at the larval stage, preventing their attachment and growth, but is too low to be harmful to the vessel's materials or the wider marine environment. Aluminium anodes are sometimes added alongside copper anodes — the Al³⁺ ions create an anti-fouling coating on the copper heat exchanger tubes, providing additional protection.

ICCP system maintenance in dry dock is a critical topic asked by multiple surveyors. In dry dock, the ICCP must be switched off because the hull is out of water and there is no seawater electrolyte for the system to function — running the ICCP in dry dock would cause the anodes to operate in air, leading to potential high-voltage arcing and possible fire hazard near flammable coatings. The complete dry dock ICCP inspection and maintenance programme covers: anode inspection and possible replacement, reference electrode replacement, cable and junction box inspection, controller calibration and testing, and hull preparation for re-coating.

The concept of protection potential is fundamental to ICCP operation and is heavily tested. Steel is protected from corrosion when its electrochemical potential vs. Ag/AgCl reference electrode is maintained between –800 mV and –1050 mV. The standard accepted criterion from NACE RP0176 and DNV class rules is –800 mV (Ag/AgCl) as the minimum protection potential — below this value (more negative), protection is achieved. The typical operating setpoint on most ships is –850 mV (Ag/AgCl), giving a safety margin above the minimum. The upper limit (most negative value allowed) is –1100 mV (Ag/AgCl) to prevent over-protection.

Over-protection occurs when the hull potential is driven more negative than –1100 mV. At these very negative potentials, the cathodic reaction produces hydrogen gas at the hull surface (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂). This causes two problems: first, hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steels used in propeller shafts, anchors, and mooring fittings; and second, cathodic disbondment — the hydrogen gas and alkaline conditions (pH up to 12–14 at the hull surface) destroy the adhesion of the hull paint coating, causing it to blister and peel away from the steel. This defeats the purpose of the cathodic protection system. Under-protection (less negative than –800 mV) simply means corrosion continues — the ICCP is not providing sufficient current to suppress the anodic dissolution reaction.

ICCP fault-finding is a practical topic that Deswal and Sanjib ask in depth. The most common faults are: reference electrode failure (causing incorrect potential display and loss of auto-control), anode circuit open circuit (no current output despite high voltage), and controller faults (rectifier failure, control card fault). Understanding the circuit helps diagnose faults systematically: the power circuit runs from ship's AC supply → ICCP transformer-rectifier → DC positive to anodes → seawater → hull → DC negative back to controller. The sensing circuit runs from reference electrode → controller (measures potential). A fault in either circuit has specific symptoms.
1.1 What is Power Factor?

Power factor (PF) is defined as the ratio of Active Power (KW) to Apparent Power (KVA) in an AC circuit. It is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1 (or expressed as a percentage), representing how efficiently electrical power is being converted into useful mechanical or thermal work. Mathematically: PF = KW / KVA = cos φ, where φ is the phase angle between the voltage and current waveforms. A power factor of 1.0 (unity) means all the apparent power drawn from the supply is being converted to useful work — there is no reactive component. A power factor of 0.8 lagging means only 80% of the apparent power is doing useful work; the remaining 20% (the KVAR component) oscillates back and forth between the source and the load without doing any net work.

On ships, the power factor is almost always lagging because the predominant loads are induction motors (pumps, fans, compressors, cargo winches, cranes) which are inherently inductive — their current lags the voltage by an angle φ. Typical ship power factor at sea: 0.7–0.85 lagging. In port with reduced motor load, PF may be even lower — more inductive magnetising currents proportionally. Typical ship PF is 0.8 lagging, and this is the standard answer surveyors expect, though the actual value depends on the vessel's loading condition and which machinery is running.
1.2 The Power Triangle — KW, KVA, KVAR

The relationship between the three power quantities forms a right-angled triangle called the power triangle. Apparent Power (KVA, hypotenuse) is the total power supplied by the generator. Active Power (KW, adjacent side) is the useful power converted to mechanical work or heat. Reactive Power (KVAR, opposite side) is the magnetising power that creates and collapses magnetic fields in inductive loads — it does no net work but must still be supplied by the generator and transported through cables. The Pythagorean relationship is: KVA² = KW² + KVAR². The angle φ between KVA and KW is the power factor angle: PF = cos φ.

Reactive power (KVAR) has real consequences onboard: it increases the current drawn from the generator for the same useful KW output, causing higher copper losses (I²R losses) in cables and windings, reduced voltage at the motor terminals, overloading of generators and cables, and reduced effective generator capacity. For example, a 1000 KVA generator at PF 0.8 lagging can only supply 800 KW of useful power; at PF 1.0 it could supply the full 1000 KW from the same machine — improving PF therefore increases effective generator capacity.
2.1 What is Droop and Why is it Necessary?

Droop is an intentional speed (or voltage) reduction characteristic built into generator control systems to enable stable parallel operation and automatic load sharing between generators. Without droop, two generators running in parallel with identical isochronous (flat, no-droop) governors would be unstable — if one generator picks up even a tiny amount of extra load, its governor would immediately increase fuel to restore speed, causing it to pick up even more load, eventually taking all the load and causing the other generator to motorise. Droop prevents this by making each generator's speed (and therefore frequency) decrease proportionally as its load increases — the generator with more load runs slightly slower, which automatically prevents it from taking further load.

There are two types of droop relevant to parallel generator operation: Governor Droop (speed/frequency droop) which controls active load sharing (KW), and AVR Droop (voltage droop) which controls reactive load sharing (KVAR). These two types work independently and must both be correctly set for stable, equal load sharing. The droop setting is expressed as a percentage: 3–5% droop means that at full load, the generator frequency falls by 3–5% below the no-load frequency setpoint. For a 60 Hz system with 5% droop: no-load frequency = 60 Hz, full-load frequency = 60 × (1 – 0.05) = 57 Hz.
