3.1 Loss of Excitation During Parallel Operation

Loss of excitation (loss of field) in one generator during parallel operation is a serious fault that is heavily tested. Excitation provides the rotor magnetic field which induces EMF in the stator windings. When excitation is lost, the rotor field collapses and the generator can no longer produce its own EMF. However, because it is still synchronised and connected to the busbars (other healthy generator is still running), the generator does not immediately trip — instead, it begins to operate as an induction generator, drawing magnetising current (reactive current, KVAR) from the busbars rather than generating it. This causes the faulty generator to appear to be taking a large leading reactive current (KVAR) from the system, overloading the healthy generator's AVR and potentially causing undervoltage on the whole system.

The sequence of events electrically when excitation is lost: (1) Rotor field collapses — generator terminal voltage starts to fall. (2) AVR detects low terminal voltage and attempts to increase excitation — but the excitation circuit is faulty so it cannot respond. (3) The generator begins absorbing reactive power (KVAR) from the other generator via the busbars. (4) This reactive absorption causes the healthy generator to increase its reactive output to compensate — its AVR increases excitation. (5) The load-sharing balance on reactive load (KVAR) is completely disrupted — the healthy generator may trip on overcurrent or AVR overload. (6) The faulty generator will eventually be detected by the under-excitation protection relay and tripped. On the switchboard, the symptom is: faulty generator's power factor reading goes leading (or near zero), KVAR meter goes reversed/negative, and the healthy generator's current increases. Action: manually trip the faulty generator immediately, increase output of healthy generator, start standby generator if needed.
3.2 Rotating Diode Faults During Parallel Operation

In a brushless alternator, the excitation current is supplied to the rotor through a rotating rectifier assembly (diode bridge) mounted on the rotor shaft. The AC output of the exciter rotor is rectified by these diodes into DC before being fed to the main field winding. Rotating diode faults during parallel operation are a specific examination scenario asked by Sanjib and Vishwanathan.
4.1 Why Poor Power Factor is Harmful

A low power factor has significant negative consequences for the ship's electrical system and must be corrected. When PF is low (e.g., 0.6 lagging), a larger current must be drawn from the generator to supply the same useful KW of power. This higher current causes: increased I²R losses (heating) in cables, transformers, and generator windings; reduced terminal voltage at the load end (increased voltage drop); generators reaching their KVA limit before their KW limit (the machine is full on current even though useful KW output is low); and increased fuel consumption by the prime mover to drive the generator at higher reactive current. Additionally, generators must be rated at a higher KVA for the same useful KW output. Improving the power factor to 0.85 or above reduces current for the same KW, directly reducing cable losses, improving voltage regulation, and increasing available generator capacity.
4.2 Synchronous Condenser — Construction, Working & Significance

A synchronous condenser is an overexcited synchronous motor running without any mechanical load — it has no coupling to any driven equipment, just a rotor spinning freely. It is connected directly to the busbars. By varying its excitation using its AVR or field rheostat, the synchronous condenser can be made to generate or absorb reactive power (KVAR). When overexcited (field current above that required for unity PF), it generates leading KVAR, acting like a capacitor bank — this is used to cancel the lagging KVAR drawn by the ship's induction motor loads, thereby improving the overall system power factor. When underexcited, it absorbs leading KVAR — used when a lightly loaded cable has a leading PF due to capacitance.

The key advantage of a synchronous condenser over a static capacitor bank is its continuous, smooth, and controllable output — the KVAR output can be varied from zero to maximum leading or lagging by adjusting the field current. On large ships with significant inductive motor load (cargo ships with many cargo pumps, tankers, bulk carriers), a synchronous condenser is an effective tool for managing reactive power. On Maersk container vessels, reactive power compensation is sometimes achieved through the use of power factor correction transformers or capacitor banks rather than a dedicated synchronous condenser, but the ETO must understand the principle for examination purposes.
5.1 What is Preferential Trip and Why is it Required?

The preferential trip (also called sequential load shedding or load reduction tripping) is a protection system fitted on the main switchboard that automatically disconnects non-essential loads in a predetermined priority sequence when the main generator is overloaded — for example, after a blackout when only one generator has been restored, or when a generator trips unexpectedly and the remaining generator(s) are suddenly asked to carry the full ship's load which may exceed their capacity. The purpose is to prevent the remaining generator from tripping on overcurrent — losing all power would be far more catastrophic than losing some non-essential loads.

Without a preferential trip, if a generator is suddenly overloaded (e.g., after blackout restoration, only one 1000 KW generator running and the ship load is 1500 KW), the generator's overcurrent protection would trip it within seconds, resulting in a second blackout. The preferential trip system detects the overload condition early and automatically disconnects loads starting with the least essential (galley, accommodation HVAC, non-essential pumps) while maintaining power to essential loads (steering gear, navigation lights, communication equipment, fire pumps, emergency lighting). SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 42/43 requires that arrangements be provided to ensure continuity of essential services in an emergency — the preferential trip system is part of this compliance.
6.1 Shore Power Connection — Checks and Issues

Shore power (cold ironing) connection is a topic closely linked to power systems and is asked by Deswal and others. The main electrical checks before connecting shore power are: verify shore voltage matches ship's voltage (440V or 6.6 KV for HV shore connection); verify shore frequency matches ship's frequency (60 Hz ship, 50 Hz shore or vice versa); check shore power cable rating and connection polarity; verify ship's shore connection box is in good condition; ensure ship's generators are in standby mode with ACBs open before shore breaker is closed; verify phase sequence is correct using a phase sequence meter.

The power factor during shore power operation: shore power is AC same as ship's generators, so the same load-PF relationship applies. However, the shore utility charges for reactive power (KVAR) in addition to KW — unlike onboard where the generator owner bears the cost of poor PF internally. This creates an incentive to improve PF while on shore power. Shore power systems typically use high-efficiency frequency converters (for frequency mismatch) or direct connection where shore and ship frequencies are identical.

Form factor is a property of an AC waveform defined as the ratio of its RMS value to its Average value: Form Factor = RMS value / Average value. For a pure sinusoidal waveform, the form factor = π/(2√2) = 1.1107 ≈ 1.11. This value of 1.11 is significant because it appears in the transformer EMF equation and generator design calculations. The RMS value is used for power calculations (represents equivalent DC heating effect), while the average value is what a simple rectifier measures.

The significance of form factor in marine electrical equipment: transformers are designed based on the 1.11 form factor of a sine wave — if the supply has a distorted waveform (due to harmonic pollution from VFDs, converters, non-linear loads), the form factor increases above 1.11, meaning the transformer core flux is higher than designed, increasing iron losses and causing overheating. In HV systems, the form factor is important when specifying transformers and switchgear for shipboard use. Generators rated in KVA: the KVA rating is determined by the product of rated voltage and rated current — both limited by insulation (voltage) and conductor size/cooling (current) — and is independent of load PF. The form factor of 1.11 is used in the EMF equation: E = 4.44 × f × N × Φm (where 4.44 = 4 × 1.11).

A specific scenario asked by Vishwanathan: Two generators have to be paralleled, PF of Generator 1 is 0.8 and PF of Generator 2 is 0.7. What is your action? This tests understanding of reactive load sharing in parallel operation. Before paralleling, each generator's PF refers to the load it was carrying on its own bus. Once paralleled, both generators see the same busbar voltage and the load is shared according to their governor and AVR droop characteristics.

The difference in PF indicates that the two generators have different reactive load (KVAR) characteristics. When paralleled, the generator with lower PF (Generator 2 at 0.7) is supplying proportionally more reactive current (KVAR) than Generator 1 at 0.8. In parallel operation, this will cause Generator 2 to be more heavily loaded on reactive power, with a higher current. The AVR droop settings control how KVAR is shared — to equalise the PF (and therefore KVAR loading) between them, the AVR droop of the generator carrying more reactive load (Gen 2) should be slightly increased, causing it to shed some KVAR to Gen 1, until both generators operate at a similar power factor. Additionally, the ETO should check whether the load itself is the cause — some loads may be connected more to one bus section than the other, causing naturally unequal KVAR distribution.

Reactive Power — Where Does It Go?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, ALL — 'where does reactive power go?' — exact surveyor wording
Reactive power (kVAR) is NOT lost or dissipated as heat. It oscillates between the source and the load at twice the supply frequency.
In an induction motor: kVAR sustains the rotating magnetic field that enables the rotor to develop torque. Without reactive power, no magnetic field, no torque.
In a transformer: kVAR maintains core magnetisation (magnetising current). Core flux is sustained by reactive current.
Returns to source every half cycle — travels back and forth between generator and load. Creates reactive current in cables, loading them without doing useful work (kW).
This is why low PF increases cable/generator/transformer current for the same useful output — leading to overheating and losses.
Answer in one sentence: 'Reactive power goes to the motor to sustain its magnetic field — it is returned to the source every half cycle, not consumed.'
Loss of Excitation in Parallel — Which Trip Activates First?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sanjib, Kamath — very specific cross-question
Sequence when one generator loses excitation while running in parallel:
Step 1: Generator output voltage drops as field collapses.
Step 2: AVR tries to compensate — increases excitation current — but if exciter fails, cannot recover.
Step 3: Generator starts importing reactive power (kVAR) from the busbar (runs like an induction generator).
Step 4: FIRST TRIP: Under-excitation relay (Loss of Field relay / minimum excitation limiter) — detects reactive power absorption and trips ACB.
Step 5: If under-excitation relay fails → reverse KVAR increases → overcurrent on remaining generators → preferential trip may activate.
Answer: Under-excitation relay (Loss of Field relay) activates FIRST.
Synchronous Motor — Why NOT Self-Starting?
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Kamath, Sanjib — always asked with synchronous condenser topic

Reason: At the instant of start, the rotating magnetic field from the stator spins at synchronous speed. The rotor (with DC field) is stationary — it cannot lock onto a field rotating at synchronous speed from standstill.
The field reverses 100 times per second (50Hz) — rotor inertia means it cannot follow. Net average torque = zero. Motor does not start.
Starting methods: (1) Most common — amortisseur/damper windings in rotor slots → motor starts as induction motor → reaches ~95% Ns → DC field applied → rotor pulls into synchronism.
(2) VFD start: Ramp frequency from 0 to rated → rotor can follow slow-rotating field → reaches synchronous speed.
(3) Pony motor: External motor runs synchronous motor to near-synchronous speed → DC field applied.
Kirchhoff's Laws
KCL — Kirchhoff's Current Law: The sum of all currents entering a node equals the sum of all currents leaving. ΣI_in = ΣI_out. Based on conservation of charge.
KVL — Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: The sum of all voltages around any closed loop equals zero. ΣV = 0. Based on conservation of energy.
Application on ships: KCL used for busbar current analysis. KVL used for circuit loop analysis in protection relay settings and voltage drop calculations.
SOLAS Regulation for AVR — Full Detail
SOLAS II-1/Reg 40.3: Automatic Voltage Regulator must maintain voltage within ±2.5% of rated voltage under any load from no-load to full-load.
Transient voltage: Must recover to ±2.5% within 1.5 seconds of sudden full-load pickup or rejection.

Why remove AVR during IR test: AVR contains thyristors, transistors, and capacitors sensitive to DC test voltage. Megger at 500V–1000V DC can damage semiconductor junctions permanently. Also: AVR may inject test voltage back into winding, giving false IR reading.
1.1 Cable Construction — Layers from Inside Out

A marine cable is a multi-layer assembly, and the ETO must be able to name every layer from the innermost conductor outward. The layers serve distinct functions: electrical conduction, insulation, filling/bedding, mechanical protection, and outer sheathing. Understanding each layer is necessary both for correct cable selection and for answering the examiner's question about 'all layers in a cable.' The standard shipboard power cable construction from inside to outside is: Conductor → Conductor Screen (HV only) → Insulation → Insulation Screen (HV only) → Metallic Screen/Tape (HV only) → Bedding/Inner Sheath → Armour → Outer Sheath.

The conductor is typically stranded copper (flexible, low resistance), though aluminium conductors are used in shore installations but rarely on ships due to corrosion concerns. The insulation material is the most critical layer — it must withstand the operating voltage, temperature, mechanical stress, and chemical environment. For LV (up to 1.1 kV) power cables, PVC (Polyvinyl Chloride) or XLPE (Cross-Linked Polyethylene) is used. For HV cables (3.3 kV, 6.6 kV, 11 kV), XLPE or EPR (Ethylene Propylene Rubber) is the standard because they have far superior dielectric strength and thermal performance compared to PVC. The armour provides mechanical protection against crushing, rodents, and tension — SWA (Steel Wire Armour) or STA (Steel Tape Armour) are standard. The outer sheath protects all inner layers from chemical, UV, and physical damage.

Ordering a cable correctly is a common practical question across all three question banks and is asked by Sanjib, Vishwanathan, and Kamath. The ETO must know every specification parameter required to ensure the correct cable is supplied. An incorrect cable — wrong voltage rating, conductor size, or fire performance — could be a safety hazard or may not meet class approval. The cable order must specify sufficient technical information so that the supplier can provide an IEC 60092-compliant cable without ambiguity.
3.1 Megger — Construction and Working Principle

The megger (insulation resistance tester) is an instrument that applies a high DC voltage across the insulation under test and measures the very small leakage current that flows through it, displaying the ratio as resistance in Megohms (MΩ). The traditional hand-cranked (analogue) megger consists of three coils: the pressure coil (voltage coil), the deflecting coil (current coil), and the crossing coil — all mounted on a single spindle between the poles of a permanent magnet. The hand generator produces high DC voltage (500V, 1000V, or 2500V depending on the type). The deflection of the pointer depends on the ratio of currents in the two coils, which corresponds to the insulation resistance. Modern digital meggars are electronic instruments generating high DC voltage via a DC/DC converter, with digital display of resistance in MΩ or GΩ.

The key reason a megger uses high DC voltage for IR testing — rather than AC or low DC — is that insulation resistance is extremely high (hundreds of MΩ for good insulation), meaning the leakage current is extremely small (microamperes). A high test voltage is necessary to drive a measurable current through this very high resistance (by Ohm's law: I = V/R — for R = 100 MΩ, at 500V: I = 5 µA). A standard multimeter applies only a few volts DC and cannot drive sufficient current through the insulation to measure it accurately. Furthermore, high voltage testing stresses the insulation in a way that reveals weak spots, voids, moisture absorption, and tracking paths that may not be detectable at low voltages — this is why a megger is specifically designed for insulation testing and a voltmeter or multimeter cannot substitute for it.

The Polarisation Index (PI) test is an advanced insulation diagnostic test that gives more information about the condition of insulation than a simple one-minute IR test. It is specifically important for HV cables and large machine windings where the insulation volume is large and the capacitive and absorptive charging characteristics are significant. The PI is defined as the ratio of the insulation resistance measured at 10 minutes to the resistance measured at 1 minute, using the same applied test voltage throughout: PI = IR(10 min) / IR(1 min).

The reason for taking a 10-minute reading is rooted in the physics of dielectric polarisation. When a DC voltage is applied to insulation, three currents flow simultaneously: capacitance charging current (decays very quickly within seconds), dielectric absorption current (decays over 10 minutes as molecular dipoles align in the electric field — this is the polarisation process), and conductive leakage current (remains constant, proportional to moisture and contamination). After 10 minutes, the capacitance charging current and most of the absorption current have decayed, leaving predominantly the leakage (conductive) current. In good, dry insulation, the 10-minute reading is significantly higher than the 1-minute reading (PI > 2). In contaminated or moisture-absorbed insulation, the leakage current dominates from the start and the resistance stays flat — PI ≈ 1.

Insulation class (also called thermal class) is an IEC/NEMA standardised classification of electrical insulation materials based on the maximum continuous operating temperature they can withstand without unacceptable deterioration in service life. The insulation class determines the maximum allowable winding temperature in a motor or generator, which in turn determines the size (physical and electrical) of the machine and its duty rating. If insulation is operated above its class temperature, its life is halved for every 10°C excess — this is the Arrhenius 10°C rule for insulation life.

The choice of earthing system for a ship's electrical distribution is a fundamental design decision with safety and operational implications. Ships use an Insulated (IT) neutral system as the standard for 440V power distribution, unlike shore installations which use a solidly earthed (TN) neutral. Understanding the advantages of the insulated neutral system is heavily tested across all question banks.

In an insulated neutral system, the generator neutral point is not connected to earth — it is completely floating (insulated from hull). In an earthed neutral system (as used on HV systems and some shore supplies), the neutral is connected directly to earth or through a Neutral Earthing Resistor (NER). On ships, the insulated neutral is standard for LV 440V distribution. An insulation monitoring device (earth fault indicator, typically measuring 25–50 kΩ resistance between neutral and earth) is connected to continuously monitor the insulation resistance of the entire system to earth and alarm if it falls below the set threshold.

Cables must frequently pass through watertight bulkheads and fire-rated decks — an improper penetration would defeat the purpose of the watertight subdivision, potentially allowing water ingress or fire spread. SOLAS requires that any penetration through a watertight bulkhead maintains the watertight integrity of the bulkhead to the same standard as the bulkhead itself. This is heavily tested and candidates are sometimes asked to draw a diagram.

The busbar is the main copper conductor assembly in the main switchboard to which all generator ACBs and load feeders connect. Busbar IR testing and hotspot detection are practical topics asked in the question banks. The busbar is made of solid copper bars or copper tube sections, plated with tin or silver to reduce contact resistance at joints. Busbars are supported on insulated standoffs (cast-resin insulators) at regular intervals.

When megger voltage is applied, three types of current flow through insulation:
1. Capacitive charging current: Decays within first few seconds. Due to cable capacitance charging up.
2. Absorption current: Decays over minutes. Due to dielectric polarisation of insulation molecules aligning with the electric field.

1.1 RADAR — Working Principle

RADAR (Radio Detection And Ranging) detects objects by transmitting short pulses of high-frequency radio energy (microwave) from a rotating antenna and receiving the echoes reflected back from targets. The time taken for the pulse to travel to the target and return (two-way travel time, t) is used to calculate the range: Range = (c × t) / 2, where c = speed of light = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The bearing of the target is determined by the orientation of the antenna at the moment of reception. The rotating antenna sweeps 360° continuously, building up a picture of all surrounding targets on the Plan Position Indicator (PPI) display. The minimum range of RADAR is limited by the pulse length — the transmitter must have finished transmitting before the echo arrives back, so very close targets cannot be detected during transmission.

Two types of RADAR are fitted on ships as required by SOLAS: X-band RADAR and S-band RADAR. X-band operates at 9 GHz (wavelength 3 cm) and gives high resolution with good target discrimination — preferred for navigation in confined waters, collision avoidance, and detecting small targets in calm weather. S-band operates at 3 GHz (wavelength 10 cm) and penetrates rain, fog, and heavy precipitation better than X-band due to its longer wavelength (less attenuation in rain) — preferred for long-range detection and bad weather use. SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires vessels >300 GT to carry two independent RADAR systems, one of which must have ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid) capability.
1.2 Magnetron — Working Principle

The magnetron is the high-power microwave transmitting tube at the heart of a marine RADAR. It is a vacuum tube oscillator that generates microwave energy at the RADAR frequency (9 GHz for X-band, 3 GHz for S-band) by the interaction of electrons with a strong magnetic field. The magnetron consists of a central cylindrical cathode (thermionic emitter) surrounded by a cylindrical anode block with resonant cavities machined into it. A strong axial magnetic field (provided by permanent magnets surrounding the tube) causes the electrons emitted from the cathode to travel in curved paths around the cathode rather than straight to the anode. As these spiralling electrons pass the openings of the resonant cavities in the anode, they induce oscillations in the cavities at the resonant frequency — the microwave energy is extracted from one of these cavities via a coupling loop connected to the waveguide.

The magnetron is a pulse device — it generates very high power (typically 10–50 kW peak power) for extremely short durations (0.05–1 µs pulse width) at a repetition rate of typically 500–3000 pulses per second. Between pulses the magnetron is off, allowing the receiver to detect reflected echoes. The T/R (Transmit/Receive) cell or duplexer switches the antenna connection between the transmitter (magnetron) and receiver — during transmission it disconnects the sensitive receiver to protect it from the high transmit power, and during reception it disconnects the transmitter and connects the receiver. Magnetrons have a finite life (typically 1000–3000 hours) and must be replaced when output power degrades. The ETO should carry a spare magnetron.
2.1 What is GMDSS and Its Purpose

GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) is an internationally agreed system using satellite and terrestrial radio communications to ensure that distress alerts and maritime safety information reach shore rescue co-ordination centres (RCCs) and nearby ships anywhere in the world. It is mandated by SOLAS Chapter IV for vessels on international voyages. GMDSS replaced the old Morse code distress system in 1999. The system is based on the concept of sea areas — the radio equipment required on a ship depends on which sea areas it operates in, because different equipment has different range capabilities.

The four GMDSS sea areas are defined by the coverage of terrestrial VHF and MF/HF radio communications combined with satellite coverage. Sea Area A1 is within VHF range (20–50 nm) of a shore-based GMDSS coast station. Sea Area A2 is within MF range (~150 nm) of a shore station, excluding A1. Sea Area A3 covers the area between 70°N and 70°S latitude (most of the globe's sea area) served by INMARSAT geostationary satellites. Sea Area A4 is the remaining polar areas not covered by INMARSAT (above 70°N and below 70°S) — served by EPIRB and HF radio.
2.2 GMDSS Battery — SOLAS Regulations

The GMDSS battery is a critical component — it must maintain all GMDSS equipment operational for the required duration without any other power source. SOLAS Chapter IV Regulation 13 specifies the battery requirements for GMDSS equipment. The battery must be of sufficient capacity to operate the radio installations for a minimum of 1 hour, or 6 hours for vessels making international voyages, after total loss of ship's main power and emergency power. The GMDSS battery is typically a sealed lead-acid battery or NiCd battery rated at 200 Ah (200 ampere-hours), designed to supply the GMDSS equipment at 24V DC.

The battery is kept permanently on trickle charge from the ship's electrical supply (via a dedicated charger unit). A battery load test is required every 12 months — the test involves discharging the battery against the actual GMDSS equipment load for the specified minimum duration (1 or 6 hours) and verifying that the terminal voltage remains above the minimum specified value at the end of the test. The ETO is responsible for the battery maintenance: checking electrolyte levels (for vented lead-acid types), checking terminal connections for corrosion, recording battery specific gravity or open-circuit voltage, and performing the annual load test. The GMDSS log must record all tests.

EPIRB and SART are among the most commonly asked topics in MMD orals from the Deswal bank and Mumbai question bank. The examiner tests whether the candidate knows exact frequencies, how many are required, where they are located, and critically the difference between the two devices.
3.1 EPIRB — Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon

The EPIRB is a self-contained battery-powered radio transmitter that, when activated, transmits a coded distress signal on 406 MHz to the COSPAS-SARSAT network of polar-orbiting and geostationary satellites. The signal contains the ship's unique 15-digit hexadecimal identification code (registered to the vessel) and, if a GPS receiver is incorporated (GPS-EPIRB), the ship's precise position. The COSPAS-SARSAT satellites relay the distress signal to a Local User Terminal (LUT) on the ground, which computes or receives the position and forwards the alert to the Mission Control Centre (MCC) and then to the Rescue Co-ordination Centre (RCC) responsible for that area. The EPIRB also transmits on 121.5 MHz (homing frequency) — search and rescue aircraft and vessels use a 121.5 MHz receiver to home in on the EPIRB once in the general search area.

The EPIRB is fitted in a hydrostatic release bracket (HRU — Hydrostatic Release Unit) on the bridge wing or upper deck. The HRU is designed to release the EPIRB bracket automatically when submerged to a depth of 1–4 metres — allowing the EPIRB to float free and self-activate if the ship sinks rapidly without time for manual release. SOLAS Chapter III Regulation 6 requires one Category I (automatic float-free) EPIRB for all passenger ships and cargo ships >300 GT on international voyages. The EPIRB battery must be replaced when it reaches its expiry date (typically 5 years) or after any activation. The EPIRB must be tested monthly using the self-test function and registered with the national maritime authority.
3.2 SART — Search and Rescue Transponder

The SART (Search and Rescue Radar Transponder) is a survival craft locating device that operates at 9 GHz — the same frequency as X-band RADAR. It is a passive device carried on survival craft (lifeboats, liferafts) that remains silent until it receives a 9 GHz RADAR pulse from a searching vessel or aircraft. When triggered, it responds by transmitting a series of 12 pulses on the same frequency, creating a distinctive 12-dot line pattern on the searching vessel's X-band RADAR PPI display, extending radially from the SART's position. The SART can respond to a ship's RADAR at a range of approximately 5 nautical miles and to an aircraft's RADAR at approximately 10 nautical miles. The SART also has a visual indicator (flashing LED) and audible alarm to alert survivors when it is being interrogated by a RADAR — this confirms that a ship or aircraft is searching and approaching.

The Doppler speed log is the primary speed measurement instrument onboard, providing both speed through water and speed over ground. It is asked in virtually every Deswal oral and is a favourite cross-question topic. The fundamental principle is the Doppler Effect — the apparent change in frequency of a wave when the source and observer are in relative motion.

The Doppler Effect states: when a wave source moves towards an observer, the received frequency is higher than the transmitted frequency (compression of wavelengths). When the source moves away, the received frequency is lower (stretching of wavelengths). Mathematically: f_received = f_transmitted × (c ± v_observer) / (c ∓ v_source), where c is the wave propagation speed and v is the velocity. For a ship's Doppler log: the transducer transmits an acoustic pulse at a fixed frequency (typically 100 kHz to 300 kHz ultrasonic) directed at an angle to the ship's bottom towards the seabed (or water layer). The pulse reflects off the seabed (bottom tracking mode — gives speed over ground) or off a layer of water below the keel (water tracking mode — gives speed through water). The reflected signal has a different frequency due to the ship's motion — the frequency shift (Doppler shift, Δf) is proportional to the ship's speed component along the beam direction: Δf = 2 × f_transmitted × v × cos θ / c, where θ is the beam angle from the vertical and v is the ship's speed. The processor computes speed from the measured frequency shift.

The echo sounder (depth sounder) measures the depth of water below the keel by transmitting a short acoustic pulse vertically downward and measuring the time for the echo to return from the seabed. Depth = (c × t) / 2, where c = speed of sound in seawater (~1500 m/s for standard conditions) and t = two-way travel time. The echo sounder uses the piezoelectric effect for both transmission and reception — the same transducer (or a separate pair of transducers) performs both functions. Operating frequency: typically 15–50 kHz for shallow water (high resolution), or 3–12 kHz for deep water (greater penetration depth). SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires an echo sounder on all ships >300 GT on international voyages.

The gyrocompass is an essential navigation instrument that indicates True North (unlike a magnetic compass which points to Magnetic North). It uses the properties of a spinning gyroscope — gyroscopic inertia and precession — combined with the Earth's rotation to seek and settle on the meridian (True North direction). The gyrocompass is an electrical instrument driven by an electric motor, making it within the ETO's maintenance scope. SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19 requires a gyrocompass on vessels >500 GT.

Navigational lights are required by COLREG (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea) and their electrical aspects — wattage, circuit design, failure detection, and survey preparation — are the ETO's responsibility. SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 22 and COLREG Annex I specify the technical requirements for navigational lights.

Doppler Speed Log — Working Principle
Transmits sound pulses at 600 kHz–1.2 MHz at an angle (typically 25–60°) to the sea bottom or water mass.
Reflected signal has a frequency shift (Doppler shift) proportional to ship's speed.
Doppler formula: Δf = 2f × v × cos(θ) / c. Where v = ship speed, θ = beam angle, c = speed of sound in water (~1500 m/s).
Two modes: Bottom-track (most accurate, reflects off seabed), Water-track (reflects off water layers — used in deep water).
ETO maintenance: Keep transducer face clean (barnacles reduce signal). Check transducer seal integrity. Calibrate against GPS-measured speed.
Echo Sounder — Working Principle
Piezoelectric transducer on keel emits ultrasonic pulse (200 kHz typical for shallow, 50 kHz for deep water).
Pulse reflects off seabed and returns to transducer.
Depth = (speed of sound × transit time) / 2. Speed of sound in water ≈ 1500 m/s (varies with salinity and temperature).
ETO maintenance: Check transducer condition (no fouling), calibrate against lead line in known depth. Check paper/display unit.

Background — Why GMDSS Was Modernised

The original GMDSS framework (SOLAS Chapter IV) was adopted in 1988 and became fully mandatory in 1999. It was designed around the Inmarsat GEO satellite system — the only option at the time. By 2020, new Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations like Iridium offered superior coverage especially in polar regions, while legacy systems like NBDP telex were used in <1% of real distress communications. IMO Resolution MSC.496(105) adopted the modernisation package, effective 1 January 2024.
Change 1 — RMSS Replaces "Inmarsat" — End of Monopoly
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: According to the updated SOLAS Chapter IV (2024), Inmarsat is no longer the ONLY approved satellite provider.
OLD regulation: SOLAS specifically named Inmarsat as the required satellite service for Sea Areas A3 and A4.
NEW regulation (from 1 January 2024): "Inmarsat" is removed from SOLAS Chapter IV. It is replaced by the term "Recognised Mobile Satellite Service" (RMSS).
RMSS = a satellite communication service formally recognised by IMO that meets all GMDSS requirements — distress alerting, distress traffic, and maritime safety information (MSI) broadcasts.
Iridium is now a recognised RMSS alongside Inmarsat. Iridium advantage: true polar coverage (LEO — no gap above 70°N/S). Inmarsat GEO satellites have limited or no coverage at high latitudes.
Practical result: Ships can equip with Iridium terminals instead of Inmarsat to comply with GMDSS for Sea Areas A3 and A4. The choice of RMSS provider is now the operator's decision.

Exam answer: "Since 1 January 2024, GMDSS uses the term RMSS — Recognised Mobile Satellite Service. Both Inmarsat and Iridium are approved. Ships are no longer required to carry Inmarsat specifically."
Change 2 — NBDP No Longer Mandatory (New Regulation)
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: According to the 2024 update, NBDP telegraphy is NO LONGER a mandatory GMDSS requirement.
OLD: NBDP (Narrow Band Direct Printing / Telex-over-Radio / SITOR) was mandatory for Sea Areas A3 and A4 — required for distress and safety text communications on MF/HF.
NEW (from 1 January 2024): NBDP is removed as a mandatory carriage and performance standard under SOLAS Chapter IV.
Reason: NBDP was used in fewer than 1% of all GMDSS distress communications. Modern DSC and satellite voice/data make it redundant.
What replaces it: MF/HF DSC (Digital Selective Calling on 2187.5 kHz) remains mandatory. RMSS satellite communication fulfils the text/data communication need.
ETO implication: Ships no longer need to maintain NBDP functionality as a GMDSS compliance item. Surveyor will not check for NBDP operation from 2024 onwards.
Note: Many MF/HF radios still have NBDP as a software feature — it is simply no longer mandatory to use or certify it.
Change 3 — VHF-EPIRB No Longer Accepted (New Regulation)
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: According to the 2024 update, VHF-EPIRBs are no longer accepted for ANY sea area — even A1.
OLD: VHF-EPIRB (operating on VHF Channel 70 DSC) was an accepted alternative for ships trading exclusively in Sea Area A1.
NEW (from 1 January 2024): VHF-EPIRBs are no longer accepted as GMDSS-compliant EPIRBs for any sea area.
All ships (including A1 only) must now carry a 406 MHz Cospas-Sarsat satellite EPIRB — or an RMSS-connected equivalent.
Reason: VHF-EPIRBs depended on local coastal VHF coverage — not reliable in all A1 areas. 406 MHz satellite EPIRBs provide global coverage with GPS position to rescue authorities.
ETO action: Check ship's EPIRB type. Verify it is 406 MHz. Check registration in national database is current. Check battery expiry date and hydrostatic release expiry date.
Summary — Updated GMDSS Equipment Requirements Post-2024
Sea Area A1: VHF DSC, 406 MHz EPIRB (VHF-EPIRB no longer accepted), SART/AIS-SART, NAVTEX
Sea Area A2: All A1 + MF DSC (2187.5 kHz), MF SSB voice, EGC receiver
Sea Area A3: All A2 + RMSS terminal (Inmarsat OR Iridium — operator's choice). OR: HF DSC + HF SSB as alternative. NBDP: no longer mandatory.
Sea Area A4: HF DSC + HF SSB mandatory. RMSS if available. NBDP: no longer mandatory.

1.1 Thermocouple — Seebeck Effect

A thermocouple is a temperature sensor consisting of two dissimilar metals joined at one end (the hot junction or measuring junction). When there is a temperature difference between the hot junction and the free ends (cold junction or reference junction), a small EMF (electromotive force) is generated — this is the Seebeck Effect, discovered by Thomas Seebeck in 1821. The Seebeck Effect states: when two dissimilar metals are joined and the two junctions are at different temperatures, an EMF is generated proportional to the temperature difference. The magnitude of the EMF is typically in the millivolt range and is a reproducible, stable function of the temperature difference for a given metal pair.

Common thermocouple types used onboard: Type K (Chromel-Alumel, -200°C to +1350°C) is the most widely used — fitted in main engine exhaust gas temperature monitoring, boiler combustion temperature, incinerator, and turbocharger inlet/outlet. Type J (Iron-Constantan, 0–750°C) for lower temperature applications. Type T (Copper-Constantan, -200°C to +350°C) for refrigeration and cryogenic applications on gas carriers. The cold junction (reference junction) must be kept at a known, stable reference temperature — modern instruments use electronic cold junction compensation (CJC) circuits that measure the reference junction temperature with a separate thermistor or RTD and electronically subtract the effect. Thermocouples are self-powered (generate their own EMF — no external excitation required), which is an advantage for explosion-hazard applications.
1.2 RTD (Resistance Temperature Detector) — PT100

An RTD (Resistance Temperature Detector) is a temperature sensor that exploits the fact that the electrical resistance of a pure metal increases predictably and linearly with temperature. The most common RTD material is platinum — a PT100 RTD has a resistance of exactly 100 Ohms at 0°C and increases approximately 0.385 Ω per °C (for standard IEC 60751 PT100). The operating range is typically -200°C to +850°C. PT stands for Platinum (the sensing element material), and 100 stands for the resistance in Ohms at 0°C. PT200 would be 200 Ω at 0°C — used where higher sensitivity or longer cable runs require higher resistance to minimise lead resistance errors.

RTDs are more accurate and stable than thermocouples, particularly in the range -200°C to +600°C, but they require an external excitation current (typically a small constant current, 1–5 mA) to measure the resistance. The measurement circuit is typically a Wheatstone bridge or a 3-wire/4-wire connection to eliminate lead resistance errors. 3-wire PT100 is standard onboard for most applications (bearing temperatures, cooling water temperatures, exhaust temperatures), and 4-wire PT100 is used where highest accuracy is required (laboratory instruments, custody transfer metering). RTDs are used onboard for: main engine bearing temperatures (shell, top, and bottom), cooling water inlet/outlet temperatures, scavenge air temperature, lubricating oil temperature, boiler feed water temperature, and cargo temperature measurement.

Pressure measurement is central to engine room monitoring — boiler steam pressure, lube oil pressure, fuel oil pressure, starting air pressure, sea chest pressure, hydraulic system pressure, and bilge system pressure. The ETO must understand the working of pressure transducers and how to calibrate them. Questions on DP (Differential Pressure) cell calibration are specifically asked by Deswal and Sanjib.
2.1 Pressure Transducer — Working Principle

A pressure transducer converts fluid pressure into an electrical signal (typically 4–20 mA current loop or 0–10V DC). The sensing element is a strain gauge bonded to a diaphragm or a piezoelectric crystal, or a capacitance-based sensor. When pressure is applied to the diaphragm, it deflects slightly. Strain gauges bonded to the diaphragm measure the strain (deformation) — the resistance of the strain gauge changes proportionally to the strain (resistance increases when stretched, decreases when compressed). This resistance change is measured by a Wheatstone bridge circuit inside the transducer and converted to a 4–20 mA signal proportional to the pressure range. The 4 mA represents zero pressure (or minimum of range) and 20 mA represents the full-scale pressure. The 4–20 mA standard is used because: live zero (4 mA, not 0 mA) allows detection of a broken wire (0 mA indicates fault, not zero pressure), and the signal is immune to cable resistance and EMI over long cable runs.
2.2 DP Cell (Differential Pressure Cell) — Construction and Working

A DP (Differential Pressure) cell measures the difference between two pressures. It has two pressure inlet ports: a high-pressure port (H) and a low-pressure port (L). The sensing element is typically a capacitance-based differential pressure sensor — a stainless steel diaphragm suspended between two capacitor plates. When the differential pressure (P_H – P_L) acts on the diaphragm, it deflects towards the low-pressure side. This changes the capacitance gap on each side — one capacitance increases, the other decreases. The electronics measure the differential capacitance and convert it to a 4–20 mA output proportional to the differential pressure. DP cells onboard are used for: tank level measurement (H port connected to bottom of tank, L port to top — the DP is proportional to the liquid head = ρ × g × h); filter differential pressure (dirty filter = higher DP → alarm); flow measurement (venturi/orifice plate flow meters use DP to calculate flow).

RPM (speed) measurement of rotating machinery — main engine, auxiliary engines, turbochargers, propeller shaft — is essential for monitoring and control. The ETO is responsible for these sensors. Two types are commonly asked: the tachometer (for main and auxiliary engine RPM) and the turbocharger speed sensor.

The viscotherm is an automatic fuel oil viscosity controller that maintains the HFO (Heavy Fuel Oil) at the correct viscosity before injection into the main engine fuel pumps. HFO must be heated to reduce its viscosity to approximately 10–17 cSt (centistokes) at the engine fuel pump inlet for proper atomisation and combustion. The viscosity is highly temperature-dependent — HFO at 20°C may have a viscosity of 700–3500 cSt, which must be reduced to 10–17 cSt by heating to typically 100–150°C depending on the oil grade.

The viscotherm measures fuel oil viscosity using a vibrating rod or torsional vibration viscometer element — a probe is immersed in the fuel oil flow, and the damping effect of the oil on the probe's vibration is directly proportional to the viscosity (higher viscosity = more damping = lower amplitude of vibration). The measured viscosity is compared with the setpoint (e.g., 12 cSt) in a controller. If the viscosity is too high (oil too cold), the controller opens the steam or electric heating valve to heat the oil. If viscosity is too low (oil too hot), the heating is reduced. This maintains correct viscosity continuously regardless of changes in fuel grade, ambient temperature, or engine load.

Gas detection instruments are essential safety equipment on tankers, gas carriers, and all ships with enclosed spaces. The ETO must know the construction, working principle, and the critical difference between a tankscope and an explosimeter. This is a direct examination question from the Sanjib and Vishwanathan banks, especially for candidates who have sailed on tankers or LPG carriers.
5.1 Explosimeter (Combustible Gas Indicator)

The explosimeter detects the percentage of Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) of flammable gas in air. It is designed to warn before the gas concentration reaches explosive levels — it measures in the range 0–100% LEL, with alarm typically at 20–30% LEL. It cannot be used in an atmosphere that is already above the LEL (above 100% LEL) because it requires oxygen to function — the catalytic combustion sensing element (pellistor) burns a small sample of gas, and if there is insufficient oxygen (inert or oxygen-depleted atmosphere), the sensor gives incorrect readings or fails. The explosimeter is used for pre-entry checks of enclosed spaces and cargo holds to verify the atmosphere is below explosive levels before sending personnel in.

The sensing element is a pellistor (catalytic bead detector) — two coils of platinum wire (an active element coated with catalyst, and a reference element without catalyst) form two arms of a Wheatstone bridge. A small sample of atmospheric gas is drawn over the active element, where flammable gas oxidises (burns catalytically) on the heated catalyst surface, raising its temperature and therefore its resistance. The bridge becomes unbalanced in proportion to the concentration of flammable gas. The reference element compensates for ambient temperature changes. The output is calibrated in %LEL.
5.2 Tankscope (Oxygen and Gas Analyser)

The tankscope (also called a multi-gas detector or portable gas analyser) is used to check the atmosphere inside cargo tanks before and during tank entry and cargo operations. Unlike the explosimeter, the tankscope can measure in gas-rich (above LEL, inerting conditions) and oxygen-deficient atmospheres. It typically measures: oxygen content (O₂ %), hydrocarbon gas concentration (% volume, above and below LEL), and on more advanced types, CO and H₂S in ppm. The oxygen measurement uses an electrochemical cell (galvanic fuel cell) — oxygen diffuses through a permeable membrane and reacts at a gold cathode and lead anode, generating a current proportional to O₂ concentration. The hydrocarbon measurement above LEL uses an infrared absorption sensor (NDIR — Non-Dispersive Infrared) — hydrocarbon molecules absorb infrared radiation at specific wavelengths; the amount of absorption is proportional to gas concentration. NDIR sensors function in oxygen-deficient or inert atmospheres, unlike pellistors.

UTI (Ullage Temperature Interface) is a portable manual cargo measurement instrument used on oil tankers and chemical tankers. Sanjib specifically asks for everything about UTI — full form, working principle, how it is powered, voltage, and what each measurement means. The UTI is essential for custody transfer measurements (determining how much cargo is in a tank accurately for bill of lading purposes) and for checking tank conditions before and after cargo operations.

Remote cargo tank level measurement systems automatically transmit tank levels to the cargo control room continuously, without requiring manual UTI measurements for every tank during cargo operations. The ETO must understand the principles and how the values reach the control room.

What is WIDAS?

WIDAS = Water Ingress Detection and Alarm System. It is a monitoring system that detects the presence of water in enclosed spaces — cargo holds, void spaces, chain lockers, ballast tanks, fore and aft peaks — and raises an alarm on the bridge before flooding becomes structurally critical. WIDAS was introduced after a series of bulk carrier losses in the 1990s where water ingress in holds was not detected until too late.

Bridge display: Central alarm panel on bridge with individual zone identification — shows WHICH space has water ingress.
Sensor types used:

1. FLOAT SWITCH (most common): A float inside a housing rises with water level. When water reaches the preset level, the float activates a microswitch — closes the alarm contact. Simple, reliable, no power required at sensor.

2. CONDUCTIVITY PROBE: Two electrodes (probes) separated by air gap — when water bridges the gap, electric current flows between probes → alarm circuit detects current. Suitable for dirty/sludgy environments where float may stick.
3. ULTRASONIC LEVEL SENSOR (less common on older WIDAS): Non-contact — measures distance to water surface. More expensive, used on more modern installations.
WIDAS Panel — Location and Features:
Main display panel: Located on the bridge — gives continuous monitoring of all zones.
Each zone shows: NORMAL (green) / ALARM (red — water detected) / FAULT (yellow — sensor or cable fault).
Audible alarm: Sounds on bridge on water ingress detection.
History log: Records alarm events with timestamp — important for post-incident investigation.
Integration: Modern systems can interface with VDR (Voyage Data Recorder) — water ingress data recorded for black-box investigation.

1. FLOAT SENSOR TESTING: Physically lift the float in each hold sensor to verify alarm activates on panel. Test all sensors per PMS — typically quarterly or as per class requirement. Access via hold manholes or sensor access ports.
2. CABLE INSPECTION: Cables running through cargo holds are exposed to mechanical damage and moisture. Inspect for damage, kinks, corroded glands during each cargo hold inspection.
3. PANEL SELF-TEST: Use panel test function — checks all sensor circuits for open-circuit faults.
4. CLEANING: Float sensors in holds may be clogged with grain dust, cargo residue, or bilge sludge — physically clean sensor housing and float during dry-dock or hold cleaning periods.
5. FALSE ALARM INVESTIGATION: Bilge water splash, condensation, or cleaning water can activate sensors. Investigate each alarm — do not silence without verifying cause.

1.1 Fire Triangle and Fire Tetrahedron

Combustion (fire) requires three elements to be present simultaneously — this is the Fire Triangle: Fuel (combustible material), Oxygen (oxidiser, typically from air — minimum ~16% O₂), and Heat (ignition energy above the fuel's ignition temperature). Remove any one of these three sides and the fire cannot be sustained. Modern fire fighting science recognises a fourth element — the Chain Reaction (free radical chain reaction of combustion) — making a Fire Tetrahedron. Some agents (halon, FM-200, Novec 1230) extinguish fire by chemical chain reaction interruption rather than by physically removing heat or oxygen, which is why the tetrahedron is a more complete model.

Fire extinguishment methods correspond to the four sides: cooling (water — removes heat), smothering (CO₂, foam, sand — removes oxygen), starvation (removing fuel — shutting off fuel supply, isolating power), and chain reaction inhibition (dry chemical powder, FM-200, halon — interrupts free radical chain reaction). The ETO must understand which method applies to each fire class to select the correct extinguisher and avoid making the fire worse — using water on a Class B (flammable liquid) fire or an electrical fire could be immediately fatal.
2.1 Smoke Detectors

Smoke detectors are the most common fire detection devices onboard ship and are found in accommodation, machinery spaces, cargo holds, and control rooms. There are two principal types: ionisation smoke detectors and photoelectric (optical) smoke detectors.

The ionisation smoke detector uses a tiny amount of radioactive material — Americium-241 (Am-241, alpha particle emitter) — to ionise the air between two charged electrodes inside a sensing chamber. The ionised air (containing free electrons and positive ions) conducts a small current between the electrodes. When smoke particles enter the chamber, they attach to the ions, reducing the conductivity and therefore reducing the current. The electronics detect this drop in current and trigger the alarm. Am-241 has a half-life of 432 years and emits alpha particles only — the source is completely shielded within the detector; it poses no radiation hazard to persons. Ionisation detectors are most sensitive to flaming fires with small combustion particles (fast-flaming fires). They respond faster to small particle smoke than optical detectors.

The photoelectric (optical) smoke detector uses a light emitter (LED or infra-red LED) and a photodetector in an optical sensing chamber. In the absence of smoke, the light beam travels across the chamber and hits a light trap — the photodetector receives no light. When smoke enters the chamber, the particles scatter the light beam in all directions — some scattered light reaches the photodetector, increasing its output signal. When the signal exceeds the threshold, the alarm triggers. Optical detectors are more sensitive to smouldering fires with large, visible smoke particles (slow smouldering fires). They are less prone to false alarms from cooking steam than ionisation types.
2.2 Heat Detectors

Heat detectors respond to elevated temperatures rather than smoke. There are five main types used onboard: fixed temperature type (bimetallic type or fusible link — triggers at a set temperature, e.g., 58°C, 72°C, or 93°C); rate-of-rise type (detects when temperature is rising faster than ~8–10°C per minute — this indicates a rapidly developing fire, triggering alarm before the absolute temperature setpoint is reached); rate-of-rise combined fixed temperature type (triggers on either condition — most versatile); pneumatic tube type (air in a tube expands when heated — a diaphragm and pressure switch triggers the alarm); and thermocouple/thermistor type (measures actual temperature continuously — used in cargo holds and machinery spaces where gradual temperature monitoring is needed).

The CO₂ total flooding system is the primary fixed fire suppression system for the main machinery space (engine room), cargo pump room, and paint locker on most cargo vessels. It is among the most heavily tested topics across all question banks — CO₂ release procedure, precautions, ETO checks in CO₂ room, and expansion ratio are all specifically asked. CO₂ is stored as a liquid under pressure in steel cylinders in a dedicated CO₂ room. When released, the liquid CO₂ rapidly expands to gas — the expansion ratio is approximately 1:450 (1 litre of liquid CO₂ expands to approximately 450 litres of gas at atmospheric pressure). This rapid expansion displaces oxygen in the protected space, reducing O₂ concentration below 15% (the minimum needed to support combustion), extinguishing the fire by oxygen deprivation.
5.1 Sprinkler System — Working and BLIS

A sprinkler system provides automatic fire detection and suppression in accommodation, public spaces, and sometimes cargo spaces. Each sprinkler head contains a heat-sensitive element — a glass bulb filled with glycerine solution or a fusible metal link — that holds a plug sealing the water orifice. When the ambient temperature around the head reaches the bulb's rated temperature (typically 68°C for standard; 93°C or 141°C for high-temperature areas), the glycerine expands and shatters the bulb, or the fusible link melts, releasing the plug. Water from the pressurised distribution system then sprays through the deflector plate, creating a spray pattern that covers the fire area.

The BLIS (Bulk Line Isolation Stop valve — sometimes called the Blank Line Indication System or simply the Sprinkler Stop valve indicator) is a supervisory valve on the main sprinkler supply line fitted with a tamper switch. If the stop valve is accidentally or deliberately closed (isolating the water supply to the sprinklers), the BLIS switch triggers an alarm at the fire panel indicating that the system has been isolated — this prevents a situation where the sprinklers are unknowingly out of service. To verify water pressure is present in the sprinkler system without activating a sprinkler head: use the test valve (test cock) at the end of each zone branch line — opening this valve simulates a sprinkler head operating by releasing water into a test drain; this confirms that water is available at the correct pressure and triggers the flow alarm and fire panel indication. The pressure gauge on the sprinkler distribution header also shows system pressure continuously.
5.2 High-Pressure Water Mist (HI-FOG / Hypermist) System

High-pressure water mist (trade names: Hi-Fog, Hypermist, Marioff) is increasingly used on modern ships as an alternative to CO₂ for machinery space protection and as a sprinkler alternative in accommodation. It works by discharging water at very high pressure (70–200 bar) through specially designed fine nozzles that atomise water into extremely fine droplets (typically 50–200 µm diameter — compared to conventional sprinkler droplets of ~1000 µm). These ultra-fine droplets have three fire suppression effects: first, rapid evaporation absorbs large amounts of heat from the fire (high latent heat of vaporisation — 2257 kJ/kg for water), cooling the combustion zone very effectively; second, as water evaporates to steam, the volume expansion (~1700 times) displaces oxygen locally around the fire; third, the fine water vapour cloud reduces radiant heat transfer from the fire, reducing re-ignition risk. Water mist is effective for Class A, Class B (flammable liquids), and Class F fires, and is safer than CO₂ for manned spaces because people can survive in a water mist atmosphere (unlike CO₂ flooding).

Portable extinguishers are the first line of defence for incipient (early-stage) fires. The ETO is responsible for their maintenance, testing, and ensuring they are correctly located per the ship's fire plan. The colour coding (BS EN 3 standard) identifies the extinguisher type: red body = water; red body + cream panel = foam; red body + black panel = CO₂; red body + blue panel = DCP; red body + yellow panel = wet chemical.

UV Flame Detector — Working Principle and Testing
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how does a UV flame detector work and how do you test it?"
What is a UV Flame Detector?

A UV (ultraviolet) flame detector is a fire detector that senses the ultraviolet radiation emitted by flames. Unlike smoke detectors (which detect combustion products) or heat detectors (which detect temperature rise), the UV detector responds to the RADIATION emitted directly from the flame itself — giving an extremely fast response time (milliseconds). This makes it ideal for locations where a fire must be detected and suppressed before it spreads.
Working Principle:
1. UV SENSOR CELL: A Geiger-Müller tube or UV photodiode responds to electromagnetic radiation in the wavelength band 185–260 nm (ultraviolet spectrum).
2. FLAME EMISSION: Hydrocarbon flames (fuel oil, LPG, gasoline) and hydrogen flames all emit strongly in this UV band during combustion — this is a characteristic signature of fire.
3. DETECTION: When UV radiation above the threshold level hits the detector, the circuit triggers an alarm output.
4. RESPONSE TIME: Typically 3–5 milliseconds — far faster than heat or smoke detectors. Critical in engine rooms and pump rooms where fuel fires spread rapidly.
Limitations of UV-only detectors:
FALSE ALARMS: Direct sunlight, arc welding, lightning, and certain fluorescent lights all emit UV radiation — can trigger false alarms if the detector has an unobstructed line to these sources.
WINDOW FOULING: Oil contamination or condensation on the detector window attenuates UV signal — regular cleaning is essential.
Solution: UV/IR combined detector — requires simultaneous UV AND infrared signal to confirm fire, rejecting false UV sources.
Ship applications:
Engine room flame detection (especially near boilers, purifiers, and engine fuel systems)
Pump room fire detection on tankers
Boiler front burner flame monitoring — confirms pilot flame and main flame are established
Gas turbine exhaust areas
Compressor room fire detection
Testing Procedure for UV Flame Detector:

1. Use a CALIBRATED UV TEST LAMP (supplied by detector manufacturer). The test lamp emits UV at the correct wavelength to simulate a flame signal. DO NOT use an open flame or gas lighter — this creates a real fire risk near fuel or flammable vapours.
2. Inform bridge and fire watch before testing — ensure fire panel in TEST mode or coordinate so alarm is expected.
3. Hold test lamp at the prescribed distance from detector window (typically 150–300 mm — per manufacturer manual).
4. Activate test lamp — alarm should activate on fire panel within 5 seconds.
5. Verify: alarm indicator lights on detector, alarm registers at fire panel with correct zone identification, any linked fire suppression pre-alarm or main alarm activates correctly.
6. Reset alarm after test.
7. Record: detector ID, test lamp serial number, result (pass/fail), date, tester name in maintenance log.

8. IMPORTANT: If detector window is dirty (oil film, dust), clean with lens tissue before testing. A dirty window will reduce UV transmission and give a false-low response — detector may not respond to real fire.
Heat Detector — Types and Testing Procedure
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how do you test a heat detector?"
Types of Heat Detectors:

1. FIXED TEMPERATURE (bimetallic or fusible element type): Activates when ambient temperature rises ABOVE a fixed setpoint (typically 58°C, 68°C, or 88°C depending on location). Bimetallic strip deflects at setpoint temperature. Simple, low maintenance, but slow response for slowly developing fires.

2. RATE OF RISE (ROR): Activates when the RATE of temperature increase exceeds approximately 8–10°C per minute, regardless of actual temperature. Detects fast-developing fires earlier than fixed temperature type. Pneumatic ROR: Contains a small air chamber — rapid heating expands air faster than it can vent through a calibration port → diaphragm operates alarm contact.
3. COMBINED (Fixed Temp + ROR): Most common. Trips on EITHER: rate of rise > threshold OR fixed temperature exceeded — whichever comes first.
Testing Procedure:
1. Inform bridge/CCR — fire panel to be in TEST mode to avoid sending crew to the location.

2. USE APPROVED HEAT GUN or calibrated hot air blower — NOT an open flame, gas torch, or hair dryer without thermometer. An open flame creates real fire risk and can cause thermal damage or permanent actuation of fusible element type detectors.
3. Hold heat gun 100–150 mm from detector — apply heat gently and steadily.
4. For FIXED TEMP type: heat until alarm activates. Note temperature using thermometer — should be within ±10% of rated setpoint.
5. For ROR type: apply heat rapidly — alarm should activate within 10–15 seconds of application.

6. ELECTRONIC TEST (addressable systems): Some modern systems allow test via fire panel — sends electronic test command to addressable detector, detector responds with TEST ALARM signal. No physical heat required. Quicker for large numbers of detectors.
7. After test: Verify alarm showed correct zone/detector address on panel. Reset alarm. Allow detector to cool. Inspect detector — ensure no damage.
8. Record: detector ID/address, test method, response observed, date, name. Log in fire detection maintenance record.
Important note — do NOT use open flame:

"Never use a naked flame to test fire detectors." — a surveyor who sees a technician using a lighter to test a detector will immediately flag this as a serious safety violation. The reason: (1) Real fire risk, especially in ER near fuel. (2) Excessive heat can permanently damage certain detector types. (3) Creates a false confidence — the detector "passed" but was actually tested incorrectly.
Container Fire in Cargo Hold — ETO Response and Containment
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "there is a fire in a container in the cargo hold — what do you do?"
Container fire in hold is one of the most dangerous scenarios for a ship. The ETO has specific responsibilities in this emergency:
Immediate actions (first 5 minutes):
1. General alarm — alert entire crew. Sound alarm manually if automatic system has not activated.
2. Inform bridge: "Fire in cargo hold [number]. Suspected container fire." Bridge calls Mayday or Pan-Pan as appropriate.
3. CLOSE ALL HOLD VENTILATION: Close ventilation flaps, fans, and trunking to the affected hold — starve fire of oxygen. This is the MOST important initial action for a container fire.
4. CLOSE WEATHERTIGHT HATCHES: Dog down hatch covers on affected hold — contain smoke and restrict air entry.
5. DO NOT OPEN HOLD HATCH: Allowing air into a semi-suffocated fire causes explosive re-ignition (backdraft). NEVER open a hatch to inspect progress of a hold fire.
Fixed fire suppression activation:
6. ACTIVATE CO₂ FIXED SYSTEM: For holds fitted with CO₂ — follow activation procedure. Verify hold is SEALED before flooding. CO₂ smothers fire by displacing oxygen.
7. If IG (inert gas) system available: Flood hold with inert gas — nitrogen or CO₂ blend. Maintain gas blanket.
8. After flooding: DO NOT OPEN HOLD for minimum 24 hours — CO₂ takes time to extinguish deep-seated fires in cargo.
9. Monitor hold temperature: Temperature probes in hold show whether fire is spreading (rising temp) or dying (falling temp).
ETO specific responsibilities during hold fire:
10. MAINTAIN EMERGENCY POWER: Ensure emergency generator is running and all critical services are on ESB — emergency lighting, fire pumps, GMDSS, PA system.
11. FIRE DETECTION MONITORING: Watch fire panel — monitor spread to adjacent holds or cargo spaces.
12. GMDSS: Ensure all GMDSS equipment operational — Distress alert, INMARSAT, VHF — in case Mayday needs to be sent.
13. PA SYSTEM: Verify ship announcement system working for crew coordination.

14. CHECK DANGEROUS GOODS MANIFEST: What is in the affected container? Chemicals? Class 1 explosives? Class 3 flammable liquids? The IMDG code substance determines firefighting strategy. Chief Officer/Master must advise firefighting team.
Why NOT to use water on container fire in hold:
Pouring water into a closed hold with CO₂: Dilutes CO₂, reduces effectiveness, can cause CO₂ gas to be expelled.
Some dangerous goods react violently with water: Class 4.3 (dangerous when wet), certain peroxides.
Water adds enormous weight to the ship — free surface effect can cause dangerous list or capsize.
Exception: If dangerous goods are confirmed water-reactive, consult IMDG emergency schedule (EmS) before any firefighting action.

PFOS Ban in Firefighting Foam — New Prohibition
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: According to new regulations, firefighting foam containing PFOS (and related PFAS chemicals) is now PROHIBITED onboard ships. Surveyor will ask about this.
What is PFOS?

PFOS = Perfluorooctane Sulfonate. A synthetic fluorochemical used in AFFF (Aqueous Film-Forming Foam) firefighting agents because of its exceptional ability to suppress flammable liquid fires by forming a thin aqueous film on the fuel surface. It was the standard foam type in engine rooms and pump rooms for decades. However, PFOS is a persistent organic pollutant (POP) — it accumulates in living organisms and the environment, causes cancer and reproductive harm, and does not break down naturally.
The new prohibition (from 1 January 2026):
USE prohibited: PFOS-containing firefighting foam may no longer be used operationally onboard ships.
STORAGE prohibited: PFOS-containing foam concentrates may not be stored/carried onboard ships.
DISCHARGE prohibited: PFOS-containing foam discharge to sea is a MARPOL violation.
Existing stocks: All PFOS-containing foam concentrates must be sent to approved shore reception facilities by the FIRST scheduled survey on or after 1 January 2026.
Survey check: Class/flag surveyor will inspect foam concentrate type. PFOS-containing stock found during survey = deficiency and removal required before departure.
PFOS-free replacements approved for use:
C6 AFFF (C6-based fluorosurfactant AFFF): Lower chain-length fluorochemicals with significantly lower environmental persistence.
AR-AFFF (Alcohol-Resistant Aqueous Film-Forming Foam): PFOS-free formulation for polar solvent fires.
F-500 (Encapsulator agent): PFOS-free, also effective on Class A fires.
Fluorine-free foams (FFF): No fluorochemicals at all — protein-based or hydrocarbon-based. Growing preference for new installations.

ETO action: Check foam concentrate data sheets (MSDS/SDS) for PFOS content. Identify all foam storage points onboard. Arrange disposal and replacement with approved PFOS-free type before first survey after January 2026.
Ro-Ro Vehicle Deck Fire Safety Overhaul (New SOLAS II-2/20 — Effective 1 January 2026)
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: According to new regulations, Ro-Ro PASSENGER ships face major new fire detection and suppression requirements from 2026. This is a hot exam topic given recent casualties.
Background:

Several serious Ro-Ro passenger ship fires in recent years (including the Grimaldi Grande America fire in 2019 and other incidents) demonstrated that vehicle deck fires spread extremely rapidly due to the open deck design, high fuel load from vehicles, and difficulty of access for firefighters. IMO amended SOLAS II-2 Regulation 20 and the FSS Code to significantly increase fire detection and suppression capability on Ro-Ro vehicle decks.

Ships affected: Ro-Ro passenger ships. Some requirements also apply to Ro-Ro cargo ships. New ships: from 1 January 2026. Existing ships: retrofit by 2028 (first scheduled survey after 2026 for most requirements).
NEW REQUIREMENT 1 — Enhanced Fire Detection in Vehicle Spaces:
Requirement: Combined smoke AND heat detectors (or linear heat detectors) must be fitted in all vehicle spaces — not smoke only.

Why combined: Vehicles fires can start with deep-seated smouldering (smoke first — smoke detector fires) OR with rapid flaming combustion (heat first, less smoke — heat detector fires). Combined type catches both scenarios faster.

Linear heat detectors: Continuous heat-sensing cable strung across the vehicle deck — detects temperature rise along its entire length. Ideal for large open vehicle decks where point detectors have wide spacing.
ETO role: Maintain the enhanced detection system. Test both smoke and heat element functions separately. Verify alarm reaches bridge and fire panel with correct zone identification. Record tests.
NEW REQUIREMENT 2 — Continuous Video Monitoring with 24-Hour Playback:
Requirement: Ro-Ro vehicle spaces must now have CONTINUOUS video monitoring — cameras covering all areas of the vehicle deck, with the ability to review at least 24 hours of recorded footage.

Why: Early fire detection from CCTV can trigger crew response before automatic systems alarm. The 24-hour playback enables investigation — identifying where and how a fire started, what vehicle was involved.
Camera requirements: Sufficient resolution and field of view to identify individual vehicles. Night-vision/thermal imaging capability preferred for 24-hour reliability.

ETO responsibilities: Install and maintain cameras and recording system. Verify recording is continuous (no gaps). Check storage capacity is sufficient for 24+ hours. Verify camera feeds are visible at bridge and ECR. Schedule camera cleaning and lens check. Include in monthly rounds.
NEW REQUIREMENT 3 — Fixed Water-Based Fire-Extinguishing Monitors on Weather Decks:
Requirement: Fixed water-based fire-extinguishing monitors (water cannons/monitors) must now be fitted on OPEN (weather) vehicle decks on Ro-Ro passenger ships.

Purpose: Where vehicles are loaded/unloaded or transported on open decks — a vehicle fire on an open deck previously had no fixed suppression. Monitors provide immediate high-volume water application remotely without firefighters entering the fire zone.
Design: Motorised or manual monitors positioned to cover the full vehicle deck area. Fed from the fire main. Flow rates designed to cover the vehicle area with adequate application rate.
ETO role: Maintain monitor mechanisms (rotation, elevation). Check nozzle condition. Verify fire main supply pressure. Test operation quarterly. Include in fire drill records.
1.1 What is SOLAS

SOLAS (Safety of Life at Sea) is an international maritime treaty administered by the IMO (International Maritime Organization) that specifies minimum safety standards in the construction, equipment, and operation of merchant ships. The current version is SOLAS 1974, as amended, which entered into force on 25 May 1980. It applies to all ships on international voyages. SOLAS sets out regulations covering structural safety, fire protection, life-saving appliances, radio communications, navigational safety, cargo management, nuclear ship safety, and high-speed craft. Flag states enforce SOLAS on ships registered under their flag; Port State Control (PSC) officers verify compliance during port inspections.

SOLAS 1974 consists of 14 chapters (as of current amendments), plus an Annex containing certificates. The number of chapters has grown over time as new regulations were added. The most commonly asked figure — total SOLAS chapters — is 14 chapters. The Convention has no separate Annexes in the MARPOL sense; additional requirements are incorporated as amendments (MSC Resolutions) and new chapters added to the main body.

The emergency generator is the most heavily tested SOLAS topic across all question banks — it appears in virtually every oral examination. SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 43 covers the emergency source of electrical power for cargo ships.

The electrical survey is the single most-asked topic in MMD orals across all question banks. It is a mandatory periodic survey carried out by the classification society surveyor to verify that the ship's electrical installation remains in compliance with the class rules and SOLAS requirements. The survey is typically carried out every 5 years as part of the Special Survey, with intermediate surveys at annual or 2.5-year intervals depending on the class society's continuous survey scheme.

The ISM Code (International Safety Management Code) is mandatory under SOLAS Chapter IX. It was adopted by the IMO in 1993 and made mandatory for cargo ships >500 GT on international voyages from 1998. The ISM Code establishes an international standard for the safe management and operation of ships and for pollution prevention. It requires shipping companies to have a documented Safety Management System (SMS) that covers all aspects of ship operation.

The ISPS Code (International Ship and Port Facility Security Code) was adopted by IMO in 2002 following the September 11 terrorist attacks, and became mandatory under SOLAS Chapter XI-2 from July 2004. It establishes an international framework for detecting and responding to security threats to ships and port facilities. The code applies to all SOLAS vessels on international voyages.
