SEEMP Part 3 — CII and ETO Role
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple candidates — surveyor asked "what is SEEMP Part 3 and what is CII?"
Background:

SEEMP = Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan. Required by MARPOL Annex VI, Regulation 22. Originally (2013) focused on identifying energy efficiency improvement measures. SEEMP Part 3 was introduced in January 2023 as part of the IMO Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) regime — a major new operational carbon rating system for ships.
CII — Carbon Intensity Indicator:
CII measures operational carbon intensity: grams of CO₂ emitted per cargo-carrying capacity per nautical mile (g CO₂ / DWT·nm).
Annual CII calculation: Based on fuel consumption data from MRV (Monitoring, Reporting and Verification) system (EU) or Data Collection System (DCS) (IMO).
Annual rating: Ships rated A (best) through E (worst) on a sliding scale.
Required rating: Ships must achieve C or better. D or E ratings trigger corrective action obligations.
D rating: Must develop and implement a corrective action plan — submitted to flag state.
E rating: Corrective action plan mandatory, with specific improvement targets. Ship may face operational restrictions.
SEEMP Part 3 content (ship-specific CII improvement plan):
1. Ship's required CII for each year (from 2023–2030, annual tightening targets)
2. Implementation plan for achieving the CII target
3. Self-evaluation: how the ship will track and review its CII performance
4. Corrective action procedure if CII rating is D or E
ETO contributions to improving ship CII rating:
1. LED LIGHTING: Replace fluorescent and halogen with LED throughout — reduces hotel load 30–60%. Each kWh saved = less fuel burned by auxiliary engine.

2. VFD ON PUMPS AND FANS: Variable frequency drives on sea water pumps, cooling fans, ventilation fans — at part load, VFD reduces speed proportionally. Power saved = speed ratio cubed. Example: Fan at 80% speed uses only 51% of power.
3. SHORE POWER (COLD IRONING): Where available, connect to shore supply in port — stop auxiliary generators completely. Zero fuel consumption at berth.
4. WASTE HEAT RECOVERY: Maintain exhaust gas economiser (waste heat boiler) efficiently — good performance means less HFO burned in auxiliary boiler for steam generation.
5. POWER FACTOR CORRECTION: Maintain capacitor banks and synchronous compensators — poor PF means generators deliver more apparent power (kVA) for same useful power (kW) = more fuel consumed.
6. POWER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM: Ensure load shedding functions correctly — avoid unnecessary generator operation. Run one generator at 70–80% load rather than two at 40% each.
7. MAINTENANCE: Clean heat exchangers on MSB cooling — overheated switchgear draws more power. Keep motor cooling paths clear. Replace worn motor bearings — friction increases motor current.
Override Authority — When and How to Override Safety Systems
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what is override authority?" or "can you override a safety trip?"
What is an override?

An override is the act of bypassing an automatic alarm or safety trip to allow equipment to continue operating despite the triggering condition. This is sometimes necessary during genuine emergencies where stopping the equipment would cause greater danger than the condition being protected against.
Who has override authority?
MASTER: Ultimate authority on the ship — can authorise overrides of any system if safety of ship and crew requires it.
CHIEF ENGINEER: Authority over machinery space overrides — approves machinery trip overrides.
ETO: May operate override switches but only with C/E or Master authorisation. NEVER unilaterally override critical safety trips.
Bridge Officer: May override UMS alarms or steering gear safeties on Master's authority only.
When override is permitted:
Emergency continuation: A critical pump is about to trip on low LO pressure, but stopping it would cause loss of steering or main engine cooling — override with increased manual monitoring.
Spurious alarm: Sensor confirmed faulty, equipment is healthy, repair requires time — override alarm while repair is underway.
Testing: Override bilge high-level alarm during tank cleaning operations to prevent nuisance alarms.
Override procedure — EVERY override must follow this process:
1. C/E or Master gives VERBAL and WRITTEN authorisation.
2. LOG: Record in engine room log and override register: date, time, system overridden, reason, authorising officer, monitoring measures.
3. INCREASED MONITORING: Watchkeeper physically checks the overridden system at increased frequency (every 15–30 minutes). Record checks in log.
4. COMPENSATORY MEASURES: Where possible, use alternate protection (manual measurement instead of automatic sensor).
5. CANCEL AS SOON AS POSSIBLE: Override must be cancelled the moment the emergency is resolved or repair is completed.
6. Override switches: Must be key-operated or sealed — prevent accidental activation. Override register maintained near MSB or in C/E's office.
Systems that must NEVER be overridden without specific procedure:
Fixed CO₂ or foam fire suppression systems — only with hot work permit and agreed safety measures
Steering gear safeties — loss of steering is catastrophic
Main engine overload trip at sea in open water — stop engine rather than override

Issued by: Flag state (or RO — Recognised Organisation acting on behalf of flag state).

MLC 2006 (Maritime Labour Convention) entered into force August 2013. It consolidates over 65 previous ILO maritime labour instruments into one comprehensive convention. It sets MINIMUM standards for working and living conditions for ALL seafarers on ships ≥500 GT on international voyages.

Accommodation electrical systems: Ensure lighting, ventilation fans, air conditioning/heating all fully functional — MLC Title 3.

MARPOL (International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships) is the main international convention covering prevention of pollution of the marine environment by ships from operational or accidental causes. It was adopted by the IMO in 1973 and modified by a 1978 Protocol — hence officially MARPOL 73/78. It is administered by the IMO and is mandatory for all vessels flagged to signatory states. MARPOL consists of 6 Annexes, each covering a different category of ship-generated pollution. For the MMD oral, the candidate must know all 6 annexes, their content, key discharge criteria, and — critically — which ones are most relevant to the ETO's role.
2.1 OWS — Oily Water Separator Working Principle

The OWS (Oily Water Separator) separates oil from oily bilge water so that only water with less than 15 ppm of oil is discharged overboard. MARPOL Annex I Regulation 14/15 requires the OWS to be fitted with an Oil Content Monitor (OCM) or Oil Content Meter that continuously monitors the effluent. If the oil content exceeds 15 ppm, the OCM automatically actuates a three-way valve that diverts the discharge back to the bilge holding tank instead of overboard. The OWS operates in two stages: the first stage is gravity/coalescing separation — oily water is fed into a separation chamber where free oil (which is less dense than water) rises to the surface and is collected. The second stage is a coalescing filter unit (cartridge) where emulsified oil droplets are captured by the coalescing medium (polypropylene or glass fibre fibres) — small droplets coalesce into larger ones that rise and separate.

The OCM continuously samples the effluent from the second stage. The ETO must understand exactly what sensor is used in the OCM for oil detection — this is a specific examination question. The standard sensor type used is an infrared absorption sensor (optical sensor). The sensor measures the turbidity or light absorption of the effluent — oil in water absorbs or scatters infrared light differently from clean water. When the oil concentration exceeds 15 ppm, the sensor output exceeds the threshold, the alarm activates, and the three-way solenoid valve operates to divert flow to the holding tank. Some OWS use light scattering sensors (nephelometry — measure scattered light at 90° to the light source, proportional to particle/droplet concentration).

MARPOL Annex VI (Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships) is the annex most directly relevant to the ETO because it covers ozone-depleting substances (ODS) used in refrigeration and air conditioning systems onboard — a direct ETO maintenance responsibility. It also covers the IAPP Certificate, the NOx Technical File, EGCS (scrubbers), and the energy efficiency regulations (EEDI, SEEMP, CII). Annex VI entered into force on 19 May 2005.

The ODME (Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control System) — also called ODMCS — is required by MARPOL Annex I on crude oil tankers and product tankers to monitor and control the discharge of oily ballast water and tank washings during cargo operations at sea. This is different from the OWS which handles machinery space bilge water. The ODME applies to cargo-related oil discharges.

ODP — Ozone Depletion Potential and Refrigerant Regulations
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what is ODP?" and "why are CFCs banned on ships?"
What is ODP?

ODP = Ozone Depletion Potential. A dimensionless number that describes the relative amount of damage a substance can cause to the stratospheric ozone layer, compared to CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane) which has a reference ODP of 1.0. The higher the ODP, the more damaging the substance is to the ozone layer that protects the Earth from harmful UV-B radiation.
ODP values of common refrigerants (must know for exam):
CFC-11 (R-11): ODP = 1.0 (reference standard). Banned under Montreal Protocol.
CFC-12 (R-12): ODP = 1.0. Banned. Was widely used in older ship refrigeration.
HCFC-22 (R-22): ODP = 0.055. Phase-out complete for developed countries. Still found on older ships in service.
HFC-134a (R-134a): ODP = 0. No ozone depletion. GWP = 1430 (global warming potential). Used in AC and medium-temp refrigeration.
HFC-404A: ODP = 0. GWP = 3922. Used in low-temperature reefer containers.
HFO-1234yf / HFO-1234ze: ODP = 0. GWP < 1. New generation refrigerants — very low environmental impact.
Montreal Protocol and MARPOL Annex VI:
Montreal Protocol (1987): International agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances. CFCs banned from new equipment by 1994 (developed countries). HCFCs (including R-22) phased out by 2020.

MARPOL Annex VI, Regulation 12: Controls deliberate emissions of ozone-depleting substances from ships. Prohibits intentional venting of ODS during maintenance. Requires Ozone-Depleting Substances Record Book.
Record Book entries: Any intentional or accidental release of ODS. Recharge or top-up of ODS-containing systems. Transfer of ODS to shore facilities.
ETO responsibility: No deliberate venting of refrigerant — must be recovered using certified recovery equipment. Use only approved ODS-free refrigerants for new installations and repairs.
Practical examination questions the surveyor may ask:
"What refrigerant does your reefer system use?" — Know the type from data plate. Know if it has ODP.
"How do you dispose of old refrigerant?" — Must be recovered using certified refrigerant recovery machine, transferred to shore facility. Cannot be vented.
"What is written in your ODS record book?" — Must contain all refrigerant additions, recoveries, and disposal.
SEEMP Part 3 — ETO Role in CII Compliance
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how does the ETO contribute to SEEMP and CII improvement?"

This question is increasingly common as IMO carbon reduction targets tighten. The surveyor wants to know that the ETO understands their SPECIFIC contribution to ship energy efficiency — not just the regulatory framework but practical actions.
ETO energy efficiency actions — with technical explanation:

1. LED LIGHTING CONVERSION: LED lamps use 60–80% less power than equivalent fluorescent. On a large vessel with 2,000 fluorescent fittings at 40W each = 80 kW load. Converting to 10W LED saves 60 kW continuously. Over 6,000 hours/year = 360,000 kWh = approximately 36 tonnes of HFO saved per year.

2. VFD ON PUMPS: Centrifugal pump/fan power follows cube law: P ∝ n³. Reducing speed by 20% reduces power by 49%. ETO fits VFDs to sea water pumps, ventilation fans, cooling fans — adjusting flow to actual demand rather than running at full capacity continuously.

3. POWER FACTOR CORRECTION: Install or maintain capacitor banks at major motor loads. Poor PF means alternator delivers high reactive kVA — more rotor current, more stator current, more I²R losses, more fuel. Improving PF from 0.75 to 0.95 on a 1000 kW ship load reduces generator current by ~21%.

4. SHORE POWER: When cold ironing is available, stop all auxiliary engines in port. Port stay = 0% of fuel consumption at berth. ETO must maintain shore connection equipment in ready state and know the connection procedure.

5. WASTE HEAT RECOVERY (EXHAUST BOILER): Keep exhaust economiser tubes clean — scale and soot buildup reduces heat transfer efficiency. A clean economiser generates more steam from exhaust heat, reducing the need to fire the auxiliary oil-fired boiler.

6. ACCURATE ENERGY MONITORING: ETO installs and maintains energy meters on main consumers. Accurate data → identify highest-consumption items → target for improvement. Required for CII calculation under DCS (Data Collection System).

7. POWER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM OPTIMISATION: Ensure PMS trips non-running generators promptly and starts standby generators only when needed. Avoid unnecessary parallel running of generators at low combined load.

3.1 Dead Front Panel — Definition and Voltage Limits

Dead front panel is one of the most specifically asked questions in the electrical survey context — surveyors and examiners ask it consistently, and candidates have reported that standard notes sometimes give incorrect answers. The correct, accepted definition from ORAL2026 and question bank cross-referencing is: a dead front panel is a switchboard or control panel design where no live conductors, busbars, or circuit breakers are accessible from the front of the panel during normal operation — the operating handles, buttons, and indicators are on the front face, but the live parts are behind barriers, shutters, or an insulating face plate. The panel can be operated from the front without risk of contact with live conductors. The term 'dead front' specifically means the front face presents NO live metal — all accessible surfaces from the operating position are at earth potential or safely insulated.

A critical distinction for MSB survey: a panel is considered dead front when it is designed so that circuit breakers CANNOT be opened or withdrawn while the front panel door or cover is open, OR the design ensures that even with the front door open, no live parts are exposed to touch. As stated in the question bank note: 'Bina circuit break kiye open nhi kar sakte' — without circuit break, you cannot open the panel. This is the safety interlock principle. The voltage limits applicable to dead front panels (relevant for ETO oral): for dead front panels, accessible metalwork must be at earth potential. The standard insulation requirement is that the front panel face must be tested to withstand the applicable test voltage — for 440V AC systems, the test voltage is typically 2000V AC (per IEC 60092-302). For DC systems, the maximum allowable voltage for accessible conductors in dead front construction is typically 50V DC (SELV — Safety Extra Low Voltage) or the panel must have additional protection.
4.1 ACB — All Trips and Their Working

The Air Circuit Breaker (ACB) on the generator has multiple protective trips, each serving a different purpose. The ETO must know the working and test method for all of them — this is a direct examination requirement across all question banks. The main trips on a generator ACB are: overcurrent trip (OCR), reverse power trip (RPR), under-voltage trip (UVT), over-voltage trip, under-frequency trip, and earth fault trip. Each is tested differently.
4.2 UVT Coil — Working and Significance

The UVT (Under-Voltage Trip) coil is a critical but often misunderstood component of the ACB. It is a continuous-duty electromagnetic coil connected across the generator terminal voltage (or via a control transformer deriving voltage from the generator terminals). As long as the generator is producing rated voltage, the coil is energised — it holds a mechanical latch in the ACB in the tripped position PREVENTED from releasing, or more precisely, it holds the ACB in the CLOSED position by maintaining the latch. When voltage falls below ~70–80% of rated, the electromagnetic force of the coil drops below the spring force holding the latch, and the latch releases — the ACB trips under its stored spring energy.

The UVT coil also serves as the fundamental safety mechanism for the ACB: the manual safety release switch in the ACB trip circuit is wired in series with the UVT coil supply. When this switch is opened (for safety isolation), the UVT coil is de-energised regardless of generator voltage — the ACB trips immediately. This is why the UVT coil is sometimes called the shunt trip coil in some designs — however, technically a shunt trip coil is a separate momentary-energised coil that actively trips the breaker when a fault signal is applied, while the UVT coil is a continuous-duty holding coil. Both may be fitted on the same ACB.

Overspeed protection is a mandatory safety system for diesel generators and the main engine, required by SOLAS and class rules. Overspeed occurs when engine speed exceeds the maximum safe operating RPM — typically 10–15% above rated speed — due to sudden loss of load (generator ACB trips while engine is at full load) or fuel injection failure (injector sticking open). The overspeed trip must stop the engine immediately to prevent mechanical failure (connecting rod, crankshaft, turbocharger overspeed). Testing the overspeed trip is specifically asked by Deswal, Kamath, and appears in the Mumbai question bank as both M/E and A/E overspeed test procedures.

The reverse power relay (RPR) protects the prime mover (diesel engine) from being motored — driven as a motor — by the busbar power when its own output drops to zero or reverses. This occurs when the engine's fuel supply fails (stuck fuel regulator, fuel pump failure) while the generator ACB remains closed and connected to the busbars. Without the reverse power trip, the generator would draw power from the busbars and motor the engine — within seconds the engine would be spinning at synchronous speed with no combustion, causing thermal damage to pistons, damage to the governor, and potential mechanical failure.

1.1 Electrical Specification of Tankers — Key Differences

Tankers carry flammable liquid cargo (crude oil, petroleum products, LPG, LNG, chemicals) which produce flammable vapours. This makes the electrical safety requirements on tankers fundamentally different from cargo ships. The hazardous areas on a tanker — pump rooms, cargo tank decks, cofferdams, void spaces, and any areas where flammable vapour may accumulate — require all electrical equipment to be of explosion-protected (Ex-rated) construction to prevent ignition of the surrounding atmosphere.

Tanker electrical systems typically operate at 440V LV for domestic services and 6.6 kV HV for large cargo pump motors on crude oil tankers. The earthing system is insulated neutral (IT system) as on all ships — first earth fault does not trip supply. However, on some gas tankers and chemical tankers, the insulated neutral is even more critical — earth faults must be detected immediately to prevent a second fault creating a spark risk. IR test (megger) values on tankers: all electrical equipment in hazardous areas is tested to more stringent insulation resistance standards — the minimum acceptable IR for equipment in hazardous areas is typically 5 MΩ (vs 1 MΩ for non-hazardous). The megger used on tankers is the same principle (high DC voltage) but the requirement is for a higher minimum value.

The Inert Gas System (IG System) on oil tankers displaces flammable hydrocarbon vapour in cargo tanks with inert gas (flue gas from the boiler or a dedicated IG generator), maintaining the tank atmosphere with oxygen content below 8% — below which no flammable mixture can exist (hydrocarbon vapour ignition requires minimum ~10% O₂). SOLAS Chapter II-2 Regulation 4 and the IBC Code (for chemical tankers) mandate IG systems on crude oil tankers >20,000 DWT and product tankers >8,000 DWT carrying petroleum products with flashpoint below 60°C. The ETO's role in the IG system is maintenance of all the electrical components — sensors, alarms, solenoid valves, motor controls, and the control panel.

The bow thruster is a transverse propulsion device fitted in a tunnel through the bow of the ship, used for manoeuvring in port without the assistance of tugs. It is driven by a large electric motor (typically 500–3000 kW) or, on older ships, a diesel engine. The ETO is responsible for the electrical system — motor, starter, power supply cables, control panel, and all interlocks. Bow thruster questions are consistently asked in orals with a focus on interlocks, motor type, and troubleshooting.

Static electricity is the accumulation of electrical charge on the surface of an insulating material (or an isolated conductor) due to the movement of charges by contact, friction, or flow. On tankers and chemical carriers, static electricity generation is a serious fire and explosion risk because the discharge of accumulated static charge (electrostatic discharge — ESD) can produce a spark energetic enough to ignite a flammable vapour-air mixture. This is specifically asked across multiple surveyors and all three question banks.

The auto-tension mooring winch automatically maintains a preset tension in the mooring rope regardless of changes in ship position due to tidal movement, draft changes, or surging. Without auto-tension, a mooring line would either become slack (snap risk in surge) or over-tight (break risk when tide rises). The auto-tension function uses feedback control to continuously adjust the drum payout or heave to maintain the set rope tension. This is specifically asked in the Mumbai bank and ORAL2026.

LPG Compressor Room — Electrical Safety Requirements
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what are the electrical requirements for LPG compressor room?"
Hazardous Area Classification:

The LPG compressor room is classified as a Zone 1 hazardous area — a place where an explosive atmosphere in the form of a cloud of flammable gas is likely to occur periodically during normal operation. Propane (LPG) has a flammable range of 2.1–9.5% in air and a vapour density greater than air (it sinks and accumulates at low points).
All electrical equipment inside LPG compressor room MUST be Ex-certified:

1. Ex d (FLAMEPROOF): Equipment enclosed in a housing strong enough to withstand internal explosion without igniting external atmosphere. Used for motor terminal boxes, compressor drive motors, junction boxes. Mark on nameplate: II 2G Ex d IIB T3 (or similar).
2. Ex e (INCREASED SAFETY): Normal equipment with enhanced safety — better seals, wider creepage distances, no sparking parts. Used for lighting fixtures, terminal boxes for non-sparking circuits.
3. Ex i (INTRINSICALLY SAFE): Circuit energy limited below ignition threshold — even if component fails. Used for instruments, sensors, 4–20mA signal circuits.
4. Ex n (Non-incendive): For Zone 2 areas adjacent to compressor room — equipment that cannot ignite atmosphere under normal operating conditions.
Electrical safety measures in LPG compressor room:
1. NO PORTABLE ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT unless certified Ex — including multimeters, clamp meters, hand lamps, mobile phones, walkie-talkies. Only Ex-certified portable test equipment allowed.
2. LIGHT SWITCHES: No standard light switches inside Zone 1. Switches in non-hazardous adjacent space, or Ex e rated switches inside.
3. CABLE ENTRIES: All cable glands must be Ex-certified — double-sealed against gas ingress into wiring. No standard brass or plastic glands.
4. EARTH BONDING: All metallic equipment bonded to ship hull earth — prevents build-up of static electricity which could cause incendive spark. Bonding strap condition checked regularly.

5. FIXED GAS DETECTION: Catalytic bead gas detectors mounted at low points (propane/butane heavier than air). First alarm (~20% LEL): auditory alarm, increased ventilation. High alarm (~40% LEL): automatic power isolation to all non-essential electrical equipment in compressor room.

6. VENTILATION INTERLOCK: Mechanical ventilation maintains minimum 20 air changes/hour. If ventilation fails → automatic trip of electrical power supply to compressor room. Ventilation fan motor must also be Ex-certified.

7. INSPECTION FREQUENCY: Electrical equipment in hazardous areas must be inspected to IEC 60079-17 standard — initial commissioning inspection, periodic inspection (typically annually by competent person), and continuous supervision by ETO during service.
ETO practical responsibilities:

Walk-down inspection: Check all Ex fittings on each watch — look for damaged enclosures, loose terminal box covers, removed plugs or blanks from conduit entries (any of these defeats the Ex protection).

Maintenance work: Any maintenance on Ex equipment requires: (1) Gas-free certificate confirming atmosphere is safe. (2) Permit to work. (3) Restore to Ex condition before re-energising — inspect all cable glands, covers, and seals.
Documentation: Maintain Ex equipment register — lists all Ex equipment in compressor room, their certification details (Ex marking, certificate number), inspection dates, and condition.
Deck Electrical Safety — LPG and Chemical Tankers
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what are the electrical requirements on tanker cargo deck?"
Hazardous Area Zones on Tanker Cargo Deck:
Zone 0: Inside cargo tanks, vapour lines, enclosed spaces with continuous presence of explosive atmosphere.
Zone 1: Within 3 metres of any tank opening, ventilation outlet, gauge opening, loading arm connection, pump flange. Cargo pump rooms. Compressor rooms.
Zone 2: Between 3 and 5 metres from Zone 1 boundaries. Cargo deck outside Zone 1 (for gas carrier).
Deck lighting:
All deck lighting fixtures in Zone 1 and Zone 2: Must be Ex-certified floodlights — typically Ex e (increased safety) or Ex d (flameproof).
No open filament or glass-exposed lamps on cargo deck.
LED fittings now standard — lower heat, longer life, less maintenance but must still be Ex-certified.
Light fitting supports and mounting: Steel conduit system with Ex-certified entries at each fitting — no flexible conduit unless Ex-rated type.
Cargo pump motors and other deck electrical equipment:
Submersible cargo pumps: Motor submerged in cargo — no electrical motor in hazardous atmosphere (motor sealed and process-liquid cooled). Safest option.
Deep well pumps: Motor above deck in non-hazardous area, long shaft extends down into cargo — safe.
Deck-mounted pump motors (older tankers): Must be Ex d flameproof certified. Motor housing designed to contain any internal ignition.
Electrical deck tools: Strictly air-powered tools on cargo deck. No 240V or 440V portable power tools. Battery-powered tools only if Ex-i certified.

Reefer Container — ETO Monitoring Routines
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what do you do for reefer container monitoring as ETO?"

Reefer containers (refrigerated containers) are powered by the ship's electrical system through receptacle connections on deck or in holds. ETO is responsible for maintaining the power supply system and monitoring container performance.
Monitoring frequency: Typically every 6–12 hours on passage (per company SMS). Every 3–6 hours for critical cargo (pharmaceuticals, live seafood).
Regular monitoring checks:

1. SET POINT vs ACTUAL TEMPERATURE: Compare required cargo temperature (on door data plate or cargo manifest) with actual supply air temperature on controller display. Deviation >1°C warrants investigation.

2. SUPPLY AND RETURN AIR TEMPERATURES: Supply air (cold air entering cargo) should be at setpoint. Return air (warm air leaving cargo) is typically 2–5°C above supply. Large difference indicates heavy heat load or door seal problem. No difference = possible airflow blockage.

3. CURRENT DRAW: Check amperage of compressor motor (via socket panel or clamp meter). Compare with expected value from manufacturer rating plate. High current = overloaded compressor or locked bearing. Low/zero current = compressor not running.
4. ALARM STATUS: Check reefer monitoring system panel (or each unit) for active alarms: high/low temperature alarm, compressor fault, defrost running, high pressure cut-out.
5. DEFROST: Check defrost cycle is occurring correctly (typically every 6–8 hours, lasts 20–30 minutes). Ice build-up on evaporator coils reduces cooling efficiency — defrost must melt this ice.
6. CONDENSER CONDITION: Touch condenser surface — should be warm (40–50°C). If cold: refrigerant charge issue. If very hot: dirty condenser — needs cleaning.
7. POWER SUPPLY: Check socket and plug condition — look for burning marks, smell of overheating. Measure supply voltage at socket — within ±10% of rated. Check socket amperage versus rating.
8. LOGBOOK ENTRY: Record all readings in reefer monitoring log: container number, position, setpoint, supply temp, return temp, current, alarm status, date/time, name.
Alarm response procedure:
TEMPERATURE EXCURSION (actual temp deviating from setpoint):
a. Check compressor is running (listen, check current).
b. Check condenser — clean if dirty.
c. Check sight glass in refrigerant circuit — bubbles indicate low charge.
d. Check defrost has not just run and recovery is in progress.
e. Check door seals — air leakage causes temperature rise.
f. If compressor fault: attempt reset. If fault persists: connect portable generator unit (Clip-on reefer unit) or advise cargo officer of potential cargo loss.
POWER FAILURE TO SOCKET: Check circuit breaker, check socket fuse, check plug condition. Restore power urgently — reefer cargo has limited thermal mass.
IGF Code 2026 Amendments — Gas-Fuelled Ships

🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: The IGF Code (International Code of Safety for Ships Using Gases or Other Low-Flashpoint Fuels) has been updated effective January 1, 2026. Surveyors will ask about gas bunkering safety, fuel preparation rooms, and alternative fuels.
Change 1 — Bunkering Safety Checklist: Mandatory New Parameters

As LNG and other low-flashpoint fuels become standard, the IGF Code was updated to close gaps in bunkering safety documentation. From 1 January 2026, the pre-bunkering safety checklist and ship-to-ship safety agreement must explicitly document and agree the following BEFORE bunkering of LNG or other gases begins:
1. Minimum and maximum transfer pressures — agreed and recorded for both ship and supplier sides.
2. Minimum and maximum transfer temperatures — agreed and recorded.
3. Relief valve settings — checked, confirmed, and recorded on both ship and bunker supply side before transfer begins.

Why: Overpressure events and temperature excursions (e.g. warm LNG causing pressure surges) have caused near-misses during gas bunkering. Documenting these parameters ensures both parties have agreed safe operating limits and that relief valves are correctly set before any transfer begins. ETO role: Verify all pressure transmitters and temperature sensors on the gas fuel bunkering line are operational before bunkering. Confirm relief valve set-point records are current and monitoring/alarm system is functioning (high pressure alarm, low temperature alarm). These sensor readings feed directly into the mandatory checklist parameters.
Change 2 — Mandatory 5 kg Dry Powder Extinguisher in Fuel Preparation Rooms

New requirement: A portable 5 kg dry powder (DCP) fire extinguisher must now be physically placed inside each fuel preparation room on gas-fuelled ships. The fuel preparation room (also called gas valve unit room or fuel conditioning room) is the enclosed space where LNG is vaporised, conditioned, and fed to the engines. It contains high-pressure gas piping, valves, and conditioning equipment — a gas leak in this space presents a significant fire and explosion risk. DCP rapidly knocks down gas jet flames and burning cryogenic liquid puddles by interrupting the chain reaction of combustion. ETO role: Confirm the 5 kg DCP extinguisher is mounted in the fuel preparation room, within date, correctly labelled, and included in the monthly portable extinguisher inspection rounds. Class/flag surveyor will check for its presence as a specific IGF Code compliance item. Record in PMS.
Change 3 — Toxic Cargoes (Ammonia) Permitted as Ship Fuel on Type 2G/2PG Ships

New permission (effective 1 January 2026): Toxic cargoes — specifically ammonia (NH₃) — carried on Type 2G or 2PG gas carriers are now legally permitted under the IGF Code to be used as the ship’s own propulsion fuel. Ammonia (NH₃) produces no CO₂ when burned, making it a zero-carbon shipping fuel. Type 2G/2PG ships are already built to carry it as cargo, so using cargo as fuel eliminates the need for separate fuel tanks. KEY HAZARD: Ammonia is TOXIC — TLV-TWA 25 ppm, IDLH 300 ppm. A fuel system leak is simultaneously a toxic gas emergency. All machinery spaces with ammonia fuel systems require continuous NH₃ gas detection, remote isolation valves, and SCBA access. ETO role: Maintain NH₃ electrochemical gas detection system. Calibrate against certified reference gas. Test alarm levels (warning: ~25 ppm, evacuation: ~50 ppm). Ensure remote solenoid shut-off valves on fuel lines are functional. Maintain SCBA sets at all entry points to fuel spaces.

1.1 Hogging and Sagging

Hogging and sagging describe the longitudinal bending deformation of a ship's hull caused by the distribution of weight and buoyancy forces along the ship's length. These are fundamental structural concepts that an ETO must understand because excessive hogging or sagging leads to structural stress in the hull plating, frames, and girders, and in extreme cases can cause hull failure.

Sagging occurs when the centre of the ship is supported by less buoyancy than its ends — the ship bends concave upward, like a hammock. This happens when: heavy cargo or ballast is concentrated amidships, the ship rides a wave trough amidships (wave crest at bow and stern), or the ship is loaded in port with heavy tanks at mid-length. The keel is in tension (stretched) and the deck plating is in compression during sagging. Hogging occurs when the centre of the ship has more buoyancy support than the ends — the ship bends concave downward, like a bridge arching up. This happens when: the bow and stern are heavily loaded (or the ship rides over a wave crest amidships), or the ship is in ballast with heavy ballast tanks at the ends. The keel is in compression and the deck plating is in tension during hogging. Both conditions create longitudinal bending stress — the hull girder (the ship's main structural beam) must be strong enough to resist these bending moments throughout the ship's operational life.

Ship stability is the ability of a ship to return to its upright position after being inclined by an external force (waves, wind, cargo shift). It is governed by the relative positions of the Centre of Gravity (G) and the Metacentre (M). The ETO is not a stability officer but must understand basic stability concepts as they affect electrical system operation — particularly emergency generator operation, power supply during heavy rolling, and the consequence of flooding on electrical spaces.

The frame number (or frame designation) of an electric motor is a standardised alphanumeric code that describes the physical dimensions and mounting configuration of the motor. It is used by engineers to ensure a replacement motor will fit the same mounting footprint, coupling dimensions, and shaft size as the original. The frame number appears on the motor nameplate and is standardised by NEMA (National Electrical Manufacturers Association) in North America and IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) internationally. This is a very repeatedly asked question across multiple surveyors — the examiner specifically wants to know what information the frame number conveys.

The Emergency Switchboard (ESB) is a separate switchboard supplied by the emergency generator (and, during normal operation, by the main switchboard through an automatic changeover arrangement) to ensure that essential services remain powered during a blackout. SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 42 specifies which services must be connected to the emergency source of power. The arrangement and equipment connected to the ESB is a specific question from ORAL2026.

Sequential starting (sequential load restoration) is the controlled, timed reconnection of machinery and equipment to the ship's busbars after a blackout (complete loss of power) has been restored. If all loads were reconnected simultaneously after a blackout, the combined starting current surge from all motors restarting at once would immediately overload the restored generator and cause a second blackout. Sequential starting prevents this by reconnecting loads in priority order with time delays between each group, allowing the generator time to recover voltage and frequency between successive motor starts.

1.1 Lifeboat Electrical Equipment — Complete List

The lifeboat is the primary survival craft on a ship. Its electrical systems must be maintained in fully operational condition at all times. The ETO is directly responsible for the electrical equipment within and associated with the lifeboat and davit system. SOLAS Chapter III and the LSA Code (International Life-Saving Appliance Code) specify the minimum electrical equipment requirements for lifeboats.

Lifeboat battery replacement and commissioning is the single most asked LSA topic across all question banks — asked in virtually every oral examination. The examiner specifically tests whether the candidate knows the ordering specifications, what to check when the new battery arrives, and the commissioning procedure. Cold weather specification is specifically asked by Gadkar and others.

The battery room (emergency battery room) stores the ship's emergency lead-acid or alkaline batteries and, on some vessels, the lifeboat battery charger and UPS batteries. During charging, lead-acid batteries produce hydrogen gas (H₂) — a highly flammable, colourless, and odourless gas that forms an explosive mixture with air at concentrations of 4–74% by volume. This makes the battery room a potential hazardous area requiring specific safety arrangements. These are repeatedly asked across all three question banks.

SCBA — Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sudhir, ALL — checks, time of operation, number onboard
SCBA: Provides breathable air from compressed air cylinder — independent of ship's atmosphere. Used for fire fighting, enclosed space entry.
Time of operation: 30 minutes (standard). Some units 45 minutes or 1 hour.

Checks before use: (1) Cylinder pressure — minimum 90% of rated pressure (typically 200–300 bar). (2) Demand valve operation — press button, feel airflow. (3) Face mask seal — no cracks. (4) Low pressure alarm test — reduce pressure by breathing down to alarm point (~55 bar) — alarm must sound.
SOLAS requirement: At least 2 SCBA per ship (cargo). Each equipped with spare cylinder. Fire-fighting equipment includes SCBA.
Maintenance: Annual inspection by approved service station. Check cylinder hydrostatic test date (every 5 years for composite cylinders). Check all seals, demand valve, pressure gauge.
EEBD — Emergency Escape Breathing Device
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Sudhir, Prakash — full form, time, number, locations
EEBD = Emergency Escape Breathing Device. For ESCAPE ONLY — not for fire fighting.
Time of operation: Minimum 10 minutes (SOLAS minimum). Most modern units 15 minutes.
Number required: SOLAS II-2: At least 2 per space where crew work (engine room, bridge). Additional units based on crew complement.
Locations: Engine control room, main engine platform, engine room entry points, bridge, accommodation escape routes — any location where crew could be trapped.
Working: Hood-type or mouthpiece-type. Contains compressed air or chemical oxygen generator. Pull on, breathe normally — filters CO and some gases OR provides clean air.
EEBD vs SCBA: EEBD = escape only, 10–15 minutes. SCBA = fire fighting + rescue, 30–60 minutes, positive pressure.
How many persons use one EEBD: ONE person per unit — not shared.
Immersion Suit — Donning and Tests
Donning time: Must be donned in 2 minutes (including lifejacket) — SOLAS requirement.
Donning drill: Annual drill for all crew. Practice donning without assistance.
Tests/inspection: Check for cracks/holes — inflate by mouth and observe. Check zip operation — smooth, no corrosion. Check reflective tape. Check buoyancy device. Check face seal.
Hydrostatic test: Not required individually — manufacturer batch testing. Service at approved station every 3 years typically.
Thermal protection: Must maintain body core temperature > 34°C after 6 hours in water at 0–2°C.
Rescue Boat vs Fast Rescue Boat — Difference
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Srivastava — 'difference between rescue boat and fast rescue boat'
Rescue boat: Minimum 5 knots speed. Can be rigid or inflatable. Carried by all cargo ships. Fitted with engine, painter line, first aid kit, bailer.
Fast Rescue Boat (FRB): Minimum 8 knots speed. Rigid hull (RIB or GRP). Required on passenger ships and some offshore vessels. Can manoeuvre quickly to retrieve persons from water.
Lowering speed: Rescue boat — no minimum, controlled descent. FRB — designed for rapid deployment.
Hoisting speed: Maximum 0.3 m/s for rescue boats. FRB — faster.
SOLAS: All cargo ships >500 GT carry at least 1 rescue boat. Typically combined with a lifeboat (survival craft/rescue boat combination).
SOLAS Liferaft — Phase A and Phase B Equipment Pack
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Srivastava — 'what is Phase A and Phase B in liferaft?'
SOLAS liferafts have two equipment packs depending on trade route:

SOLAS A Pack (Offshore pack — ships going beyond 20nm): Full survival equipment. Includes: (1) Seasick pills and bags (6 per person). (2) Thermal protective aids — 10% of capacity or 2. (3) Survival rations — 10,000 kJ per person. (4) Fresh water — 1.5 litres per person + desalting kits. (5) Signalling: 4 rocket parachute flares, 6 hand flares, 2 buoyant smoke. (6) First aid kit. (7) Fishing tackle. (8) Jackknife. (9) Luminescent electric light. (10) Radar reflector. (11) Instructions.
SOLAS B Pack (Inshore pack — ships within 20nm of land): Reduced pack. Fewer rations and water. Fewer flares. Simpler equipment.
How to generate water if finished: Collect rainwater using canopy. Use desalting kit (chemical). Do NOT drink seawater.
Lifeboat Battery — Specifications
Lifeboat battery powers: Starting motor for engine, lights, communications (radio), alarm.
Specifications: Must be capable of starting engine in cold conditions (typically -15°C). Lead-acid or nickel-cadmium (NiCd) batteries used — NiCd better for cold weather.
SOLAS requirement: Battery must be capable of operating for 12 hours (lights, communications, engine starting).
Maintenance: Check electrolyte level (lead-acid), check specific gravity, check terminal connections, charge fully after any use, test load regularly.
Trickle charging: Continuous low-level charging to keep battery fully charged during storage. Prevents sulphation of lead-acid battery. ETO must verify charger is operating — check charging current.
Pyrotechnic Signals — Regulations
Rocket parachute flare: Burns red, minimum 30 seconds, height 300m minimum. Used for distress signalling over long range.
Hand flare: Burns red, 1 minute minimum. Short range, close rescue operations.
Buoyant smoke signal: Orange smoke, 3 minutes minimum. Daytime distress — visible to aircraft.
SOLAS requirement on cargo ships: 12 rocket parachute flares (bridge), 6 hand flares (2 per lifeboat/liferaft), 2 buoyant smoke signals.
Shelf life: 3 years from date of manufacture. Must be replaced before expiry.
Storage: Watertight containers. Not near heat sources. Bridge or embarkation station.

Lifeboat Sprinkler System — Complete Design and Operation
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "explain the lifeboat fire protection/sprinkler system — design and operation"
Background — why fire protection on lifeboat?

On oil and chemical tankers, a fire or explosion may result in burning oil spreading across the sea surface. The crew must abandon ship through this burning oil layer. Without fire protection, a conventional glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) lifeboat hull would melt or ignite within seconds in this environment. Fire protection systems allow the lifeboat to pass through the burning area and survive long enough to clear the fire zone.
SOLAS Requirement:
SOLAS III/31.1 and LSA Code 4.8: On oil tankers, chemical tankers, gas carriers, and ships carrying dangerous goods — totally enclosed lifeboats must be either:
(a) Built from fire-resistant materials (which can withstand 8 minutes in burning petroleum), OR
(b) Fitted with an approved fire protection system (water spray)
Most ships use option (b) — water spray system — as it is retrofit-compatible and provides continuous protection.
System Design:
1. SEA COCK: Bottom-mounted sea water intake. Opens automatically when lifeboat is water-borne and engine starts.
2. ENGINE-DRIVEN PUMP: Centrifugal pump driven directly from lifeboat engine crankshaft via belt or gear drive. Pump starts when engine starts.
3. DISTRIBUTION PIPING: Stainless steel or copper alloy piping runs along the spine of the lifeboat, with branches to each side.
4. SPRAY NOZZLES: Full-spray nozzles positioned to completely cover the outer hull surface — top deck, sides, and forward/aft surfaces. Designed to produce a continuous water film, not just spray.
5. MANUAL VALVE: Inside lifeboat — coxswain opens this to activate spray system. Also serves as system isolation for maintenance.
6. FLOW RATE: Designed to cover total hull surface area with a minimum flow rate (typically 3–5 litres/m²/minute).
7. DRAINAGE: Spray water drains off hull by gravity — must not pool on deck (weighted down) or block drainage channels.
Operation:
Before entering fire area: Coxswain starts lifeboat engine, opens sea cock, opens spray valve.
Continuous operation: As long as engine runs and sea cock is in water — system self-sustaining.
Duration: Indefinite — seawater supply is unlimited from surrounding sea.
Limitation: System only works when lifeboat is water-borne (sea cock submerged). Cannot be tested out of water (in davit) with full system — only partial test possible.
Maintenance and testing:
1. VISUAL INSPECTION (monthly): Check all spray nozzles for blockage or corrosion. Check piping joints for leaks or corrosion. Check sea cock condition.

2. FLOW TEST (quarterly or per PMS): Launch lifeboat in sheltered water. Start engine. Open sea cock and spray valve. Observe all nozzles spraying uniformly, check flow from each side, check no blocked nozzles.
3. NOZZLE CLEANING: If any nozzle blocked — disassemble and clean with wire or compressed air. Salt deposits are common in tropical service.
4. RECORD: Log test date, which nozzles tested, any defects found and corrected.
5. SURVEY: Class surveyor will witness quarterly test and inspect system condition.
Lifeboat Battery — Air Bottle Maintenance and Capacity Testing
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked about lifeboat battery and air bottle maintenance
Lifeboat Engine Starting Battery:
Type: Sealed lead-acid (VRLA/AGM) or conventional flooded lead-acid — 12V or 24V system.
Function: Powers electric starter motor to crank lifeboat diesel engine. Also powers lifeboat interior lighting, bilge pump, and engine panel instruments.
SOLAS requirement: Battery must be capable of starting the engine after being stored for 1 month at the lowest expected temperature without recharging.

Trickle charger: Shore power-connected trickle charger keeps battery at full charge while lifeboat in davit. ETO must verify trickle charger output voltage (~13.5–13.8V for 12V system) and current during routine checks.
Battery maintenance procedure:
1. MONTHLY CHECK: Verify trickle charger is connected and charging (charger indicator green). Measure battery terminal voltage — fully charged: 12.6–12.8V (12V system). Record.
2. ELECTROLYTE (flooded type): Check electrolyte level above plates. Top up with DISTILLED water only — NEVER tap water (mineral impurities). Check specific gravity: >1.265 = fully charged.
3. TERMINALS: Inspect for corrosion (white/green deposits). Clean with dilute bicarbonate solution if corroded. Apply terminal grease after cleaning.

4. CAPACITY TEST (annual or as required by class): Fully charge battery. Disconnect trickle charger. Discharge at rated 20-hour current and measure total Ah delivered — must equal or exceed rated capacity.
5. REPLACE IF: Capacity test fails. Voltage drops below 10.5V under load during start attempt. Age >3–4 years (regardless of apparent condition).
Compressed Air Bottle maintenance:
1. MONTHLY: Check pressure gauge — must be at or above 90% of rated working pressure. Low pressure → recharge.

2. RECHARGING: Use BREATHING QUALITY air compressor only (Class E compressed air per ISO 8573-1). NEVER industrial compressed air — oil aerosol contamination creates toxic breathing air and can destroy lung tissue. Record recharge in lifeboat log.

3. ANNUAL: Physical inspection of cylinder body — corrosion, heat exposure, mechanical damage. Check valve condition. Pressure test cylinder per national regulation (typically every 5 years — hydrostatic test at 1.5× working pressure).
4. CERTIFICATE: Pressure vessel certificate must be current and available for class/SOLAS survey inspection.
Latest LSA Code Amendments (2026 and Beyond)

🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Four new LSA Code amendments directly relevant to the ETO oral exam. Surveyors are actively asking about lifeboat ventilation, hook safety design, lowering speed limits, and updated lifejacket testing requirements.
Amendment 1 — Totally Enclosed Lifeboat Ventilation System (From 1 January 2029)

New requirement: Totally enclosed lifeboats installed on or after 1 January 2029 must be fitted with a dedicated ventilation system capable of providing a minimum of 5 cubic metres of fresh air per hour per person, independently of the lifeboat engine.

Why introduced: Investigations into lifeboat incidents found that in hot climates and when fully loaded with persons, CO₂ levels inside totally enclosed lifeboats rise rapidly and temperatures can exceed 50°C within 30 minutes. Several incidents involved crew incapacitation from heat and CO₂ buildup before the lifeboat could escape the casualty vessel. The ventilation system addresses both heat stress and CO₂ accumulation independently of the main engine (which may not be running during first minutes of launch).

ETO role: Maintain the electric ventilation fan motor, its DC power supply (battery-backed), and ducting. Verify the system operates independently of the main engine. Test airflow quarterly. Check fan motor insulation and connection at monthly lifeboat rounds. For existing lifeboats (pre-2029), check whether retrofitting is required by the ship's class society — some flag states may require earlier compliance.
Amendment 2 — Lifeboat Single Fall and Hook Safety Design

New requirement: For lifeboats using a single fall and hook system, the hook mechanism must be designed so that it CANNOT support any load unless the hook is completely and correctly reset in the closed/locked position.

Why introduced: Several fatal accidents occurred when a lifeboat hook appeared to be reset (latched) but was only partially engaged. When the lifeboat was next hoisted and reached the boat deck level, the hook released under load, dropping the loaded lifeboat. The new design requirement makes it physically impossible for the hook to support ANY load unless the mechanism is fully seated and locked — a partial reset cannot bear weight. This eliminates the failure mode where a partially reset hook appears secure but releases under load.

ETO role: During monthly and quarterly lifeboat checks, verify the hook reset mechanism is functioning correctly — check that the positive locking indicator (where fitted) shows fully locked before any hoisting test. Check the interlock between the hook position and the on-load release operating handle. Report immediately to C/E if the hook mechanism shows signs of wear, corrosion, or incomplete seating. This is a safety-critical item — do NOT attempt to hoist the lifeboat if there is any doubt about hook integrity.
Amendment 3 — Maximum Lowering Speed for Survival Craft Capped at 1.3 m/s
New requirement: The maximum permitted lowering speed for survival craft (lifeboats and rescue boats) is now explicitly capped at 1.3 metres per second (approximately 78 metres per minute).

Why: High lowering speeds cause hard water impacts that have injured persons inside lifeboats, and have also caused hook release difficulties (boat bouncing and re-loading falls). The 1.3 m/s cap standardises a safe maximum speed across all survival craft designs.

ETO role: During davit motor maintenance and brake adjustment, verify that the centrifugal brake (gravity davit) or the motor speed control (powered davit) limits lowering speed to not more than 1.3 m/s. Check the manufacturer's specification — if the davit has a centrifugal speed governor, verify its set-point. If the davit uses a motor brake system, verify the speed governor or VFD maximum speed parameter is set to comply. Record the lowering speed check in the lifeboat maintenance log. Surveyor will ask: “What is the maximum lowering speed?” — answer: 1.3 m/s.
Amendment 4 — Lifejacket In-Water Performance Testing (From 1 January 2026)
New requirement: Lifejackets supplied onboard after 1 January 2026 must pass new mandatory in-water performance tests covering buoyancy retention and stability in water.

What the new tests require: Buoyancy test: lifejacket must maintain required buoyancy (minimum 150 N for adult lifejackets) after 24 hours continuous immersion in water at the test temperature — confirming buoyancy material does not absorb water over time. Stability test: a mannequin wearing the lifejacket must be turned face-up from a face-down position in water within 5 seconds without assistance (self-righting test) — confirming the lifejacket correctly supports an unconscious person in the correct floating position. These tests must be passed for type approval of new lifejackets.

Why introduced: Post-accident analysis of drowning fatalities involving lifejackets found that some approved lifejackets lost buoyancy after extended immersion (foam absorbed water) and many failed to reliably turn an unconscious person face-up in real sea conditions (waves, clothing drag). The new in-water tests are conducted in a pool under controlled conditions to directly verify the performance that matters in an actual survival situation.

ETO awareness: The ETO does not conduct these type approval tests — they are performed by the manufacturer. However, the ETO should know that lifejackets procured after 1 January 2026 must be of a type that has passed these tests (evidenced by the type approval certificate). When ordering replacement lifejackets, verify with the supplier that the type is approved under the new standard. Existing onboard lifejackets (pre-2026 type) remain valid until their service life expires.
LSA Amendments — Quick Revision Summary

Amendment 1 — Lifeboat ventilation (from Jan 2029): Totally enclosed lifeboats must have ventilation providing 5 m³/hr/person, independent of main engine. Addresses CO₂ and heat buildup. ETO: maintain fan motor and battery backup.

Amendment 2 — Hook safety design: Single fall hook CANNOT support load unless completely reset. Prevents accidental drop from partial hook engagement. ETO: verify locking indicator and interlock at every quarterly check.

Cold ironing (also called shore power connection or Alternative Maritime Power — AMP) is the practice of connecting a ship to shore-based electrical power while berthed at port, shutting down the ship's diesel generators, and taking all power from the shore supply. This eliminates exhaust emissions from running generators at berth — a significant environmental benefit in port cities. Cold ironing is increasingly mandated at ports in California, northern Europe, and major Asian ports as part of local air quality regulations. The term 'cold ironing' comes from the historical practice when ships used coal fires and the firemen (stokers) were given shore leave while in port — the boilers and engines went cold — the irons (the colloquial name for the ship's machinery/engines) went cold. Hence 'cold ironing.'

The wrong way alarm (also called reverse rotation alarm or wrong direction alarm) is a safety device fitted on certain critical machinery — particularly the main engine, steering gear pumps, and essential motors — that detects if the shaft or rotor is rotating in the wrong direction (opposite to commanded direction) and raises an alarm to prevent mechanical damage or operational failure.

Permit to work (PTW) systems ensure safe working on electrical equipment by formally documenting the isolation, testing, and working procedure. On ships, several distinct types of permits may be issued for different types of electrical work. Understanding all permit types is specifically asked in multiple banks.
