Cable Ordering — Full Specification List
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how do you order a replacement marine cable? What specifications do you give?"

This is a very practical question. Surveyors want to confirm the ETO understands what makes a marine cable different from a standard industrial cable. A marine cable order must specify ALL of the following:
1. CONDUCTOR MATERIAL: Copper (standard for all ship cables — good conductivity, flexibility). Specify: STRANDED copper (most cables — flexible) or SOLID copper (fixed installations only).
2. NUMBER OF CORES: 1C (single), 2C, 3C (3-phase no neutral), 4C (3-phase + neutral), or multi-core instrumentation cable (specify exact count).
3. CONDUCTOR CROSS-SECTION: in mm² — e.g. 1.5mm², 2.5mm², 4mm², 6mm², 10mm², 16mm², 25mm², 35mm², 50mm², 70mm², 95mm². Never specify by AWG on marine cables.

4. INSULATION MATERIAL: XLPE (cross-linked polyethylene — best thermal performance, 90°C rated, water-resistant). EPR (ethylene propylene rubber — flexible, excellent for LV and MV). PVC (acceptable up to 70°C — lower-spec but common for internal wiring).

5. OUTER SHEATH: LSZH (Low Smoke Zero Halogen — mandatory for new-build ships, reduces toxic gases in fire). PVC (older ships — produces HCl in fire — being phased out). Rubber (flexible duty, deck use).

6. ARMOUR: SWA (Steel Wire Armoured — mechanical protection, general use). DSTA (Double Steel Tape Armoured — for cables in contact with machinery, trays without fixing). None (unarmoured — use in conduit or protected trays).
7. VOLTAGE RATING: 0.6/1 kV (600V phase-to-neutral / 1000V phase-to-phase) for 440V distribution systems. 3.6/6 kV for HV feeders. Specify voltage class matching system voltage.

8. MARINE STANDARD: IEC 60092-350 (ships and mobile offshore units — this is the key marine standard). Or BS 6883 (UK ships). The marine standard means cable is tested for flame retardance, oil resistance, salt water resistance.
9. FLAME RETARDANCE: IEC 60332-1 (single cable flame test) minimum. For bunched cables in trays: IEC 60332-3 (category A, B, or C). LSZH sheath required by IEC 60092-376 on new ships.

10. SCREEN (for control/instrumentation cables): Overall copper braid or aluminium foil screen — specifies EMI (electromagnetic interference) shielding. Required for 4–20mA, 0–10V, and communication cables near heavy electrical equipment.
11. LENGTH: In metres — continuous (no joints). Specify slightly longer than needed — allow for connections and routing.
12. DRUM vs COIL: Specify delivery on drum for long lengths (easier unrolling) or coiled for short lengths.
Example cable order:
"3 core × 10 mm² stranded copper, XLPE insulated, LSZH sheathed, SWA armoured, 0.6/1 kV, IEC 60092-350, Category A flame retardance, 75 metres continuous on drum."
440V Circuit — Low IR Reading Systematic Troubleshooting
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "440V motor circuit megger reading is 0.3 MΩ — what do you do systematically?"

This is a classic practical question. Surveyor wants to see systematic fault isolation — not just "I rewind the motor." The correct approach is to ISOLATE each component and test individually to find the fault.
Procedure — fault isolation:
1. OBTAIN PERMIT TO WORK: Isolate at MSB (lock off, tag out). Prove dead at load end with approved voltage indicator.
2. DISCONNECT BOTH ENDS OF CABLE: Remove cable from motor terminal box. Remove cable from MSB feeder terminal. Now the cable is isolated from all equipment.
3. MEGGER THE CABLE ALONE: Test each core to earth (each core to armour/screen). Test each core to each other core. Megger voltage: 500V DC (for 0.6/1kV cable). Result:
HIGH IR (>100 MΩ): Cable is healthy. Fault is in motor or starter.
LOW IR on cable: Cable has an insulation fault. Continue to step 4.
4. IF CABLE IS FAULTY: Test each core individually. Note which core(s) are faulty.
Both faults on one core: Localised damage (pinch point, hot spot, water ingress at gland).
All cores to earth faulty: Water ingress in cable run — flooding of cable tray or conduit.
Core-to-core fault: Cable pinched — mechanical damage.
5. IF CABLE IS HEALTHY — TEST MOTOR: Disconnect motor terminal links (separate star point). Megger each individual phase winding to earth: U1–E, V1–E, W1–E. Megger voltage: 500V for 440V motor.
Minimum acceptable: 1 MΩ for 440V motor at test temperature.
If motor IR is low: Check motor temperature (IR decreases with temperature — correct to 40°C using temperature coefficient). Check for moisture ingress.
6. IF MOTOR WINDING IR IS LOW:

Can motor be dried out? Yes if: No physical damage, IR responds slowly (moisture not contamination). Method: Run motor at low load to warm windings. Or use electric heater inside motor frame overnight.
If drying does not raise IR: Motor requires rewinding — condemned.
7. TEST STARTER COMPONENTS SEPARATELY: Contactor coil, overload relay, cable to motor — test each component to earth to identify if starter wiring is at fault.
8. BEFORE RE-ENERGISING: Confirm all IR values above 1 MΩ. All cable terminations remade correctly. Motor rotation direction verified. C/E or senior officer signs off.
Common mistake surveyors look for: ETOs who say "I would megger the circuit" without explaining HOW they isolate and identify WHICH component is faulty. Always describe the isolation process.
Shore Connection (Cold Ironing) — Full Connection Procedure
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked step-by-step shore power connection procedure as ETO

Shore power (cold ironing / AMP — Alternative Maritime Power): Connecting ship's electrical distribution to shore supply when in port — stopping auxiliary generators and reducing emissions. ETO leads this operation.
Pre-arrival preparation:
1. Confirm with port agent: shore supply voltage (typically 6.6 kV, 11 kV, or 440V), frequency (50 or 60 Hz), connector type (IEC 62613 or port-specific), available power (kVA).
2. Check ship shore connection box: ratings match shore supply. Protection relay settings reviewed.
3. Prepare shore power cable: visual inspection for insulation damage, connector condition, cable length.
4. Brief deck crew: who assists with cable handling, what signals to use.
Connection procedure — step by step:
1. REDUCE SHIP LOAD: Transfer non-essential loads off or to minimum — reduces inrush when switching. Running generators share load before transfer.
2. CONNECT CABLE (DE-ENERGISED): Connect cable from shore connection box to shore connection point — with shore power circuit breaker OPEN (not live). Never connect live cable.
3. MEASURE SHORE VOLTAGE AT SHIP END: Use calibrated voltmeter at ship side of shore connection terminals. Verify shore voltage = ship voltage (within ±5%).

4. CHECK PHASE SEQUENCE: Use phase sequence meter (phase rotation meter). Verify shore phase rotation matches ship system (ACB, BCA, or whatever is ship's standard). WRONG PHASE SEQUENCE will cause all motors to run in REVERSE — catastrophic.
5. CHECK FREQUENCY: Confirm shore frequency equals ship frequency (50 Hz vs 50 Hz, or 60 Hz vs 60 Hz). Incompatible frequency cannot be directly paralleled.

6. SYNCHRONISE: Close shore connection breaker at MSB. Use synchroscope (or auto-synchroniser if fitted) to match shore voltage phase angle with running generator phase angle. Close shore ACB when synchroscope pointer at 12 o'clock.
7. TRANSFER LOAD: Increase shore load (close shore bus-tie, transfer feeders). Simultaneously reduce generator load. Watch kW meters.
8. TRIP GENERATOR: When shore is carrying full ship load and generator is at minimum load — trip generator ACB. Verify no reverse power condition.
9. ISOLATE GENERATOR: Stop prime mover. Log: shore connection time, shore power parameters, generator stop time.
10. RECORDS: Log all readings. Enter in electrical log. Port authority may require connection data for billing.
Disconnection (restoration to ship power):
1. Start generator — warm up and bring to rated voltage and frequency.
2. Synchronise generator with shore supply.
3. Transfer load from shore to generator.
4. Open shore connection breaker.
5. Disconnect cable from ship — after confirming shore circuit is de-energised.
6. Stow cable — inspect for damage, log condition.
Blackout Test — Procedure, Requirements, and Recovery
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple candidates — "describe a blackout test from start to finish"
What is a blackout test?

A blackout test (also called emergency generator test or dead ship test) verifies that if the main power supply is completely lost, the emergency generator will automatically start, reach rated voltage and frequency, and supply all emergency services within the SOLAS mandated time of 45 seconds. This is a statutory test required by SOLAS and class rules.
Pre-test preparation:
1. C/E and Master notification — bridge must be informed. Ship in safe water, good weather, not in port or restricted waters.
2. Pre-test checks on emergency generator: Fuel level (tank topped up), lube oil level, coolant level, starting batteries fully charged, air starting bottle pressure (if applicable).
3. Verify emergency generator in AUTO-START mode — when blackout occurs, it must start automatically.
4. UPS systems confirmed charged — will carry GMDSS, ECDIS, alarms through transition.
5. Tester with stopwatch ready.
Test procedure:
1. START TIMING when all generators are tripped — from this moment, 45-second clock starts.
2. TRIP ALL RUNNING GENERATORS from MSB (use normal ACB trip — do NOT press emergency stop).
3. OBSERVE EMERGENCY GENERATOR: Must auto-start. Engine must reach rated speed and voltage.
4. TIMING MILESTONES:
0 seconds: Blackout — main power lost.
~10–15 seconds: Emergency generator engine reaches governed speed.
~20–30 seconds: Emergency generator voltage and frequency stabilised.
≤45 seconds: Emergency switchboard connected and all required loads energised — SOLAS limit.

5. VERIFY EMERGENCY SERVICES ON: Emergency lighting (all accommodation, ER, muster stations). Fire pump. Bilge pump. Navigation lights. General alarm system. GMDSS. Steering gear (if within 45 seconds is required by flag state). Public address system.
6. RECORD all times with stopwatch. Record which loads came on and when.
7. RUN ON EMERGENCY POWER: Minimum 30 minutes — verify stable operation, no overheating, voltage and frequency stable under load.
8. RESTORE MAIN POWER: Start main generator. Synchronise onto ESB. Transfer loads from EM bus to main bus. Trip EM generator. Restore normal power distribution.
9. POST-TEST CHECKS: Verify all EM generator automatic controls reset to AUTO. Log test results. Both C/E and Master sign test record.
SOLAS requirements for emergency source of power:
SOLAS II-1/Reg 43: Emergency generator to supply power within 45 seconds.
Transitional source: Battery or UPS must supply emergency services for 30 minutes while emergency generator starts.
Emergency generator location: Above bulkhead deck, outside machinery space — SOLAS II-1/Reg 42.
Class test: Emergency generator test witnessed by class surveyor at annual/renewal survey.
IR Testing at High Temperature — Correction and Interpretation
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: "You megger a motor and the reading is low because it is hot — what do you do?"
Why temperature affects insulation resistance:

Insulation resistance is highly temperature-dependent — it DECREASES as temperature INCREASES (approximately halving for every 10°C rise). This means a motor that reads 10 MΩ at 80°C might read 160 MΩ if cooled to 40°C — both readings represent the same insulation. This is why IR values must ALWAYS be recorded with the temperature at time of test.
Temperature correction procedure:
1. RECORD TEMPERATURE AT TIME OF TEST: Use calibrated thermometer on motor frame (or PT100 reading if fitted). Note temperature T_test.
2. APPLY IEC 60034 CORRECTION FORMULA:
IR_corrected (at 40°C) = IR_measured × 2^((T_measured − 40) / 10)
3. EXAMPLE CALCULATION:
Motor at 80°C reads IR = 10 MΩ.
This is an EXCELLENT reading — no action required.
4. COMPARE CORRECTED VALUE: Against minimum acceptance criterion (typically 1 MΩ for 440V motor) AND against previous historical readings for this motor.
5. TRENDING: Compare corrected IR over time — downward trend indicates insulation degradation even if absolute value still above minimum.
Polarisation Index (PI) — additional test:
PI = IR reading at 10 minutes / IR reading at 1 minute (using megger, same voltage applied throughout).
Healthy insulation: PI ≥ 2.0 (insulation is clean and dry — PI increases over time as surface charge builds up on healthy insulation).
Contaminated or wet insulation: PI < 1.5 (conductive moisture or dirt prevents charge build-up).
PI test is independent of temperature effect — more reliable than single IR reading for assessing insulation health.
When to allow motor to cool vs correct for temperature:
For routine maintenance trending: Allow motor to cool to 40°C for best accuracy before testing.
For emergency assessment (fault diagnosis): Test at current temperature, apply correction formula.
For class survey: Surveyor may want cooled readings. Confirm requirements in advance.
Electrical Contact Cleaning — Correct Procedure
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how do you clean electrical contacts?"
Contaminated or oxidised contacts cause high contact resistance → localised overheating → arcing → contact erosion. Proper cleaning technique is important — wrong technique causes more harm.
Types of contacts and their cleaning method:

1. COPPER CONTACTS (ACB, MCCB, contactors): Light oxidation — use isopropyl alcohol (IPA) spray and clean lint-free cloth. Pitting or arc erosion — dress with smooth flat file (NOT emery cloth — abrasive particles embed and increase resistance). Remove minimum metal — preserve contact shape and pressure. After dressing — verify contact gap meets manufacturer spec.

2. SILVER-PLATED CONTACTS (many modern contactors): DO NOT FILE. Silver plating is only 5–20 microns thick — filing removes it and exposes base metal which corrodes rapidly. Clean with IPA only. Accept minor discolouration — silver tarnishes naturally without affecting resistance significantly.
3. GOLD-PLATED CONTACTS (relay, instrument contacts): IPA only. Gold is used for low-level signal contacts — extreme sensitivity to contamination. Never abrade.

4. BUSBAR JOINTS (bolted copper-to-copper): Clean contact faces with fine emery paper or wire brush. Apply contact paste (Duolube or equivalent) to prevent future oxidation. Re-torque bolts to specified torque value.
Contact resistance measurement:

Use micro-ohmmeter (DLRO — Digital Low Resistance Ohmmeter): Measures contact resistance in µΩ. For MSB busbar joints: should be <50–100 µΩ per joint. High resistance joint generates heat — thermographic camera shows it as hot spot.
After cleaning: Measure contact resistance — verify improvement. Record before and after values.
Important: Never measure contact resistance with standard megger or digital multimeter — they use too low a test current. Only micro-ohmmeter gives accurate contact resistance readings.
Electrical Shock — First Aid Response and Rescue
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple surveyors — "a crew member gets electric shock in the engine room — what is your immediate action?"
🔴 MOST IMPORTANT RULE: DO NOT TOUCH THE VICTIM WHILE THEY ARE STILL IN CONTACT WITH THE ELECTRICAL SOURCE. You will become a second casualty.
Step-by-step response:
1. ISOLATE THE SUPPLY — FIRST AND ALWAYS:
Option A: Switch off nearest circuit breaker or isolator (fastest).
Option B: Pull the plug (for plug-in equipment).

Option C: If circuit cannot be isolated quickly — use a DRY non-conducting object to push or pull victim away from source. Examples: dry wooden plank, rubber-insulated hook, dry rope. DO NOT use metal tools, damp materials, or bare hands.
2. CALL FOR HELP: Shout for assistance. Call bridge on radio: "Medical emergency in engine room, electric shock casualty."
3. ASSESS CASUALTY — DO NOT WASTE TIME IF CPR NEEDED:
Check responsiveness: "Are you okay?" — tap shoulders.
Check airway: Tilt head, lift chin.
Check breathing: Look, listen, feel — 10 seconds.
Check circulation: Carotid pulse (neck).
4. IF NOT BREATHING AND NO PULSE: Start CPR IMMEDIATELY.
30 chest compressions: Rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6cm, centre of chest.
2 rescue breaths: Tilt head, seal nose, watch chest rise.
Repeat 30:2 until: AED arrives, casualty recovers, or medical authority takes over.

5. DEFIBRILLATION: Electric shock frequently causes VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION (chaotic heart rhythm — no effective pumping). AED (Automated External Defibrillator) is the only treatment. Apply AED as soon as available — every minute without defibrillation reduces survival by 10%.
6. IF BREATHING AND CONSCIOUS:
Place in RECOVERY POSITION (lateral, airway open).
Keep warm with blanket.
Monitor continuously — cardiac arrest can occur minutes after apparent recovery.

7. CHECK FOR BURNS: Entry wound (where current entered body — often hand/forearm) and exit wound (where current left body — often foot/earth contact). Both are burns — dress with sterile non-adhesive dressing.

8. INTERNAL INJURIES: Electric current causes internal tissue damage not visible externally. Even if casualty appears recovered — MUST have medical assessment. Contact MedAdvice (MSAT, CIRM, or national medical advisory service) via GMDSS.
9. DO NOT: Give food or water until medically cleared. Leave casualty unattended. Assume recovery is complete based on appearance.
10. REPORT AND INVESTIGATE: Accident log entry. Preserve scene. Report to Master, C/E, DPA. Investigate root cause — what failed? Why was the person in contact? Prevent recurrence.
Daily ETO Duties — Full Routine
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "describe your typical daily routine as ETO — what do you check every day?"
Morning rounds (first thing every day):
1. ALARM PANEL CHECK: Review overnight alarm printout (UMS alarm printer) or panel — note all activated alarms, investigate any that appear unusual. Clear acknowledged alarms after noting.

2. MSB ROUNDS: Check all generator panel readings — kW output, power factor, voltage, frequency. Note if PF is low (may need reactive power adjustment). Check earth fault indicator lamps — all three lamps bright = no earth fault.

3. RUNNING MACHINERY: Walk-around all running generators, compressors, purifiers, pumps. Listen for unusual sounds. Note bearing temperatures if PT100 or thermometer available. Check lube oil levels visible sight glasses.
4. FIRE DETECTION PANEL: All zones show HEALTHY — no latched fire alarms, no fault indicators. Log check.
5. GMDSS EQUIPMENT CHECK: All displays operational. GPS position valid. DSC controller shows distress watch maintained. Battery charger output normal.
6. NAVIGATION EQUIPMENT: All bridge equipment at watch status — ECDIS, radar, AIS transmitting, NAVTEX receiving. Check with OOW.
7. REEFER CONTAINERS: Check monitoring panel or walk each reefer — temperatures within setpoint range, no alarms. Record.
8. BATTERY CHARGER STATUS: Emergency lighting battery charger — check float voltage. UPS units — check charge status, battery voltage, bypass status.
9. BILGE ALARM PANEL: Check level indicators — no high-level alarms. Auto pump status.
10. PLANNED MAINTENANCE SYSTEM (PMS): Check today's planned maintenance tasks. Prioritise and start work. Assign ETR as needed.
End-of-day log entry:
Record ALL work done during the day in electrical log: jobs completed, tests performed, alarms responded to, materials used.
Record any outstanding defects that require follow-up.
Hand over to watch officer or UMS system — ensure all alarms are set and working.
Class requirement: Electrical log to be maintained as official ship's record — may be inspected by surveyor.
MCA-Approved 6-Step Framework for Troubleshooting and Emergency Scenarios

🔴 EXAM CRITICAL — STRUCTURE OF YOUR ANSWER: Surveyors frequently fail candidates who give technically correct but unstructured answers to troubleshooting and emergency scenarios. An answer that lists facts without a clear action sequence sounds like reading from a manual, not demonstrating practical seamanship. ALL troubleshooting and emergency scenario answers must follow this 6-step structure.
The MCA 6-Step Response Framework

Step 1 — IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (Safety-Critical): The first actions you take the moment the fault or emergency is recognised — before any investigation. These are actions whose delay would cause immediate danger to life, ship, or environment. Examples: isolate a live fault to prevent electrocution, raise the fire alarm before investigating smoke, LOTO before opening any panel. State these clearly and first — it shows the examiner you prioritise safety over technical curiosity.

Step 2 — ASSESSMENT (Gather Information): Once immediate safety is established, systematically gather information to understand the fault or situation. Check alarm panels, read gauges, review recent alarm history, talk to watch-keeper about what happened before the alarm. For electrical faults: check MCBs, earth fault lamps, insulation readings. For mechanical faults: check temperatures, sounds, vibration, oil level. For emergencies: assess extent, locate source, count personnel. The goal is to diagnose before acting — avoid changing things randomly.

Step 3 — COMMUNICATION (Master/Bridge/C/E): Report to the appropriate authority. For machinery faults: inform the Chief Engineer (C/E). For safety-critical faults affecting navigation (blackout, steering failure, GMDSS failure): inform the Officer of the Watch (OOW) or Master directly. For emergencies: sound the general alarm and report to the bridge via telephone. Examiners want to see that you understand the chain of command — you are not operating as a lone technician but as part of a ship's crew with clear reporting responsibilities. State WHO you report to and WHAT information you give them.

Step 4 — FURTHER ACTIONS (Investigate and Rectify): Now provide the detailed technical response — the actual fault-finding steps, component checks, testing sequence, or repair procedure. This is where your technical knowledge goes. Apply systematic fault-finding: start from symptoms, work through cause → effect using knowledge of the system. Include any interim measures (switching to standby equipment, reducing load, using bypass) to maintain ship operations while the fault is addressed. This step may take the most time in your answer.

Step 5 — DOCUMENTATION: Record everything. Electrical log entry: fault, time of occurrence, what was done, components replaced, results of testing, who was involved. PMS update: mark the corrective maintenance task as completed. For emergencies: accident log entry, incident report to DPA, relevant certificates or survey notifications (if a statutory item is affected). Documentation shows that the event is officially recorded and handled — examiners mark you up for remembering this step, as many candidates forget it under pressure.

Step 6 — FOLLOW-UP (Prevent Recurrence): After the immediate situation is resolved, investigate root cause and implement preventive measures. Was this fault predictable? Should the PMS interval be changed? Was there a design weakness? Does the rest of the crew need to be briefed? For emergencies: conduct a post-incident review (toolbox talk or safety meeting) to share lessons learned. Order replacement spares if a component was consumed. Submit a near-miss or defect report to the company if appropriate. This final step demonstrates you think systemically, not just reactively — which is what surveyors want to see from an officer, not just a technician.
How to Apply the Framework — Example Answer Structure
Examiner: “The main generator trips on overload at 0200. What do you do?”

Poor answer (fails): “I would check the overload relay setting, check the generator, check the load, check the busbar...” [lists facts, no structure, no safety first, no communication, no documentation]

Correct answer using 6-step framework: Step 1 — Immediate: Emergency generator should start automatically within 45 seconds — I confirm ESB is energised and essential services (bridge, nav lights, GMDSS) are powered. Step 2 — Assessment: Check alarm panel for cause — was it a genuine overload, short circuit, or relay malfunction? Check kW meter reading before trip, check fault relay indication. Step 3 — Communication: Immediately telephone the bridge (OOW) to inform of blackout and restoration status. Call C/E to report. Step 4 — Further actions: Start standby generator, synchronise, restore main services in sequential load-shedding order. Investigate cause of overload — which load tripped last? Check for earth fault. Check generator itself — winding insulation. Step 5 — Documentation: Log the blackout time, duration, cause, and restoration steps in the electrical log. Step 6 — Follow-up: Check whether overload relay setting is correct. Investigate whether load shedding system should have prevented the trip. Review load list and sequential starting parameters with C/E. Report to company if required.
6-Step Framework — Memory Card

Remember: 1. IMMEDIATE (safety first) → 2. ASSESS (gather info) → 3. COMMUNICATE (C/E, Master, OOW) → 4. FURTHER ACTIONS (technical fix) → 5. DOCUMENT (log, PMS, report) → 6. FOLLOW-UP (prevent recurrence). Apply this to EVERY scenario question. Begin your answer with “My first action is...” (Step 1). This signals to the examiner immediately that you prioritise safety. End your answer with Step 6 — this signals you think like an officer, not just a technician.
How Batteries Are Rated — Ampere-Hour (Ah) Explained
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Multiple surveyors — "how is a battery rated?" and "what is Ah?"
Battery capacity rating — Ampere-Hours:

A battery's capacity is stated in Ampere-Hours (Ah). This tells you how much total charge the battery can deliver before it is fully discharged. 1 Ah = ability to supply 1 Ampere for 1 Hour continuously.
Practical examples:
A 100 Ah battery can supply: 100A for 1 hour, OR 50A for 2 hours, OR 10A for 10 hours, OR 1A for 100 hours (approximately — see C-rate note below).
The relationship is NOT perfectly linear — batteries lose effective capacity at higher discharge rates due to internal resistance losses.
C-rate — discharge rate specification:
C-rate specifies the discharge rate relative to capacity. C10 = complete discharge in 10 hours. C20 = discharge in 20 hours.
A 100 Ah C20 battery: Rated capacity of 100 Ah when discharged at 100Ah/20h = 5A over 20 hours.
Same battery at C1 rate (100A discharge): Will only deliver ~60–70 Ah before voltage drops — the high rate causes more voltage drop due to internal resistance.
This is why high-capacity batteries for engine starting (CCA rating) specify performance differently from UPS batteries (Ah at C10 or C20).
Why Ah rating matters on ships:
SOLAS II-1/Reg 43: Emergency batteries must supply all emergency loads for the FULL required duration (typically 30 minutes for cargo ships, 18 hours for passenger ships during flooding).
Battery capacity test: Class surveyor requires proof that batteries can deliver rated Ah — tested by discharging at rated current and measuring total Ah delivered.
Design calculation: Identify all emergency loads (kW) → calculate total current → select battery: Ah = current (A) × duration (hours), then add 20% safety margin.
Lead-Acid Battery — Design, Working, and Specific Gravity
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "explain lead-acid battery construction and how you check its state of charge"
Lead-acid battery is the most common battery type on ships — used for engine starting, emergency lighting, and GMDSS. Understanding its construction is essential for maintenance.
Construction:
POSITIVE PLATE: Lead dioxide (PbO₂) — dark brown/chocolate colour. High energy density material.
NEGATIVE PLATE: Sponge lead (Pb) — grey, porous structure — maximises surface area for reaction.
ELECTROLYTE: Dilute sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and water — typically 30–40% H₂SO₄ by mass.
SEPARATORS: Porous polyethylene or glass mat separators between plates — prevent short circuit while allowing ion flow.
CELL CONTAINER: Polypropylene or hard rubber — acid resistant, transparent (allows level checking).
TERMINAL POST: Lead alloy posts through container lid — positive (red/+) larger diameter, negative (black/−).
VENT PLUG: Allows hydrogen gas to escape during charging. Some types are fully sealed (VRLA/AGM — no vent).
Electrochemistry — discharge and charge reactions:
DISCHARGE (battery supplying current): PbO₂ + Pb + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O
Both plates become lead sulphate (PbSO₄). Acid becomes diluted (water forms). Specific gravity DECREASES.
CHARGE (charger applying current — reverse reaction): 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O → PbO₂ + Pb + 2H₂SO₄
Plates restored to PbO₂ and Pb. Acid concentration increases. Specific gravity INCREASES.
Key consequence: Specific gravity of electrolyte directly indicates state of charge — this is how we measure charge level.
Specific gravity and state of charge (using hydrometer):
Fully charged: SG = 1.260–1.285 (varies slightly by temperature and battery design).
Half charged: SG = 1.200–1.220.
Fully discharged: SG = 1.150–1.180.
Temperature correction: SG decreases 0.0007 per 1°C rise. Standard reference temperature is 25°C.
Hydrometer use: Draw electrolyte into float hydrometer — float rises to level indicating SG. Read at eye level. Temperature-correct if ambient is very different from 25°C.
IMPORTANT: Never use hydrometer on alkaline batteries (NiCd) — SG does NOT change. This distinction is a favourite exam question.
Cell voltage and open circuit voltage:
Fully charged cell: ~2.12V open circuit. Fully discharged: ~1.90V.
12V monobloc battery: 6 cells × 2.0V = 12.0V nominal.
24V battery bank: 12 cells (or two 12V batteries in series).
NiCd Battery — Design, Working, and Comparison with Lead-Acid
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "explain a NiCd battery" and "how is it different from lead-acid?"
Nickel-Cadmium (NiCd) Battery:
POSITIVE PLATE: Nickel oxyhydroxide (NiOOH) — sometimes called nickel hydroxide electrode.
NEGATIVE PLATE: Cadmium (Cd) — metallic cadmium in porous matrix.
ELECTROLYTE: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution — ALKALINE, approximately 30% KOH in distilled water.
CELL VOLTAGE: 1.2V nominal per cell (lower than lead-acid's 2.0V per cell).
SPECIFIC GRAVITY: Does NOT change significantly during charge/discharge — KOH electrolyte is not consumed in the reaction. SG remains approximately 1.20–1.25 throughout charge/discharge cycle.
Electrochemistry:
DISCHARGE: Cd + 2NiOOH + 2H₂O → Cd(OH)₂ + 2Ni(OH)₂
CHARGE (reverse): Cd(OH)₂ + 2Ni(OH)₂ → Cd + 2NiOOH + 2H₂O
The KOH electrolyte participates only indirectly — it provides OH⁻ ions but its overall concentration remains constant. This explains why SG does not change.
Advantages of NiCd over lead-acid:
1. TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE: NiCd retains capacity at low temperatures (-20°C) far better than lead-acid. Essential for lifeboats in cold climates — lifeboat batteries on all ships are often NiCd.
2. CYCLE LIFE: 1,000–2,000 charge/discharge cycles (lead-acid: 300–500 cycles). Much longer service life.
3. STORAGE IN DISCHARGED STATE: NiCd can be stored fully discharged without damage — just recharge when needed. Lead-acid stored discharged → sulphation → permanent capacity loss.
4. OVERCHARGE TOLERANCE: NiCd handles overcharging better than lead-acid — internal chemistry accommodates slight overcharge.
5. ROBUST: Less susceptible to vibration damage (sealed, solid plates).
Disadvantages of NiCd:
1. MEMORY EFFECT: If NiCd battery is repeatedly discharged to 50% and recharged, it "forgets" the remaining 50% and treats it as unavailable. Capacity appears to reduce.
Solution: Full discharge/charge cycle (conditioning) periodically restores full capacity.
2. COST: More expensive per Ah than lead-acid.
3. CADMIUM TOXICITY: Cadmium is highly toxic — disposal requires certified hazardous waste handler. More expensive end-of-life disposal.
4. LOWER ENERGY DENSITY: NiCd requires more volume and weight for same Ah as modern lithium batteries (though comparable to lead-acid).
Ship applications of NiCd:
Emergency lighting battery packs in accommodation — rated for cold temperatures.
GMDSS portable equipment (EPIRB, SART, handheld VHF) — NiCd rechargeable batteries.
Lifeboat starting battery — cold weather performance critical.
UPS for bridge navigation equipment.
CRITICAL EXAM DISTINCTION — remember this:
Lead-acid: SG CHANGES with charge state → use hydrometer to check state of charge.
NiCd and Alkaline: SG does NOT change → CANNOT use hydrometer. Use voltmeter (open circuit voltage) or capacity test to check state of charge.
Alkaline Battery (Primary) — Components and Characteristics
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked about alkaline batteries — "can you check specific gravity of an alkaline battery?"
Primary alkaline batteries (non-rechargeable disposable type):
ANODE (negative): Zinc (Zn) — powdered zinc in gel for maximum surface area.
CATHODE (positive): Manganese dioxide (MnO₂).
ELECTROLYTE: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) — alkaline (hence the name).
SEPARATOR: Non-woven fabric soaked in electrolyte.
CELL VOLTAGE: 1.5V nominal (drops during discharge).
CAPACITY: Commonly available from AA (2-3 Ah) to D-cell (15–20 Ah).
Key characteristics:
NON-RECHARGEABLE: Primary cell — chemical reaction is not easily reversible. Attempting to recharge can cause leakage, rupture, or fire.
SPECIFIC GRAVITY: DOES NOT CHANGE during discharge. KOH concentration remains approximately constant. Hydrometer is USELESS for checking state of charge.
State of charge check: Only method — measure open circuit voltage. Full: ~1.5V. Half: ~1.35V. Discharged: <1.1V. (Or conduct load test.)
Self-discharge: Very low — shelf life 5–10 years (stored below 25°C). Unlike lead-acid which self-discharges ~3–5% per month.
Low temperature: Good performance down to -20°C (better than lead-acid, similar to NiCd).
Ship applications of alkaline primary batteries:
Emergency torches and hand-lamps — replaceable cells.
SART (Search and Rescue Transponder): Uses lithium primary or alkaline cells with 5–8 year shelf life.
Handheld VHF radios: Primary alkaline as backup if rechargeable battery fails.
Smoke and CO detectors in accommodation.
Various portable instruments (flow meters, gas detectors).
CCA — Cold Cranking Amperes (Battery Starting Rating)
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what is CCA rating on a starter battery?"
What is CCA?

CCA = Cold Cranking Amperes. The internationally standardised performance rating for starter batteries, measuring their ability to start an engine in cold conditions. It defines the maximum current a fully charged battery can deliver for 30 seconds at −18°C (0°F) while maintaining terminal voltage above 7.2V for a 12V battery (or 14.4V for 24V).
Why cold temperature is critical:
Cold temperature INCREASES battery internal resistance → reduces available current for same voltage.
Cold temperature INCREASES engine oil viscosity → engine needs MORE torque (more current) to crank.
Both effects combine at low temperature — double penalty. A battery adequate at 25°C may completely fail at -18°C.
This is why a lifeboat battery rated 400 CCA in a tropical climate might fail to start the engine at -18°C — the rating tells you exactly what to expect in the worst case.
CCA values and applications:
Small lifeboat diesel (e.g. 30 kW): 400–600 CCA minimum.
Medium auxiliary engine (e.g. 250 kW): 800–1000 CCA.
Large diesel generator starting battery: 1000–1500 CCA (often 24V, 2× 12V batteries in series).
Emergency generator battery: Must be rated for worst expected ambient temperature AND generator starting requirements.
Related ratings — understand the differences:
MCA (Marine Cranking Amperes): Measured at 0°C instead of -18°C. MCA > CCA for same battery. Used in some marine specifications.
RC (Reserve Capacity): Minutes a fully charged 12V battery can supply 25A before dropping below 10.5V. Indicates how long battery supports electronics if alternator fails.
Ah (Ampere-Hours): Deep cycle capacity — not the same as starting ability. A high-Ah deep cycle battery may have lower CCA than a smaller starting battery.

ETO exam answer on CCA: "CCA is the cold cranking ampere rating — the current a battery can supply for 30 seconds at minus 18°C while maintaining useful voltage. Higher CCA means better cold-start performance. For lifeboat and emergency generator batteries, CCA must be adequate for the coldest service temperature in the ship's trading area."
Battery Ordering — Complete Specification
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "how do you order a replacement battery for the lifeboat/emergency generator?"
When ordering a marine battery, provide ALL of the following to the supplier to ensure you receive the correct replacement:
1. BATTERY TYPE: Lead-acid (flooded/wet cell), VRLA/AGM (sealed lead-acid), Gel, NiCd, Li-ion. Important — same chemistry as original.
2. VOLTAGE: 6V, 12V, or 24V. (Or specify cell voltage and number of cells for large banks.)
3. CAPACITY: Ah rating at specified C-rate (e.g. 100 Ah at C20). For UPS/emergency lighting: specify Ah at required discharge time.
4. STARTING PERFORMANCE (for starter batteries): CCA rating at −18°C (e.g. 800 CCA). Or MCA at 0°C if specified.
5. PHYSICAL DIMENSIONS: Length × Width × Height in mm. Critical — must fit existing battery box/tray.
6. TERMINAL TYPE: Top-post (bolt terminals), side terminal (bolt threads in case), L-shaped (threaded stud). Incorrect terminal means cables won't connect.
7. TERMINAL POLARITY LAYOUT: Left-positive / Right-negative or Right-positive / Left-negative when viewed from front. Incorrect polarity layout means cables cross and may cause short circuit.
8. MAINTENANCE TYPE: Flooded (requires topping up with distilled water, has removable vent caps) or Sealed/VRLA (maintenance-free, cannot top up, recombinant gas design).
9. TEMPERATURE RANGE: Specify minimum expected ambient temperature — especially for lifeboat batteries that may be stored in cold climates.

10. MARINE/SOLAS APPROVAL: For life-saving appliance batteries (GMDSS, lifeboat, emergency generator) — must be type-approved. State certificate requirement: "IMO SOLAS-compliant, class-approved (Lloyd's/DNV/ABS etc)"
11. SHELF LIFE REQUIREMENT: Some batteries (SART, EPIRB) have mandatory minimum shelf life — specify this for replacements.
12. HAZMAT SHIPPING REQUIREMENTS: NiCd and lithium batteries have shipping restrictions (IATA/IMDG classifications). Note if ordering for air freight.
Battery at Half Capacity — SOLAS Acceptance Criteria
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "the emergency battery is at 50% capacity — can you accept it?"
Short answer: NO — a battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS.
Why not:

SOLAS II-1/Reg 43 requires the emergency source of electrical power to supply ALL emergency services for the FULL required duration — typically 30 minutes for general cargo ships, 18 hours for passenger ships.
A battery at 50% capacity can only supply HALF the required duration.

If a blackout occurs and the emergency battery provides only 15 minutes (instead of required 30 minutes) before failing — the ship is left without navigation lights, fire detection, bilge pumps, and GMDSS — a potentially fatal situation.
Required action when battery capacity is found degraded:
1. If capacity is 80–100% of rated: ACCEPTABLE. Monitor more frequently.
2. If capacity is 50–80%: FLAG for early replacement. Ship may still sail but replacement must be ordered urgently. Class surveyor notification may be required.
3. If capacity is below 50%: MUST REPLACE before vessel sails. Battery is not fit for SOLAS purpose.

4. Emergency: If shore is available — arrange emergency battery replacement before departure. If at sea with degraded battery discovered — notify Master, notify C/E, notify company/DPA, increase monitoring, identify alternative emergency power sources, log all actions taken.
How battery capacity is measured:

Capacity test (discharge test): Fully charge battery. Rest 1 hour. Discharge at rated current (Ah/10 or as specified) while measuring voltage. Stop when terminal voltage reaches cut-off voltage (10.5V for 12V battery). Calculate: Ah delivered = current × time.
Compare delivered Ah against rated capacity. Example: 100 Ah battery delivers 45 Ah → 45% capacity → NOT acceptable.
Frequency: Class requires capacity test annually (or as specified in class rules). Test result must be recorded with date and signature.

Exam answer: "A battery at 50% capacity cannot be accepted for emergency service under SOLAS. The SOLAS requirement is that emergency batteries supply all emergency loads for the full required period. At 50% capacity, only half the required duration can be met. The battery must be replaced before the ship sails."
Battery Room Safety Requirements
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "what are the safety requirements for the battery room?"

Battery rooms are HAZARDOUS AREAS. Lead-acid and NiCd batteries both produce HYDROGEN GAS during charging (from electrolysis of water in the electrolyte). Hydrogen is highly flammable (LEL 4%, UEL 75% in air) and accumulates at the ceiling (lighter than air).
Key safety requirements (based on IEC 60092, class rules, and SOLAS):

1. VENTILATION: Forced or natural ventilation designed to prevent accumulation of hydrogen above 25% of LEL (Lower Explosive Limit). Minimum ventilation rate calculated per number of cells and charging current. Inlet at low level, exhaust at high level (hydrogen rises). Ventilation must be independent — not shared with other spaces.
2. NO IGNITION SOURCES: No non-Ex light switches, sockets, fuses, or electrical equipment INSIDE battery room. All electrical equipment must be Ex-certified (Ex e or Ex d for Zone 1/2).
3. EX-RATED LIGHTING: All light fixtures Ex e or Ex d certified. Controlled by switch OUTSIDE the room.

4. ACID/ALKALI-RESISTANT FLOOR: Lead-acid acid spillage: floor must resist sulphuric acid. NiCd KOH spillage: floor must resist alkaline. Typically: acid-resistant tiles, painted concrete, or drip tray.
5. EYEWASH STATION: Immediately outside or just inside battery room — in case of electrolyte splashing in eyes. Running water or eyewash bottle.
6. EMERGENCY SHOWER (large rooms): Where large battery banks are maintained, shower capability required.
7. FIRE EXTINGUISHER: CO₂ or dry powder type at entrance. NOT water — water reacts with acid, spreads corrosive liquid and can cause arc flash in live terminals.
8. PPE REQUIREMENT POSTED: Sign on door: "Safety glasses, acid-resistant gloves, and apron mandatory." PPE must be available at or near the room.

9. NO SPARKS NEAR TERMINALS: Use insulated tools only. Remove metallic wrist watches, bangles, rings before entering. Short-circuit between battery terminals causes explosive current — melts tools, can ignite hydrogen.
10. SELF-CLOSING FIRE DOOR: Battery room door must be fire-rated (A-class on SOLAS ships) and self-closing.
11. IDENTIFICATION: Door must be marked "BATTERY ROOM — NO NAKED FLAMES — NO SMOKING".
UPS Battery Systems — Ship Applications and Maintenance
🔴 EXAM CRITICAL: Surveyor asked "explain a UPS on a ship — what batteries does it use and how do you maintain it?"
What is UPS?

UPS = Uninterruptible Power Supply. Provides continuous power to critical equipment during interruption of the main AC supply — bridge switchboard failure, port power interruption, or short blackout. The UPS prevents data loss, system restart delays, and gaps in safety-critical functions.
Ship UPS applications:
GMDSS equipment: DSC controller, satellite terminal (Inmarsat), MF/HF radio — SOLAS IV requires independent power supply for 6 hours (reduced load) or 1 hour (full load).
ECDIS and chart systems: Continuous power prevents chart data loss and navigation interruption.
VDR (Voyage Data Recorder): Must continuously record — any power gap = data loss.
Bridge alarm and monitoring system: Loss of alarm system during blackout is unacceptable — UPS covers transition.
Autopilot and heading control: Short power interruption causes course deviation.
Engine room automation system (DCS/PLC): Power interruption may cause automatic trips and false alarms.
UPS types:

ONLINE (double conversion): AC input → rectified to DC → charges battery AND powers inverter → inverts back to AC for load. Load ALWAYS runs from inverter — no switchover delay. Battery is always in circuit. Best for sensitive equipment.

OFFLINE (standby): Normally load runs direct from AC mains. On failure → automatic switch to battery/inverter. Switchover gap ~10–20ms. Acceptable for most equipment but not ideal for very sensitive loads.
LINE-INTERACTIVE: Continuously regulates voltage from mains. On failure → battery + inverter. Compromise between online and offline.
Battery type in ship UPS:

VRLA (Valve-Regulated Lead-Acid) / AGM: Most common in ship UPS. Sealed — no electrolyte topping up. Absorbed glass mat retains electrolyte — no spill risk even if inverted. Maintenance-free under normal operation.
NiCd: Used in older UPS, more expensive but longer life and better temperature performance.
UPS maintenance procedure:
1. VISUAL CHECK (monthly): Inspect battery pack for swelling, leakage, heat damage. Check charger indicator status.
2. BATTERY VOLTAGE (monthly): Measure float voltage — VRLA 12V battery float: 13.5–13.8V. If low → charger fault or battery failing.

3. DISCHARGE TEST (quarterly or annually): Simulate mains failure — switch UPS to battery mode. Time how long it supplies load before low battery cutoff. Compare with rated backup time. Record result.
4. BATTERY REPLACEMENT: VRLA batteries in UPS: expected life 3–5 years (temperature dependent — for every 10°C above 25°C, life halves). Replace before failure, not after.

5. BYPASS TEST: Operate manual bypass — transfer load to direct AC supply. Verify load continues without interruption. Then restore UPS. This allows UPS internal servicing without switching off the load.
6. FIRMWARE/SOFTWARE: Check UPS management software for logged events, battery health indicators, fault history.
